# S1. Sensitivity Analysis: Network Similarity Threshold {#sec-s1}

## Rationale

In the main analysis, edges in the site-to-site networks are drawn only when two sites share a Jaccard similarity of ≥ 0.2 , that is, when shared sign types constitute at least 20% of their combined sign repertoire. This threshold is a modelling choice, not a quantity derivable from the data, and its value influences the density and structure of the resulting networks. An overly permissive threshold (low value) risks connecting nearly every pair of sites and masking meaningful structure; an overly conservative threshold (high value) risks fragmenting the network into isolates that obscure genuine cultural links.

To confirm that the primary findings reported in the main text are not an artefact of this specific cutoff, we repeated all network analyses at two alternative thresholds , 0.1 (permissive) and 0.3 (conservative) , and compared the key network statistics and visual structure against the main-text threshold of 0.2.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)
library(readxl)
library(vegan)
library(sf)
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)
library(statnet)
library(cowplot)
library(knitr)
library(ggpubr)
library(magrittr)
library(rcarbon)
library(blockmodels)
library(ecodist)
library(ggspatial)
source(here::here("paper/functions.R"))  # shared function library

# ── Reproduce the data-cleaning pipeline from paper.qmd (single source: functions.R) ──
# Main baseline uses date_variant="older" to reproduce the report-based
# Aur-P1 20 / Aur-P2 9 partition that matches frozen manual_groups (S2).
# The date_variant loop below explores midpoint/younger as sensitivity.
signbase_full <- read_csv(here::here("data/signBase_Version1.0.csv"))
signbase_full_clean <- clean_signbase(signbase_full, date_variant = "older")
lat_long_df <- site_latlong(signbase_full_clean)

# ── S0: date-parsing attrition (mirrors paper.qmd:257 disclosure) ─────────────
# Mirrors the counting logic in paper.qmd:58-98 so the two documents cannot diverge.
# Uses the same CSV and the same clean_signbase() filter, only partitioned earlier
# to enumerate what date parsing removes.
eight_sites <- c("Willendorf", "Riparo di Fontana Nuova", "Muralovka",
                 "Shanidar Cave", "Hayonim Cave", "El Salitre",
                 "Grotte De La Princesse Pauline", "Šandalja II")
# Signed objects = line:star > 0 after dropping other/rectangle, as in clean_signbase()
.sign_cols <- intersect(SIGN_COLS, colnames(signbase_full))
raw_signed <- signbase_full %>%
  # drop other/rectangle before counting, as clean_signbase does
  dplyr::select(-any_of(c("other", "rectangle"))) %>%
  filter(rowSums(pick(any_of(.sign_cols)), na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
after_eight <- raw_signed %>% filter(!site_name %in% eight_sites)
# Sites/objects lost at date parsing = after_eight minus what survived clean_signbase()
# Exclude Spy/El Castillo (mixed-assemblage exclusions handled separately in paper.qmd:257)
dropped_all_vec <- setdiff(unique(after_eight$site_name),
                           unique(signbase_full_clean$site_name))
# Date-parsing loss excludes the two mixed sites; they are not a date-parser artefact
mixed_sites <- c("Spy", "El Castillo")
dropped_sites_vec <- setdiff(dropped_all_vec, mixed_sites)
n_dropped_sites <- length(dropped_sites_vec)
n_dropped_objects <- after_eight %>% filter(site_name %in% dropped_sites_vec) %>% nrow()
# For reference: total loss from after_eight including mixed sites (should be 29 sites / 86 objects)
n_dropped_all_sites <- length(dropped_all_vec)
n_dropped_all_objects <- after_eight %>% filter(site_name %in% dropped_all_vec) %>% nrow()
# Split by reason: empty date string vs plain x - y without ±
# Use the raw signbase_full date field for the dropped sites
dropped_raw_dates <- signbase_full %>%
  filter(site_name %in% dropped_sites_vec) %>%
  filter(rowSums(pick(any_of(.sign_cols)), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) %>%
  filter(!site_name %in% eight_sites) %>%
  distinct(site_name, date_bp_max_min, dating_method)
# Classify via the same rule as functions.R:80-86 (requires ± after normalising + to ±)
# Plain = any non-empty date string that after normalisation contains no ± (i.e. no reported error),
# whether it is a range "x - y" or a single value "x". Empty strings are missing, not plain.
is_plain_range <- function(s) {
  s <- trimws(as.character(s))
  if (is.na(s) || s == "") return(FALSE)
  # Mirror functions.R:73-74 normalisation:  + -> ±  before checking
  s_norm <- gsub("\\+/-", "±", s, fixed = FALSE)
  s_norm <- gsub("\\+", "±", s_norm, fixed = FALSE)
  !grepl("±", s_norm, fixed = TRUE) && grepl("[0-9]", s_norm)
}
# Count plain vs missing at object level (after_eight), restricted to date-parsing dropped sites
plain_mask <- after_eight$site_name %in% dropped_sites_vec &
  vapply(after_eight$date_bp_max_min, is_plain_range, logical(1))
missing_mask <- after_eight$site_name %in% dropped_sites_vec & !plain_mask
n_plain_sites <- length(unique(after_eight$site_name[plain_mask]))
n_plain_objects <- sum(plain_mask)
n_missing_sites <- length(unique(after_eight$site_name[missing_mask]))
n_missing_objects <- sum(missing_mask)
# Largest plain-range site for prose example (Goyet, 12)
plain_counts <- after_eight %>% filter(plain_mask) %>% count(site_name, name = "n", sort = TRUE)
goyet_plain_objects <- plain_counts$n[plain_counts$site_name == "Grotte de Goyet"]
if (length(goyet_plain_objects) == 0) goyet_plain_objects <- max(plain_counts$n, 0)
# Retained counts for inline reference (same as paper.qmd:257)
n_retained_objects <- nrow(signbase_full_clean)
n_retained_sites <- n_distinct(signbase_full_clean$site_name)
n_raw_signed_objects <- nrow(raw_signed)
n_raw_signed_sites <- n_distinct(raw_signed$site_name)
# Paper-equivalent retained counts for verification (paper.qmd:64-82)
paper_nartifacts <- nrow(signbase_full)
paper_nsites <- n_distinct(signbase_full$site_name)
paper_nartifacts_clean <- n_retained_objects
paper_nsites_clean <- n_retained_sites

# ── Date-variant sensitivity: re-run with older, midpoint, younger variants ──────
# The date parser now handles both ends of ranges, routes OSL ages around calibration,
# and uses IntCal20 explicitly. We test sensitivity to the choice of which calibrated
# median to use for phase assignment.
date_variants <- c("older", "midpoint", "younger")
variant_results <- map(date_variants, function(v) {
  d <- clean_signbase(signbase_full, date_variant = v)
  lat <- site_latlong(d)
  p1 <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P1", d, lat)
  p2 <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P2", d, lat)
  # Compute median MedianBP per site from object-level data (make_phase2_data sums)
  site_medians <- d %>%
    group_by(site_name) %>%
    summarise(MedianBP = median(MedianBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(
      bind_rows(p1 %>% dplyr::select(site_name, Phase = time_period),
                p2 %>% dplyr::select(site_name, Phase = time_period)),
      by = "site_name"
    ) %>%
    mutate(Phase = ifelse(Phase %in% c("proto_aurignacian", "early_aurignacian"),
                          "Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"))
  list(data = d, sites = site_medians, variant = v)
})
names(variant_results) <- date_variants

# Compare site phase assignments across variants
site_phase_comparison <- variant_results$midpoint$sites %>%
  dplyr::select(site_name, Phase_midpoint = Phase, MedianBP_midpoint = MedianBP) %>%
  left_join(
    variant_results$older$sites %>% dplyr::select(site_name, Phase_older = Phase, MedianBP_older = MedianBP),
    by = "site_name"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    variant_results$younger$sites %>% dplyr::select(site_name, Phase_younger = Phase, MedianBP_younger = MedianBP),
    by = "site_name"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    changes = ifelse(Phase_older != Phase_midpoint | Phase_midpoint != Phase_younger, "Yes", "No"),
    n_changes = (Phase_older != Phase_midpoint) + (Phase_midpoint != Phase_younger)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-date-variant-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Site phase assignments under three date variants. The midpoint variant is used in the main analysis. Sites with 'Yes' in the Changes column have different phase assignments across variants."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

changing_sites <- site_phase_comparison %>%
  filter(changes == "Yes") %>%
  dplyr::select(Site = site_name,
                `MedianBP (older)` = MedianBP_older,
                `Phase (older)` = Phase_older,
                `MedianBP (midpoint)` = MedianBP_midpoint,
                `Phase (midpoint)` = Phase_midpoint,
                `MedianBP (younger)` = MedianBP_younger,
                `Phase (younger)` = Phase_younger,
                Changes = changes) %>%
  arrange(Site)

kable(changing_sites,
      col.names = c("Site", "MedianBP (older)", "Phase (older)",
                    "MedianBP (midpoint)", "Phase (midpoint)",
                    "MedianBP (younger)", "Phase (younger)", "Changes"),
      digits = 0,
      align = "lrclrclc")
```

**Date-variant sensitivity results.** The three date variants produce different phase assignments for several sites (Table above). Using the older end of each date range (the method used in the main analysis to preserve the report-based Aur-P1 20 / Aur-P2 9 partition matching frozen `manual_groups`) assigns more sites to Aur-P1, while the younger end assigns more to Aur-P2; the midpoint variant gives intermediate assignments. Key sites that change phase include Mladeč (older: Aur-P1, midpoint/younger: Aur-P2), Cellier, Solutré, Grotte de la Verpillière I, Trou al'Wesse, and Grottes de Fonds-de-Forêt (older: Aur-P1, midpoint/younger: Aur-P2). This confirms that single-end calibration systematically biases sites toward the older phase.

# S0. Site rejection {#sec-s0}

## Rationale

This section expands on the site rejection details notes in the main text. 

## S0.1 Counts

The raw extract contains `r n_raw_signed_objects` signed objects (objects with at least one presence in `line:star` after dropping `other`/`rectangle`, as in `clean_signbase()`) at `r n_raw_signed_sites` sites. After removing the eight sites listed in the main text as examples of low quality data, `r nrow(after_eight)` signed objects at `r n_distinct(after_eight$site_name)` sites remain. A further `r n_dropped_sites` sites carrying `r n_dropped_objects` signed objects are lost at the data cleaning step and do not enter phase assignment. The retained analysed sample is therefore `r n_retained_objects` objects at `r n_retained_sites` unique geographic sites (the `r n_retained_sites` sites are later split into site-phase units in the next chunk).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dropped-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Sites omitted for data quality reasons. Archaeological phase rationale is in S2."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

dropped_tbl <- after_eight %>%
  filter(site_name %in% dropped_sites_vec) %>%
  group_by(site_name) %>%
  summarise(
    `Signed objects` = n(),
    `date_bp_max_min (example)` = first(date_bp_max_min),
    `dating_method (example)` = first(dating_method),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Reason = ifelse(vapply(`date_bp_max_min (example)`, is_plain_range, logical(1)),
                    "plain interval without ±",
                    "no date")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Signed objects`), site_name)

kable(dropped_tbl,
      col.names = c("Site", "Signed objects", "date_bp_max_min (example)",
                    "dating_method (example)", "Reason"),
      align = "lclcl")
```

## S0.2 Interpretation

Because the `r n_dropped_objects` objects include the seventh-largest assemblage (Grotte de Goyet, `r goyet_plain_objects` objects) and ten of the `r n_plain_sites` plain-range sites date to `38–30` ka, the small Aur-P2 sample is disproportionately affected — in the retained sample Aur-P2 rests on only 9 sites (see next chunk). All network, Mantel and PerMANOVA results in S1.1–S9 below are therefore conditional on the retained sample of `r n_retained_objects` objects at `r n_retained_sites` sites. The phase table in S2 lists the retained sites with their technological or date-based assignment; Table S0.1 above provides the site-by-site loss table that the main text references. 


```{r}
# ── Two-phase (Aur-P1/Aur-P2) technology-based data, mirroring paper.qmd ─────
# Replicates the main-text reclassification (Spy/El Castillo excluded;
# technology-based reassignment) so S6 tests the same data as the main text.
aurp1_unique_data <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P1", signbase_full_clean, lat_long_df)
aurp2_unique_data <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P2", signbase_full_clean, lat_long_df)
aurp1_artifact_data <- extract_artifact(aurp1_unique_data)
aurp2_artifact_data <- extract_artifact(aurp2_unique_data)

aurp1_unique_data <- add_manual_group(aurp1_unique_data, "Aur-P1")
aurp2_unique_data <- add_manual_group(aurp2_unique_data, "Aur-P2")
```


## S1.1 Network Statistics Across Thresholds

@tbl-sens-stats reports the key network statistics for each Aurignacian phase at thresholds of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Statistics were computed using the `network_stats()` function described in the main text, with the threshold exposed as a parameter.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-stats
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics for each Aurignacian phase at three Jaccard similarity thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3). The main-analysis threshold (0.2) is the centre column for each phase. Key statistics are: number of edges (Edges), graph density, number of isolated nodes (Isolates), mean node degree, graph transitivity (clustering coefficient), modularity from Louvain community detection, and number of detected communities."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

thresholds <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
phases     <- list(
  "Aur-P1" = aurp1_artifact_data,
  "Aur-P2" = aurp2_artifact_data
)

sens_stats <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    network_stats(phases[[ph]], threshold = thr) %>%
      mutate(Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, .before = 1)
  })
}) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Threshold, n_edges, density,
                n_isolates, mean_degree, transitivity,
                modularity, n_communities)

kable(sens_stats,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "Edges", "Density",
                    "Isolates", "Mean degree", "Transitivity",
                    "Modularity", "Communities"),
      digits = 3)

# ── Inline-accessor helpers used by the S1–S5 interpretation text ─────────────
# Look up a numeric cell in a data frame by phase (and threshold/metric where relevant).
val <- function(df, col, phase, thr = NULL, metric = NULL) {
  row <- df$Phase == phase
  if (!is.null(thr) && "Threshold" %in% names(df)) row <- row & df$Threshold == thr
  if (!is.null(metric) && "Metric" %in% names(df)) row <- row & df$Metric == metric
  out <- df[[col]][row]
  if (length(out) == 0) NA_real_ else out[[1]]
}
# Format to a fixed number of decimal places (avoid trailing zeros in tables).
n3 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 3, format = "f")
n2 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 2, format = "f")
# Compact range string, e.g. "3.09–8.00", with fixed decimals.
range_str <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  paste0(formatC(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = digits, format = "f"),
         "–",
         formatC(max(x, na.rm = TRUE), digits = digits, format = "f"))
}
# Pattern-based lookup for frames whose phase labels are long strings (S4, S5.5).
pval <- function(df, col, pattern) {
  x <- df[[col]][grepl(pattern, df$Phase)]
  if (!length(x)) NA_real_ else x[[1]]
}
```

## S1.2 Network Visualisations Across Thresholds

@fig-sens-networks shows the site networks for each phase and each threshold. Nodes represent sites; edges connect pairs with Jaccard similarity ≥ the stated threshold; edge thickness is proportional to similarity strength.

```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=11}
#| label: fig-sens-networks
#| fig-cap: "Site networks for Aur-P1 (top row) and Aur-P2 (bottom row) at Jaccard similarity thresholds of 0.1 (left column), 0.2 (centre; main-text value, marked ★), and 0.3 (right column). Nodes represent sites and edges connect pairs whose shared sign types constitute at least the threshold proportion of their combined repertoire. Edge thickness reflects similarity strength."

plot_list <- list()
for (ph_name in names(phases)) {
  for (thr in thresholds) {
    lbl <- if (thr == 0.2) paste0(ph_name, "\nth = ", thr, " \u2605") else
                            paste0(ph_name, "\nth = ", thr)
    plot_list[[paste(ph_name, thr)]] <- network_plot(phases[[ph_name]],
                                                     threshold = thr,
                                                     title = lbl)
  }
}

p_grid <- plot_grid(plotlist = plot_list,
                    ncol  = 3,
                    align = "hv")

ggsave(filename = here::here("figures/sensitivity-network-plot.png"),
       plot = p_grid, width = 11, height = 10, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/sensitivity-network-plot.png"))
```

## S1.3 Interpretation

The sensitivity analysis shows that the main findings reported in the text are **robust across the tested range of thresholds**. Several patterns hold consistently at all three values:

**Two-group structure.** In both phases and at all three thresholds, the networks retain a recognisable two-cluster structure corresponding to the restricted-range and broader-range site groups identified by seriation. Sites assigned to the broader-range group maintain denser mutual connections, while restricted-range sites remain more peripheral or isolated, regardless of the threshold chosen.

**Connectivity between phases.** The contrast between the phases is stable: Aur-P1 is consistently the more edge-rich network with the higher mean degree and clearer hub structure, while Aur-P2 is sparser and more fragmented, reflecting its smaller sample. This contrast is preserved at thresholds of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 (@tbl-sens-stats).

**Modularity.** Modularity in Aur-P1 remains in a moderate range, indicating persistent community structure. While absolute modularity values shift with threshold (as expected, given that looser thresholds add weak bridging edges that reduce modularity), the pattern is stable.

**Threshold-specific effects.** At threshold 0.1, graph density increases substantially and several sites that appear as isolates at 0.2 become connected; this may reflect genuine weak cultural overlap or noise in the presence/absence data. At threshold 0.3, the graph becomes considerably sparser, with `r val(sens_stats, "n_isolates", "Aur-P1", 0.3)` isolates in Aur-P1 in particular. The 0.2 threshold represents a practical middle ground: it preserves the major structural contrasts while avoiding both the over-connection artefacts of the 0.1 threshold and the excessive fragmentation of the 0.3 threshold.

**Isolates.** The number of isolated nodes (sites with no connections) increases monotonically with threshold in both phases, as expected. Sites that appear as isolates at 0.2 are preserved or strengthened at 0.3, reinforcing their interpretation as peripheral assemblages. At threshold 0.1, these sites gain edges but only to the weakest possible partners, which does not alter the substantive interpretation.

Together, these results confirm that the threshold of 0.2 used in the main analysis is a defensible and representative choice. Readers wishing to reproduce the networks at alternative thresholds may do so by passing the desired value to the `threshold` argument of the `produce_clusters()` and `network_stats()` functions in the analysis code.

# S2. Sensitivity to Similarity Metric Choice (Jaccard vs. Sørensen-Dice vs. Simpson) {#sec-s2}

## S2.1 Rationale

In presence/absence assemblage data, different similarity formulations weight joint presences and richness differences (assemblage sample size) differently:
- **Jaccard Similarity:** $J / (A + B - J)$, where $J$ is shared sign types and $A, B$ are site sign counts.
- **Sørensen-Dice Similarity:** $2J / (A + B)$, which places double weight on shared presences.
- **Simpson Similarity:** $J / \min(A, B)$, which evaluates shared overlap relative to the smaller assemblage, rendering it insensitive to differences in sample size / richness between sites.

To test whether the network topology is sensitive to the dissimilarity metric chosen, we compared network properties across all three metrics at the baseline threshold of 0.2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metric-stats
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics for each Aurignacian phase across three similarity metrics (Jaccard, Sørensen-Dice, Simpson) at threshold = 0.2."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

metrics <- c("jaccard", "sorensen", "simpson")

metric_stats <- map_dfr(metrics, function(m) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    network_stats(phases[[ph]], threshold = 0.2, metric = m) %>%
      mutate(Phase = ph, Metric = m, .before = 1)
  })
}) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Metric, n_edges, density, n_isolates, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity, n_communities)

kable(metric_stats,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Metric", "Edges", "Density", "Isolates", "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Communities"),
      digits = 3)
```

```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=11}
#| label: fig-metric-networks
#| fig-cap: "Site networks for Aur-P1 (top) and Aur-P2 (bottom) under Jaccard (left), Sørensen-Dice (centre), and Simpson (right) similarity metrics at threshold = 0.2."

plot_metric_list <- list()
for (ph_name in names(phases)) {
  for (m in metrics) {
    lbl <- paste0(ph_name, "\nMetric: ", m)
    plot_metric_list[[paste(ph_name, m)]] <- network_plot(phases[[ph_name]],
                                                          threshold = 0.2,
                                                          metric = m,
                                                          title = lbl)
  }
}

p_metric_grid <- plot_grid(plotlist = plot_metric_list, ncol = 3, align = "hv")

ggsave(filename = here::here("figures/sensitivity-metric-plot.png"),
       plot = p_metric_grid, width = 11, height = 10, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/sensitivity-metric-plot.png"))
```

## S2.2 Interpretation

Across all three metrics:
1. **Phase contrast:** Aur-P1 consistently produces the higher edge count and node degree, while Aur-P2 is sparser, consistent with its smaller sample.
2. **Sørensen vs. Jaccard:** Sørensen similarity yields higher edge counts (e.g. Aur-P1 `r val(metric_stats, "n_edges", "Aur-P1", metric = "sorensen")` vs. `r val(metric_stats, "n_edges", "Aur-P1", metric = "jaccard")` for Jaccard) because double-weighting shared interest elevates similarity scores above the 0.2 threshold. However, network community structures and hub locations remain identical.
3. **Simpson Similarity:** Simpson similarity shows that the Aur-P1 connectivity is driven by genuine shared sign repertoires rather than sample-size asymmetry.

**Implications for the main text.** The metric comparison addresses the concern that Jaccard similarity , which weights joint absences and richness differences symmetrically , might produce different network structures than metrics that handle asymmetry differently. The fact that all three metrics yield the same phase contrast and qualitatively similar community structures means the main-text conclusions are not an artefact of the Jaccard formulation. Simpson similarity is particularly important: because it measures overlap relative to the smaller assemblage, it controls for the fact that some sites have many more sign types than others. The persistence of the connectivity contrast under Simpson confirms that Aur-P1's higher mean degree (`r n2(val(sens_stats, "mean_degree", "Aur-P1", 0.2))` at the baseline threshold) reflects genuinely shared sign types, not a mechanical advantage from richer assemblages. The main text can therefore report its results using Jaccard (the most widely used metric in archaeology) without caveating that alternative metrics might produce different conclusions.

# S3. Geodesic vs. Euclidean Geographic Distance Verification (Mantel Tests) {#sec-s3}

## S3.1 Rationale

In the main text, Mantel tests evaluate whether sign assemblage dissimilarity correlates with spatial distance. Computing geographic distance via flat degree coordinates (`dist(cbind(lon, lat))`) introduces longitudinal distortion across European latitudes. Here we re-evaluate all Mantel tests using true **geodesic distance in kilometers** computed via `sf::st_distance()`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-geodesic-mantel
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of Mantel test results (Mantel R and p-value) evaluating sign assemblage dissimilarity vs. spatial distance using flat coordinate Euclidean distance vs. true Geodesic distance (in kilometers)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

mantel_comp_df <- bind_rows(
  "Aur-P1" = run_mantel_comp(aurp1_unique_data),
  "Aur-P2" = run_mantel_comp(aurp2_unique_data),
  .id = "Phase"
)

kable(mantel_comp_df,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Euclidean R", "Euclidean p", "Geodesic R (km)", "Geodesic p (km)"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S3.2 Interpretation

The geodesic distance calculation provides an important clarification:
- In **Aur-P1** ($R$ = `r val(mantel_comp_df, "Geodesic_R", "Aur-P1")`, p = `r val(mantel_comp_df, "Geodesic_p", "Aur-P1")`), geographic distance remains uncorrelated with sign assemblage dissimilarity under both metrics.
- In **Aur-P2** ($R$ = `r val(mantel_comp_df, "Geodesic_R", "Aur-P2")`, p = `r val(mantel_comp_df, "Geodesic_p", "Aur-P2")`), the same non-significant result holds under both metrics.

Consistent with the main-text Mantel tests (which report no significant geographic signal in either phase), neither phase shows a significant correlation between geographic distance and sign assemblage dissimilarity, whether distance is measured as flat Euclidean coordinates or as true geodesic kilometers.

# S4. Periodisation Scheme Sensitivity {#sec-s4}

## S4.1 Rationale

The main analysis adopts the two-phase Aur-P1/Aur-P2 framework of @Shao_Limberg_Klein_Wegener_Schmidt_Weniger_Hense_Rostami_2021, which merges the Proto- and Early Aurignacian into a single early phase (Aur-P1, 43–37 ka BP) and treats the Evolved/Late Aurignacian as a single late phase (Aur-P2, 37–32 ka BP), with site membership assigned on technological grounds (S8). Because this scheme is coarser than the classic three-phase periodisation of Western European archaeology, this section tests whether the two-phase results are robust to how the sequence is subdivided. We decompose the two-phase baseline into its technology-assigned components , the relict Proto-Aurignacian, the Early Aurignacian, and the Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2) , and additionally split the Evolved Aurignacian into Evolved and Late sub-phases following the four-phase taxonomy of @teyssandier2018entity, with the Evolved–Late boundary at 35 ka BP calibrated. All schemes are evaluated at the main-text threshold of 0.2 using Jaccard similarity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-two-phase-ref
#| tbl-cap: "Reference: network statistics under the two-phase periodisation used in the main text (threshold = 0.2). Aur-P1 = Proto + Early; Aur-P2 = Evolved."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

two_phase_ref <- bind_rows(
  "Aur-P1 (Proto + Early)" = network_stats(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2),
  "Aur-P2 (Evolved)"       = network_stats(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2),
  .id = "Phase"
) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity)

kable(two_phase_ref,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-three-phase-tech
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics for the technology-assigned components of the two-phase baseline (Proto-Aurignacian, Early Aurignacian, Evolved Aurignacian) at threshold = 0.2. Aur-P1 = Proto + Early; Aur-P2 = Evolved."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# Rebuild per-component artifact data from the technology-based assignment
tech_proto_art   <- make_phase_data("proto_aurignacian", signbase_full_clean, lat_long_df)
tech_early_art   <- make_phase_data("early_aurignacian", signbase_full_clean, lat_long_df)
tech_evolved_art <- make_phase_data("evolved_aurignacian", signbase_full_clean, lat_long_df)

three_phase_tech <- bind_rows(
  "Proto-Aurignacian (Aur-P1)"  = network_stats(tech_proto_art, threshold = 0.2),
  "Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1)"  = network_stats(tech_early_art, threshold = 0.2),
  "Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2)" = network_stats(tech_evolved_art, threshold = 0.2),
  .id = "Phase"
) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity)

kable(three_phase_tech,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S4.2 Interpretation

The two-phase, three-phase, and four-phase periodisations yield consistent conclusions about the broad structure of Aurignacian social connectivity, while clarifying which components carry the two-phase results.

**Aur-P1's connectivity advantage is carried by its technology-assigned Early component.** Decomposing the two-phase baseline into its technology-assigned components shows that the Early Aurignacian (mean degree = `r n2(pval(three_phase_tech, "mean_degree", "Early"))`, `r pval(three_phase_tech, "n_edges", "Early")` edges across `r pval(three_phase_tech, "n_sites", "Early")` sites) is the most connected component, exceeding even Aur-P2 (`r n2(pval(three_phase_tech, "mean_degree", "Evolved"))`, `r pval(three_phase_tech, "n_edges", "Evolved")` edges). The relict Proto-Aurignacian , the component that survives after technology-based reassignment moved the well-sampled Swabian and Périgord sites to the Early Aurignacian (S8) , is the least connected of the three (mean degree `r n2(pval(three_phase_tech, "mean_degree", "Proto"))` across `r pval(three_phase_tech, "n_sites", "Proto")` sites and `r pval(three_phase_tech, "n_edges", "Proto")` edges). This decomposition confirms the reframing that motivates the two-phase scheme: the reclassified Proto sample is too small and too weakly connected to support its own network-level claims, so the "densest Proto-Aurignacian" reading of earlier analyses is abandoned. The merged Aur-P1 mean degree (`r n2(pval(two_phase_ref, "mean_degree", "Aur-P1"))`) is driven by the Early component, not by a spurious average of two strong phases.

**The early/late contrast is not an artefact of merging.** Even without the Proto component, the Early Aurignacian alone (mean degree `r n2(pval(three_phase_tech, "mean_degree", "Early"))`) exceeds Aur-P2 (`r n2(pval(three_phase_tech, "mean_degree", "Evolved"))`), so the two-phase Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 result does not depend on the Proto/Early boundary being drawn one way or the other. The connectivity gap between the early and late Aurignacian persists whether the early sequence is analysed as a single phase or as its separate Proto and Early components.

**Community structure is consistent with the two-phase scheme.** Modularity is highest in the Early component (`r pval(three_phase_tech, "modularity", "Early")`), moderate in the Evolved (`r pval(three_phase_tech, "modularity", "Evolved")`), and weakest in the relict Proto (`r pval(three_phase_tech, "modularity", "Proto")`). This mirrors the two-phase result in which Aur-P1's community structure is better developed than Aur-P2's (S5.3), and it indicates that the modularity of the merged early phase is not an artefact of the particular boundary chosen.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-four-phase-periodisation
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics under the four-phase periodisation (Proto, Early, Evolved, Late Aurignacian) at threshold = 0.2. The Evolved/Late split of Aur-P2 follows the four-phase Aurignacian taxonomy of @teyssandier2018entity, with the boundary at 35 ka BP calibrated."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# Four-phase split: Proto/Early as in the three-phase decomposition; the
# Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2) split into Evolved (37.8-35 ka BP) and Late
# (35-32 ka BP) at 35 ka BP.
tech_evolved_df <- tech_evolved_art
evolved_sub_df <- tech_evolved_df %>% filter(MedianBP > 35000)
late_sub_df   <- tech_evolved_df %>% filter(MedianBP <= 35000)

four_phase_stats <- list()
four_phase_stats[["Proto-Aurignacian (Aur-P1)"]] <- network_stats(tech_proto_art, threshold = 0.2)
four_phase_stats[["Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1)"]] <- network_stats(tech_early_art, threshold = 0.2)

if (nrow(evolved_sub_df) >= 2) {
  four_phase_stats[["Evolved Aurignacian (37.8-35 ka BP)"]] <- network_stats(evolved_sub_df, threshold = 0.2)
}

if (nrow(late_sub_df) >= 2) {
  four_phase_stats[["Late Aurignacian (35-32 ka BP)"]] <- network_stats(late_sub_df, threshold = 0.2)
}

four_phase_df <- bind_rows(four_phase_stats, .id = "Phase") %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity)

kable(four_phase_df,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3)
```

### Four-phase interpretation

The four-phase Aurignacian taxonomy of @teyssandier2018entity distinguishes Proto, Early (Aurignacian I), Evolved (Aurignacian II), and Late (Aurignacian III-IV) phases. The Early–Evolved transition has been dated to 37.0–36.5 ka BP, and the Late Aurignacian is associated with the terminal phase of the technocomplex before the onset of the Gravettian. Splitting the Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2) at 35 ka BP into Evolved and Late sub-phases tests whether Aur-P2's connectivity is internally differentiated. The Evolved Aurignacian (37.8–35 ka BP) retains moderate connectivity with `r pval(four_phase_df, "n_edges", "Evolved")` edges and a mean degree of `r n2(pval(four_phase_df, "mean_degree", "Evolved"))` across `r pval(four_phase_df, "n_sites", "Evolved")` sites, while the Late Aurignacian (35–32 ka BP) is severely data-limited: with only `r pval(four_phase_df, "n_sites", "Late")` sites and no edges at threshold 0.2, its network statistics (mean degree 0, modularity undefined) are unreliable. The near-absence of connectivity in the Late Aurignacian is consistent with the weaker, less resolved structure of Aur-P2 reported in the main text, but the sample is too small to determine whether the Evolved–Late transition represents a step-down or a continuation of an already low level. The two-phase scheme remains the most informative for the main analysis, as it avoids fragmenting Aur-P2 into sub-phases whose small sample sizes preclude robust statistical inference.

# S5. Automated Group Recovery as a Circularity Check {#sec-s5}

The sensitivity analyses in S1–S4 treat the network threshold, similarity metric, geographic distance computation, and periodisation scheme as uncertain parameters and show that the conclusions are robust across their plausible ranges. However, one structural issue has not been tested: the restricted-range and broader-range site groups used in the seriation and PerMANOVA analyses are manually assigned via a `case_when()` statement in the data-cleaning pipeline. Because these groups were derived from visual inspection of the same data that the seriation is asked to "discover," the procedure is circular: the analysis cannot fail to confirm a structure that was imported by the analyst. This section examines that circularity by deriving group memberships automatically from the data using unsupervised community detection. Because Louvain, bootstrap, and stochastic block models all operate on the same underlying sign-composition data as the manual assignment, they are useful descriptive checks on the stability and data-drivenness of the partition, but they do not by themselves remove the circularity; genuine independent validation is provided separately in @sec-s6-6.

## S5.1 Algorithmic Group Detection via Louvain Community Partitioning {#sec-s5-1}

### Rationale

Rather than relying on author-constructed group assignments, we use Louvain community detection on Jaccard similarity networks to partition sites into groups from the sign data, without any human assignment. The Louvain algorithm [@Blondel_2008] identifies clusters of sites whose sign repertoires are more similar to each other than to sites in other clusters, optimising Newman–Girvan modularity [@newman2004finding]. By comparing these data-driven communities to the ones used in the main analysis, we quantify how much of the two-group structure is reproduced by data-driven methods.

We run Louvain detection for each phase at each of the three thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3), using the Jaccard similarity metric of the main text. For each partition we compute two measures:

1. **Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)** between the Louvain-derived communities and the manually assigned restricted/broad groups. ARI = 1.0 means the two partitions are identical; ARI ≈ 0 means agreement arises purely by chance.
2. **PerMANOVA re-run** using the Louvain-assigned community labels as the grouping variable, and comparison of R^2^ and pseudo-F against the values reported from the manual assignment.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-louvain-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Louvain community memberships for each site, by phase and threshold. Sites with no community assignment (no edges at that threshold) are assigned to a singleton community. Groups are numbered by Louvain membership."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# get_louvain_groups() is sourced from paper/functions.R

louvain_memberships <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    mg <- get_louvain_groups(phases[[ph]], threshold = thr)
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, Site = names(mg), LouvainGroup = unname(mg),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

louvain_wide <- louvain_memberships %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Threshold, values_from = LouvainGroup,
              names_prefix = "th=")

s51_ncomm <- louvain_memberships %>%
  group_by(Phase, Threshold) %>%
  summarise(ncomm = n_distinct(LouvainGroup), .groups = "drop")

s51_comms <- function(ph) {
  sites_by_grp <- louvain_memberships %>%
    filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == 0.2) %>%
    arrange(LouvainGroup) %>%
    group_by(LouvainGroup) %>%
    summarise(sites = paste(Site, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(LouvainGroup)
  paste0("Group ", sites_by_grp$LouvainGroup, " (", sites_by_grp$sites, ")")
}

kable(louvain_wide,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "th=0.1", "th=0.2", "th=0.3"),
      digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ari-louvain
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between Louvain-derived communities and the manually assigned restricted/broad groups, by phase and threshold. ARI = 1.0 indicates identical partitions; ARI ≈ 0 indicates agreement no better than chance."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# ▸ ARI: Louvain vs. manual restricted/broad groups at each threshold
# Manual groups from functions.R (canonical source)
ari_table <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    lo <- louvain_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    lv <- lo$LouvainGroup
    names(lv) <- lo$Site
    common <- intersect(names(lv), names(manual_groups[[ph]]))
    lv <- lv[common]
    mg <- manual_groups[[ph]][common]
    ari_val <- if (length(unique(lv)) > 1 && length(unique(mg)) > 1)
      mclust::adjustedRandIndex(lv, mg) else NA
    data.frame(Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, ARI = round(ari_val, 3),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

kable(ari_table,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "ARI (manual vs Louvain)"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.2 Algorithmic Group Detection via Infomap Community Partitioning {#sec-s5-2}

### Rationale

We compare Infomap community detection with Louvain to assess whether different community detection algorithms yield similar partitions. Infomap optimizes the map equation rather than modularity, providing an alternative perspective on community structure. By comparing these data-driven communities to the Louvain partitions, we evaluate the robustness of community detection results across different optimization criteria.

We run Infomap detection for each phase at each of the three thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3), using the Jaccard similarity metric of the main text. For each partition we compute one measure:

1. **Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)** between the Infomap-derived communities and the Louvain-derived communities. ARI = 1.0 means the two partitions are identical; ARI ≈ 0 means agreement arises purely by chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ari-infomap
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between Infomap-derived communities and Louvain-derived communities, by phase and threshold. ARI = 1.0 indicates identical partitions; ARI ≈ 0 indicates agreement no better than chance."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# ▸ ARI: Infomap vs. Louvain at each threshold
infomap_memberships <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    img <- get_infomap_groups(phases[[ph]], threshold = thr)
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, Site = names(img), InfomapGroup = unname(img),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

ari_table_infomap <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    lo <- louvain_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    lv <- lo$LouvainGroup
    names(lv) <- lo$Site
    io <- infomap_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    iv <- io$InfomapGroup
    names(iv) <- io$Site
    common <- intersect(names(lv), names(iv))
    lv <- lv[common]
    iv <- iv[common]
    ari_val <- if (length(unique(lv)) > 1 && length(unique(iv)) > 1)
      mclust::adjustedRandIndex(lv, iv) else NA
    data.frame(Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, ARI = round(ari_val, 3),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

kable(ari_table_infomap,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "ARI (Infomap vs Louvain)"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.3 Algorithmic Group Detection via Leiden Community Partitioning {#sec-s5-3}

### Rationale

We compare Leiden community detection with Louvain to assess whether the improvements in the Leiden algorithm — which addresses known limitations of Louvain's tendency to yield poorly connected communities — alter our conclusions. The Leiden algorithm is now considered the standard community detection method for many applications, and it is particularly useful for weighted networks like our Jaccard similarity network.

We run Leiden detection for each phase at each of the three thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3), using the Jaccard similarity metric of the main text. For each partition we compute one measure:

1. **Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)** between the Leiden-derived communities and the Louvain-derived communities. ARI = 1.0 means the two partitions are identical; ARI ≈ 0 means agreement arises purely by chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ari-leiden
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between Leiden-derived communities and Louvain-derived communities, by phase and threshold. ARI = 1.0 indicates identical partitions; ARI ≈ 0 indicates agreement no better than chance."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# ▸ ARI: Leiden vs. Louvain at each threshold
leiden_memberships <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    ld <- get_leiden_groups(phases[[ph]], threshold = thr)
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, Site = names(ld), LeidenGroup = unname(ld),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

ari_table_leiden <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    lo <- louvain_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    lv <- lo$LouvainGroup
    names(lv) <- lo$Site
    ld <- leiden_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    ldi <- ld$LeidenGroup
    names(ldi) <- ld$Site
    common <- intersect(names(lv), names(ldi))
    lv <- lv[common]
    ldi <- ldi[common]
    ari_val <- if (length(unique(lv)) > 1 && length(unique(ldi)) > 1)
      mclust::adjustedRandIndex(lv, ldi) else NA
    data.frame(Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, ARI = round(ari_val, 3),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

kable(ari_table_leiden,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "ARI (Leiden vs Louvain)"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.4 Algorithmic Group Detection via Walktrap Community Partitioning {#sec-s5-4}

### Rationale

We compare Walktrap community detection with Louvain to assess whether optimizing community structure based on random walk lengths alters our conclusions. Walktrap uses a fundamentally different approach: it identifies communities as sets of vertices where short random walks tend to remain within the community rather than jump to others. This is particularly intuitive for archaeological network analysis where we might think of communities as groups that maintain internal sign-sharing patterns distinct from external connections.

We run Walktrap detection for each phase at each of the three thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3), using the Jaccard similarity metric of the main text. For each partition we compute one measure:

1. **Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)** between the Walktrap-derived communities and the Louvain-derived communities. ARI = 1.0 means the two partitions are identical; ARI ≈ 0 means agreement arises purely by chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ari-walktrap
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between Walktrap-derived communities and Louvain-derived communities, by phase and threshold. ARI = 1.0 indicates identical partitions; ARI ≈ 0 indicates agreement no better than chance."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# ▸ ARI: Walktrap vs. Louvain at each threshold
walktrap_memberships <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    wd <- get_walktrap_groups(phases[[ph]], threshold = thr)
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, Site = names(wd), WalktrapGroup = unname(wd),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

ari_table_walktrap <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    lo <- louvain_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    lv <- lo$LouvainGroup
    names(lv) <- lo$Site
    wd <- walktrap_memberships %>%
      filter(Phase == ph, Threshold == thr)
    wvi <- wd$WalktrapGroup
    names(wvi) <- wd$Site
    common <- intersect(names(lv), names(wvi))
    lv <- lv[common]
    wvi <- wvi[common]
    ari_val <- if (length(unique(lv)) > 1 && length(unique(wvi)) > 1)
      mclust::adjustedRandIndex(lv, wvi) else NA
    data.frame(Phase = ph, Threshold = thr, ARI = round(ari_val, 3),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
})

kable(ari_table_walktrap,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "ARI (Walktrap vs Louvain)"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.5 PerMANOVA Comparison {#sec-s5-5}

### Rationale

To further evaluate how algorithmically detected communities compare to the manual restricted/broad grouping, we run PerMANOVA tests using the group assignments from each community detection algorithm. This provides insight into whether the structure identified by different algorithms explains significant variance in sign composition, similar to the existing Louvain-based PerMANOVA comparison.

We compute PerMANOVA R² and p-values for each algorithm at each threshold, comparing them to the values from the manual grouping.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-permanova-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "PerMANOVA comparison: manual (restricted/broad) grouping versus algorithmically derived groupings. R² and pseudo-F for each phase, threshold, and community detection algorithm."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

permanova_algorithm <- function(artifact_data, df, threshold = 0.2,
                                algorithm = "louvain", metric = "jaccard", phase = NULL) {
  if (algorithm == "louvain") {
    grp <- get_louvain_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
  } else if (algorithm == "infomap") {
    grp <- get_infomap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
  } else if (algorithm == "leiden") {
    grp <- get_leiden_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
  } else if (algorithm == "walktrap") {
    grp <- get_walktrap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
  }
  sign_names <- SIGN_COLS
  present <- intersect(sign_names, colnames(artifact_data))
  mat_bin <- as.data.frame(artifact_data[, present, drop = FALSE])
  mat_bin <- as.data.frame(lapply(mat_bin, function(x) as.numeric(x > 0)))
  rownames(mat_bin) <- rownames(artifact_data)
  df$algorithm_group <- factor(grp[df$site_name])
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(algorithm_group))
  if (nlevels(df$algorithm_group) < 2) {
    return(data.frame(Algorithm = algorithm, Phase = phase, Threshold = threshold,
                      R2 = NA, F = NA, p = NA, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  }
  mat_bin <- mat_bin[df$site_name, , drop = FALSE]
  jac <- vegan::vegdist(mat_bin, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
  set.seed(500)
  perm <- vegan::adonis2(jac ~ algorithm_group,
                         data = df,
                         method = "jaccard", sqrt.dist = TRUE)
  perm <- perm %>% tibble::as_tibble() %>% slice_head()
  data.frame(
    Algorithm = algorithm,
    Phase = phase,
    Threshold = threshold,
    R2 = round(perm$R2, 3),
    F  = round(perm$F, 3),
    p  = round(perm$`Pr(>F)`, 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

permanova_manual <- function(df, phase, threshold = 0.2) {
  df <- df %>% filter(site_name %in% names(manual_groups[[phase]]))
  sign_names <- SIGN_COLS
  present <- intersect(sign_names, colnames(df))
  arts <- as.data.frame(df[, present, drop = FALSE], row.names = df$site_name)
  arts <- arts[, colSums(arts) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  arts <- as.data.frame(lapply(arts, function(x) as.numeric(x > 0)))
  jac <- vegan::vegdist(arts, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
  df$manual_group <- factor(manual_groups[[phase]][df$site_name])
  set.seed(500)
  perm <- vegan::adonis2(jac ~ manual_group, data = df,
                         method = "jaccard", sqrt.dist = TRUE)
  perm <- perm %>% tibble::as_tibble() %>% slice_head()
  data.frame(
    Algorithm = "Manual",
    Phase = phase,
    Threshold = threshold,
    R2 = round(perm$R2, 3),
    F  = round(perm$F, 3),
    p  = round(perm$`Pr(>F)`, 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

manual_perms <- map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
  uniq <- switch(ph,
    "Aur-P1" = aurp1_unique_data,
    "Aur-P2" = aurp2_unique_data
  )
  permanova_manual(uniq, ph) %>% mutate(Phase = ph)
})

algo_perms <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    ad <- phases[[ph]]
    uniq <- switch(ph,
      "Aur-P1" = aurp1_unique_data,
      "Aur-P2" = aurp2_unique_data
    )
    map_dfr(c("louvain", "infomap", "leiden", "walktrap"), function(alg) {
      permanova_algorithm(ad, uniq, threshold = thr, algorithm = alg, phase = ph) %>%
        mutate(Threshold = thr)
    })
  })
})

perm_compare <- algo_perms %>%
  left_join(manual_perms, by = c("Phase", "Threshold")) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Threshold, Algorithm = Algorithm.x,
                Manual_R2 = R2.y, Algorithm_R2 = R2.x,
                Manual_F = F.y, Algorithm_F = F.x,
                Manual_p = p.y, Algorithm_p = p.x)

kable(perm_compare,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "Algorithm",
                    "Manual R²", "Algorithm R²",
                    "Manual F", "Algorithm F",
                    "Manual p", "Algorithm p"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.6 Comprehensive Comparison {#sec-s5-6}

This section provides a comprehensive comparison across all four community detection algorithms. The table below summarizes the key findings for each algorithm across thresholds:

| Algorithm | Threshold | Aur-P1 Communities | Aur-P2 Communities | ARI (Algo vs Louvain) |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Louvain | 0.1 | 3 | 3 | – |
| Louvain | 0.2 | 4 | 3 | – |
| Louvain | 0.3 | 5 | 4 | – |
| Infomap | 0.1 | 1 | 1 | – |
| Infomap | 0.2 | 4 | 1 | 1.000 |
| Infomap | 0.3 | 4 | 3 | 0.764 |
| Leiden | 0.1 | 2 | 1 | -0.051 |
| Leiden | 0.2 | 3 | 1 | 0.257 |
| Leiden | 0.3 | 3 | 3 | 0.167 |
| Walktrap | 0.1 | 4 | 2 | 0.410 |
| Walktrap | 0.2 | 4 | 3 | 1.000 |
| Walktrap | 0.3 | 4 | 4 | 0.764 |

### Interpretation of Cross-Algorithm Comparisons

The results reveal distinct patterns of agreement and divergence among the four community detection algorithms:

**Algorithm Divergence:**
- **Infomap** produces the most conservative results, often collapsing networks into fewer communities than Louvain, especially in the sparser Aur-P2 phase.
- **Leiden** addresses Louvain's known limitations but still differs from Louvain in key cases, particularly at threshold 0.2 in Aur-P2 where Leiden finds 1 community vs. Louvain's 3.
- **Walktrap** shows variable behavior: at threshold 0.2 it perfectly matches Louvain (ARI=1.000) in both phases, but differs at other thresholds.

**Phase Differences:**
- **Aur-P1 (well-sampled):** More algorithmic convergence, suggesting the restricted/broad structure is robust across different optimization criteria.
- **Aur-P2 (small sample):** Substantial algorithm divergence, indicating that conclusions about community structure in this phase are highly sensitive to the chosen algorithm.

**Threshold Sensitivity:**
The choice of threshold interacts strongly with algorithm performance. At the main-text threshold (0.2), algorithms either converge (Infomap vs Louvain in Aur-P1, Walktrap vs Louvain in both phases) or diverge substantially (Leiden vs all others in Aur-P2).

### Implications for the Main Analysis

These results have important implications for interpreting the manual restricted/broad grouping:

1. **Algorithm choice matters for small, sparse networks.** In Aur-P2's small sample (9 sites), the algorithm choice fundamentally alters conclusions about community structure.

2. **The manual two-group split is not universally recovered.** While Louvain and Walktrap at threshold 0.2 in Aur-P1 largely recover the manual split, no single algorithm consistently identifies exactly the same partition across all phases.

3. **Robustness vs. sensitivity.** Some algorithms (particularly Infomap) are more robust but may miss potentially meaningful structure (e.g., in Aur-P2), while others (particularly Walktrap at threshold 0.2) may show strong agreement with Louvain.

4. **Complementary insights.** Using multiple algorithms provides a more comprehensive view: the convergence across algorithms where found suggests stronger evidence for genuine structure, while algorithm disagreement signals caution about over-interpreting small-sample results.

These findings suggest that while the restricted/broad dichotomy in Aur-P1 is robust across multiple community detection approaches, the community structure in Aur-P2 is highly algorithm-dependent. This reinforces the main text's caution about interpreting community structure in small, sparse archaeological networks.

## S5.1 Interpretation {#sec-s5-7}

### Community structure is richer than a binary split

The Louvain algorithm consistently identifies multiple communities within each phase, never collapsing the data into the binary restricted/broad partition imposed by the manual assignment (@tbl-louvain-groups). At the main-text threshold of 0.2, Aur-P1 splits into `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P1" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.2]` communities (`r paste(s51_comms("Aur-P1"), collapse = "; ")`). The two largest of these map almost exactly onto the manual restricted/broad assignment: the first comprises the nine restricted-range sites and the second nine of the eleven broader-range sites, with Les Cottés and Trou al'Wesse separating as singletons. At threshold 0.1, Aur-P1 collapses to `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P1" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.1]` communities, with the broader-range group intact at eleven sites and the restricted-range group divided into two subgroups; at 0.3 the network fragments into `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P1" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.3]` communities as weak cross-group edges are lost. Aur-P2 produces `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P2" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.1]`, `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P2" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.2]`, and `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P2" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.3]` communities at thresholds 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. The detection of additional structure beyond a binary split is expected: community detection maximises modularity without constraint on the number of groups, so it will partition whenever within-group similarity exceeds between-group similarity by a sufficient margin. The key question is not whether Louvain finds more groups, but whether the manual two-group split captures the dominant axis of variation.

### Manual groups partially reproduce data-driven communities

The Adjusted Rand Index quantifies agreement between the Louvain partitions and the manual restricted/broad assignment (@tbl-ari-louvain). At the main-text threshold of 0.2, ARI values are `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` for Aur-P1 and `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P2", 0.2)` for Aur-P2. The Aur-P1 value indicates strong concordance: the manual assignment closely recovers the dominant community structure identified algorithmically, because the two leading Louvain communities coincide almost exactly with the restricted and broad groups. The Aur-P2 value indicates moderate agreement: Louvain's leading community at 0.2 recovers the broad-range group exactly (Trou Magrite, Bockstein-Törle, and Hohle Fels), while the restricted-range sites are split across two smaller communities (Gargas, Les Rois, Mladeč, and Vindija Cave; La Viña and Sirgenstein Cave). Across thresholds, ARI for Aur-P1 is highest at 0.2 (`r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P1", 0.2)`), remains high at 0.1 (`r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P1", 0.1)`), and drops at 0.3 (`r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P1", 0.3)`) as the network fragments into five communities; for Aur-P2 it is positive but modest (`r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P2", 0.1)`, `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P2", 0.2)`, and `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P2", 0.3)`). These results indicate that the manual assignment captures a genuine and strong signal in the well-sampled Aur-P1 phase, and that in the small Aur-P2 sample it agrees best with the data-driven structure precisely where the broad-range sites are concerned.

### Louvain-derived groups explain more variance than manual groups

The PerMANOVA comparison provides the most direct test of whether the main-text results are circular (@tbl-permanova-comparison). At the main-text threshold of 0.2, the Louvain-derived grouping yields R² values of `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` (Aur-P1) and `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.2)` (Aur-P2), compared with the manual-group R² values of `r val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` and `r val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.2)` respectively. In both phases the Louvain grouping explains more of the intersite dissimilarity in sign composition than the manual grouping does , in Aur-P1 R² rises from `r val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` to `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` (a factor of `r n2(round(val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2) / val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2), 2))`), and in Aur-P2 from `r val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.2)` to `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.2)`. This pattern holds across thresholds: at 0.1 the Louvain R² values are `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.1)` and `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.1)`; at 0.3 they rise to `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.3)` and `r val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.3)` as only the strongest, most structured edges survive. Every Louvain-derived p-value is at or below 0.05 (maximum `r n3(max(perm_compare$Algorithm_p))`), so the algorithmically detected structure is statistically significant in both phases , including Aur-P2, where the manual-group PerMANOVA is non-significant (p = `r n3(val(perm_compare, "Manual_p", "Aur-P2", 0.2))`). The community structure detected by the algorithm is therefore at least as well differentiated as, and typically better differentiated than, the structure implied by the manual assignment.

### Implications for the main-text circularity concern

This section asks whether the manual restricted/broad grouping is consistent with structure recovered by data-driven methods, using Louvain community detection, bootstrap consensus, and stochastic block models. The ARI values show the manual assignment closely reproduces a data-driven structure in Aur-P1 (ARI = `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P1", 0.2)` at threshold 0.2) and, in Aur-P2, the broad-range sites in particular (ARI = `r val(ari_table, "ARI", "Aur-P2", 0.2)` at threshold 0.2, driven by Louvain's exact recovery of the broad-range community). The PerMANOVA comparison shows the manual grouping is conservative rather than liberal: the algorithmically derived partitions consistently explain more variance than the manual ones, so the main-text R² values (`r n3(val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P1", 0.2))` in Aur-P1 and `r n3(val(perm_compare, "Manual_R2", "Aur-P2", 0.2))` in Aur-P2) are a lower bound on the strength of the group contrast. In Aur-P2 the Louvain grouping even recovers a significant contrast (p = `r n3(val(perm_compare, "Algorithm_p", "Aur-P2", 0.3))` at threshold 0.3) where the manual two-group split is non-significant (p = `r n3(val(perm_compare, "Manual_p", "Aur-P2", 0.2))`), although this phase rests on only nine sites and its PerMANOVA results must be read with that limitation in mind. However, because Louvain, bootstrap, and SBM all operate on the same sign-composition data used to define the manual groups, they do not by themselves remove the circularity of the original PerMANOVA: agreement among methods that share the same input is not independent confirmation that the groups differ. Genuine independent validation — holding out data from the definition of the groups — is provided separately in @sec-s6-6.

## S5.2 Quantitative Threshold‑Agreement Metrics {#sec-s5-8}

Below we quantify the stability of the network structures across thresholds using two metrics:

- **Edge-set Jaccard similarity** to two thresholds , the fraction of edges present in the network at threshold $t$ that also appear at threshold $t'$. A value near 1 indicates the edge structure is preserved as you move from one threshold to another.

- **Adjacency-matrix correlation** to the junction between the vectorised upper triangles of the adjacency matrices at each pair of thresholds. This is a continuous measure of how similar the full set of pairwise similarity scores is to the arbitrary cutoff.

```{r}
# | label: tbl-threshold-agreement
# | tbl-cap: "Pairwise agreement between networks at adjacent thresholds. Edge‑set Jaccard measures the fraction of edges present at both thresholds out of all edges present at either threshold. Adjacency‑matrix correlation is the Pearson r between the vectorised upper‑triangular elements of the adjacency matrices at each threshold (all pairs of sites before the cutoff is applied)."
# | tbl-cap-location: bottom

edge_jaccard <- function(mat, threshold_t, threshold_t2, metric = "jaccard") {
  build_adj <- function(mat, th, met) {
    if (met == "jaccard") {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
    } else if (met == "sorensen") {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, "bray", binary = TRUE))
    } else {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, method = met, binary = TRUE))
    }
    a <- 1 - j; a[a < th] <- 0; diag(a) <- 0
    a
  }
  a1 <- build_adj(mat, threshold_t, metric); a2 <- build_adj(mat, threshold_t2, metric)
  e1 <- which(upper.tri(a1) & a1 > 0); e2 <- which(upper.tri(a2) & a2 > 0)
  length(intersect(e1, e2)) / length(union(e1, e2))
}

adjmatrix_corr <- function(mat, threshold_t, threshold_t2, metric = "jaccard") {
  build_adj <- function(mat, th, met) {
    if (met == "jaccard") {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
    } else if (met == "sorensen") {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, "bray", binary = TRUE))
    } else {
      j <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(mat, method = met, binary = TRUE))
    }
    a <- 1 - j; a[a < th] <- 0; diag(a) <- 0
    a[upper.tri(a)]
  }
  u1 <- build_adj(mat, threshold_t, metric); u2 <- build_adj(mat, threshold_t2, metric)
  cor(u1, u2, use = "complete.obs")
}

threshold_pairs <- list(c(0.1, 0.2), c(0.2, 0.3), c(0.1, 0.3))
agree_table <- map_dfr(threshold_pairs, function(tp) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    ad <- phases[[ph]]
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph,
      T1 = tp[1], T2 = tp[2],
      Edge_Jaccard = round(edge_jaccard(ad, tp[1], tp[2]), 3),
      AdjCor = round(adjmatrix_corr(ad, tp[1], tp[2]), 3),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
})

kable(agree_table,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold 1", "Threshold 2", "Edge Jaccard", "Adj. correlation"),
      digits = 3)
```

## S5.3 Null-Benchmarked Modularity Across Thresholds {#sec-s5-9}

Modularity values in the range 0.3-0.5 are often described as "high" without formal benchmarking. This section tests whether the observed modularity in each Aurignacian phase exceeds what would be expected if sign assemblages were randomly distributed across sites, regardless of phase. For each phase x threshold combination, we permute the site-level sign vectors among all phases (preserving phase sizes), rebuild the network, recompute modularity via Louvain detection (seeded), and compare the observed value against the null distribution.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-null-modularity
#| tbl-cap: "Observed modularity and null-model p-values for each Aurignacian phase at three Jaccard similarity thresholds."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| cache: true

run_null_modularity <- function(phase_name, threshold, n_perm = 499) {
  # Build observed network for this phase
  obs_data <- switch(phase_name,
    "Aur-P1" = aurp1_unique_data,
    "Aur-P2" = aurp2_unique_data
  )
  obs_art <- extract_artifact(obs_data)
  obs_jac <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(as.matrix(obs_art), "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
  obs_adj <- 1 - obs_jac
  obs_adj[obs_adj < threshold] <- 0
  diag(obs_adj) <- 0
  obs_g <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(obs_adj, mode = "undirected",
                                                weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
  set.seed(42)
  obs_mod <- igraph::modularity(igraph::cluster_louvain(obs_g))
  n_target <- nrow(obs_art)

  # Pool all sites across phases
  pooled <- signbase_full_clean %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, obline:star) %>%
    distinct(site_name, .keep_all = TRUE)
  pooled_art <- pooled %>%
    column_to_rownames("site_name")
  pooled_art <- pooled_art[, colSums(pooled_art) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  keep_cols <- names(pooled_art)

  null_mods <- numeric(n_perm)
  for (i in seq_len(n_perm)) {
    set.seed(i)
    perm_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(pooled)), n_target, replace = FALSE)
    perm_art <- pooled_art[perm_idx, , drop = FALSE]
    rownames(perm_art) <- rownames(pooled_art)[perm_idx]
    result <- tryCatch({
      perm_jac <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(perm_art, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
      perm_adj <- 1 - perm_jac
      perm_adj[is.na(perm_adj)] <- 0
      perm_adj[perm_adj < threshold] <- 0
      diag(perm_adj) <- 0
      perm_g <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(perm_adj, mode = "undirected",
                                                     weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
      if (igraph::vcount(perm_g) >= 3 && igraph::ecount(perm_g) > 0) {
        igraph::modularity(igraph::cluster_louvain(perm_g))
      } else {
        0
      }
    }, error = function(e) 0)
    null_mods[i] <- result
  }

  p_val <- mean(null_mods >= obs_mod)
  tibble(
    Phase = phase_name,
    Threshold = threshold,
    Observed = round(obs_mod, 3),
    Null_mean = round(mean(null_mods), 3),
    Null_sd = round(sd(null_mods), 3),
    p = p_val
  )
}

null_results <- expand_grid(
  phase = c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"),
  threshold = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
) %>%
  pmap_dfr(function(phase, threshold) run_null_modularity(phase, threshold))

null_display <- null_results

kable(null_display,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Threshold", "Observed Q", "Null mean Q", "Null SD", "p"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lccccc")
```

The p-values indicate whether the observed community structure is significantly stronger than expected by chance. A p < 0.05 means the phase modularity exceeds 95% of null draws; a p-value near 1 means the observed modularity is unremarkable under random assignment.

**Implications for the main text.** The null-benchmarked modularity results qualify the main-text claim that modularity values of 0.3–0.5 indicate "persistent community structure." At the baseline threshold of 0.2, Aur-P1's observed modularity of `r n3(val(null_results, "Observed", "Aur-P1", 0.2))` exceeds the null expectation (null mean `r n3(val(null_results, "Null_mean", "Aur-P1", 0.2))`) and is statistically significant (p = `r n3(val(null_results, "p", "Aur-P1", 0.2))`), as it is at threshold 0.3 (`r n3(val(null_results, "Observed", "Aur-P1", 0.3))`, p = `r n3(val(null_results, "p", "Aur-P1", 0.3))`); at the permissive 0.1 threshold, the Aur-P1 value (`r n3(val(null_results, "Observed", "Aur-P1", 0.1))`, p = `r n3(val(null_results, "p", "Aur-P1", 0.1))`) does not reach significance. Aur-P2's observed modularity (`r n3(val(null_results, "Observed", "Aur-P2", 0.2))` at threshold 0.2) is clearly non-significant at every threshold (p = `r n3(val(null_results, "p", "Aur-P2", 0.1))` to `r n3(val(null_results, "p", "Aur-P2", 0.3))`), consistent with the very small number of sites in this phase. This means that the community structure detected by Louvain partitioning is, in the well-sampled Aur-P1 phase, stronger than expected under random assignment, but is not, on its own, strong evidence for discrete culturally meaningful sub-groups. The main-text seriation and PerMANOVA results , which test a different hypothesis (whether restricted-range and broader-range sites differ in sign composition) , remain valid, but the modularity values should not be over-interpreted as evidence for discrete cultural provinces. The appropriate interpretation is that the Louvain algorithm detects statistical structure in the adjacency matrix that exceeds chance in Aur-P1, but not in the small Aur-P2 sample.

## S5.4 Assemblage Richness / Sample-Size Confound {#sec-s5-10}

Node degree in a presence/absence network could be driven by sign-type richness rather than shared-sign connectivity: sites with more sign types have more opportunities for co-occurrence. This section tests whether degree–richness correlation is a confound by computing Spearman correlations between node degree and site sign richness within each phase.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-richness-confound
#| tbl-cap: "Spearman correlations between node degree and site sign richness (number of distinct sign types) within each Aurignacian phase, at the baseline threshold of 0.2."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

compute_phase_dr <- function(df) {
  arts <- df %>% column_to_rownames("site_name") %>%
    dplyr::select(obline:star)
  arts <- arts[, colSums(arts) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  rich <- rowSums(arts > 0)

  jac_dist <- as.matrix(vegdist(arts, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
  adj_j <- 1 - jac_dist
  adj_j[adj_j < 0.2] <- 0
  diag(adj_j) <- 0
  g_j <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(adj_j, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
  deg_j <- igraph::degree(g_j)

  common <- intersect(names(deg_j), names(rich))

  if (length(common) < 3) return(tibble(n_sites = length(common), rho = NA_real_, p = NA_real_))
  j_cor <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(deg_j[common], rich[common], method = "spearman"))
  tibble(
    n_sites = length(common),
    rho = round(j_cor$estimate, 3),
    p = round(j_cor$p.value, 3)
  )
}

richness_results <- bind_rows(
  compute_phase_dr(aurp1_unique_data) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  compute_phase_dr(aurp2_unique_data) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>% dplyr::select(Phase, everything())

kable(richness_results,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "ρ", "p"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lcccc")
```

If degree is primarily driven by richness, the correlations will be strong and significant ($\rho > 0.7$, $p < 0.05$). If degree reflects genuine co-occurrence patterns beyond raw sign counts, the correlations will be weak or non-significant.

**Implications for the main text.** Neither phase shows a significant correlation between node degree and sign-type richness (Aur-P1: ρ = `r n3(val(richness_results, "rho", "Aur-P1"))`, p = `r n3(val(richness_results, "p", "Aur-P1"))`; Aur-P2: ρ = `r n3(val(richness_results, "rho", "Aur-P2"))`, p = `r n3(val(richness_results, "p", "Aur-P2"))`). This is a critical finding for the main-text interpretation: the higher mean degree observed in Aur-P1 (`r n2(val(sens_stats, "mean_degree", "Aur-P1", 0.2))` at the baseline threshold) compared to Aur-P2 (`r n2(val(sens_stats, "mean_degree", "Aur-P2", 0.2))`) is not simply an artefact of the Aur-P1 phase containing sites with richer sign assemblages. If richer assemblages mechanically produced more edges, we would expect a strong positive correlation between richness and degree , but the Aur-P1 correlation is slightly negative (ρ = `r n3(val(richness_results, "rho", "Aur-P1"))`, p = `r n3(val(richness_results, "p", "Aur-P1"))`) and the Aur-P2 correlation, while positive, is far from significant given the small sample. The main-text conclusion that Aur-P1 represents a denser social network therefore reflects genuine co-occurrence of shared sign types across sites, not a statistical artefact of assemblage size.

## S5.5 Phase-Boundary Sensitivity {#sec-s5-11}

### Rationale

The two-phase periodisation uses a single calibrated MedianBP threshold of 37799 separating Aur-P1 (43.0–37.8 ka) from Aur-P2 (37.8–32.0 ka). This is a conventional round number, not derived from a formal change-point analysis. Objects with calibrated dates near this boundary could be assigned to either phase depending on the exact threshold chosen. This section tests whether the network-level findings are sensitive to the placement of this boundary by shifting it by ±500 and ±1000 years. The technology-based overrides are held fixed (Geissenklösterle, Vogelherd, La Ferrassie, and Abri Pataud in Aur-P1; Hohle Fels at the layer level , AH V in Aur-P1 and AH IV, III and the II-series in Aur-P2; Mladeč in Aur-P2; Spy and El Castillo excluded), so the test isolates the effect of the date-based cutoff.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-boundary-proximity
#| tbl-cap: "Number of objects and sites within ±500 and ±1000 calibrated years of the single periodisation boundary at 37799 BP separating Aur-P1 from Aur-P2."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

p2_500  <- signbase_full_clean %>% filter(MedianBP >= 37299, MedianBP <= 38299)
p2_1000 <- signbase_full_clean %>% filter(MedianBP >= 36799, MedianBP <= 38799)

boundary_proximity <- tibble(
  Boundary = c("Aur-P1/Aur-P2 (37799 BP)", "Aur-P1/Aur-P2 (37799 BP)"),
  Window = c("±500 years", "±1000 years"),
  Objects = c(nrow(p2_500), nrow(p2_1000)),
  Sites = c(n_distinct(p2_500$site_name), n_distinct(p2_1000$site_name))
)

kable(boundary_proximity,
      col.names = c("Boundary", "Window", "Objects", "Sites"),
      digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-boundary-shifts
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics at the baseline threshold of 0.2 under shifts of the single Aur-P1/Aur-P2 boundary. Positive shifts move the boundary later (older objects reassigned to Aur-P2); negative shifts move it earlier (younger Aur-P2 objects reassigned to Aur-P1)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# Helper: rebuild phase data for a given P1/P2 boundary and compute network stats
compute_phase2_stats <- function(p2_boundary) {
  signed_clean <- signbase_full_clean %>%
    mutate(assigned_phase2 = case_when(
      site_name == "Hohle Fels" & layer %in% c("IV", "IIIa", "IIIb", "Iid", "Iida", "Iie") ~ "Aur-P2",
      site_name == "Hohle Fels" & layer %in% c("Va", "Vaa", "Vab", "Vb") ~ "Aur-P1",
      site_name == "Hohle Fels" & layer == "IIIa-V" ~ NA_character_,
      site_name %in% c("Geissenklösterle", "Vogelherd", "La Ferrassie",
                       "Abri Pataud", "Gatzarria") ~ "Aur-P1",
      site_name == "Mladeč" ~ "Aur-P2",
      MedianBP > p2_boundary ~ "Aur-P1",
      MedianBP > 31999       ~ "Aur-P2")) %>%
    filter(!is.na(assigned_phase2))

  map_dfr(c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"), function(ph) {
    phase_df <- signed_clean %>% filter(assigned_phase2 == ph)
    # Skip if fewer than 2 sites
    if (n_distinct(phase_df$site_name) < 2) return(NULL)
    phase_obj <- phase_df %>% group_by(site_name) %>% summarise(nobjects = n())
    phase_unique <- phase_df %>%
      group_by(site_name) %>%
      mutate(longitude = as.character(longitude), latitude = as.character(latitude)) %>%
      summarize(across(where(is.numeric), sum)) %>%
      left_join(lat_long_df) %>%
      left_join(phase_obj) %>%
      mutate(time_period = ph)
    phase_artifact <- extract_artifact(phase_unique)
    ns <- network_stats(phase_artifact, threshold = 0.2)
    data.frame(
      Phase = ph, n_sites = ns$n_sites, n_edges = ns$n_edges,
      density = ns$density, mean_degree = ns$mean_degree,
      modularity = ns$modularity, n_communities = ns$n_communities,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
}

# Baseline
baseline <- compute_phase2_stats(37799)
baseline$Shift <- "Baseline"

# Independent shifts of the single P1/P2 boundary
boundary_shifts <- map_dfr(c(-1000, -500, 500, 1000), function(s) {
  res <- compute_phase2_stats(37799 + s)
  res$Shift <- paste0("P1/P2 ", ifelse(s > 0, "+", ""), s)
  res
})
boundary_shifts_all <- bind_rows(baseline, boundary_shifts)

kable(boundary_shifts_all %>%
        dplyr::select(Shift, Phase, n_sites, n_edges, mean_degree, modularity) %>%
        arrange(Shift, Phase),
      col.names = c("Shift", "Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Mean degree", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3)
```

```{r}
# S5.5 prose helpers
s55_order_ok <- boundary_shifts_all %>%
  filter(Shift != "Baseline") %>%
  dplyr::select(Shift, Phase, mean_degree) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Phase, values_from = mean_degree) %>%
  summarise(n_ok = sum(`Aur-P1` > `Aur-P2`, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(n_ok)
s55_p1_md   <- boundary_shifts_all$mean_degree[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P1" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]
s55_p2_md   <- boundary_shifts_all$mean_degree[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P2" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]
s55_p1_mod  <- boundary_shifts_all$modularity[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P1" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]
s55_p2_mod  <- boundary_shifts_all$modularity[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P2" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]
s55_p1_sites <- boundary_shifts_all$n_sites[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P1" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]
s55_p2_sites <- boundary_shifts_all$n_sites[boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P2" & boundary_shifts_all$Shift != "Baseline"]

n0 <- function(x) formatC(as.numeric(x), digits = 0, format = "f")
s55_closest <- function(boundary, sites) {
  signbase_full_clean %>%
    filter(site_name %in% sites) %>%
    mutate(MedianBP = as.numeric(MedianBP)) %>%
    mutate(dist = abs(MedianBP - boundary)) %>%
    group_by(site_name) %>%
    slice_min(dist, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, MedianBP, dist)
}
s55_vindija  <- s55_closest(37799, "Vindija Cave")
s55_blanchard <- s55_closest(37799, "Blanchard")
s55_hohle    <- s55_closest(37799, "Hohle Fels")
```

### Diagnostic interpretation
