`r boundary_proximity$Objects[boundary_proximity$Window == "±1000 years"]` objects from `r boundary_proximity$Sites[boundary_proximity$Window == "±1000 years"]` sites fall within ±1000 calibrated years of the boundary at 37799 BP, and `r boundary_proximity$Objects[boundary_proximity$Window == "±500 years"]` objects from `r boundary_proximity$Sites[boundary_proximity$Window == "±500 years"]` sites within ±500 years. The sites closest to the boundary are Hohle Fels (MedianBP `r n0(s55_hohle$MedianBP[s55_hohle$site_name == "Hohle Fels"])`, just `r n0(s55_hohle$dist[s55_hohle$site_name == "Hohle Fels"])` years below the threshold) and Vindija Cave (`r n0(s55_vindija$MedianBP[s55_vindija$site_name == "Vindija Cave"])`, `r n0(s55_vindija$dist[s55_vindija$site_name == "Vindija Cave"])` years below), while the closest site above the threshold is Blanchard (`r n0(s55_blanchard$MedianBP[s55_blanchard$site_name == "Blanchard"])`, `r n0(s55_blanchard$dist[s55_blanchard$site_name == "Blanchard"])` years above). Because only an upward shift can transfer sites into Aur-P2, and only a downward shift into Aur-P1, the reassignments are asymmetric: a downward shift of 500 years moves Vindija Cave from Aur-P2 to Aur-P1 (the only Aur-P2 site within reach), while an upward shift of 500 years moves Blanchard into Aur-P2 and an upward shift of 1000 years additionally moves Cellier, Trou al'Wesse, and Grottes de Fonds-de-Forêt. Hohle Fels lies just below the boundary, but its near-boundary objects belong to AH IV, which the technology-based override fixes in Aur-P2 (its Aur-P1 horizon, AH V, is well above the boundary), so it does not change phase under any shift. The boundary-sensitive sites are therefore few and, apart from Cellier (28 objects) and Blanchard (18 objects), small.

### Independent-shift interpretation

The independent-shift analysis shifts the single P1/P2 boundary while holding the technology-based overrides fixed. Across the four shifts tested, the Aur-P1 mean degree ranges from `r range_str(s55_p1_md, 2)` and Aur-P2 from `r range_str(s55_p2_md, 2)`. The Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity ordering is preserved in all `r s55_order_ok` shifts: a downward shift adds Vindija Cave to Aur-P1, raising its mean degree to `r n2(max(s55_p1_md))` (82 edges) while shrinking Aur-P2 to `r min(s55_p2_sites)` sites (mean degree `r n2(min(s55_p2_md))`); an upward shift transfers sites the other way, with Aur-P1 at `r min(s55_p1_sites)` sites after the ±1000 year shift yet still averaging `r n2(min(s55_p1_md))`, above Aur-P2's `r n2(max(s55_p2_md))`. Modularity is stable: Aur-P1 ranges from `r n3(min(s55_p1_mod))` to `r n3(max(s55_p1_mod))` across shifts (baseline `r n3(boundary_shifts_all$modularity[boundary_shifts_all$Shift == "Baseline" & boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P1"])`) and Aur-P2 from `r n3(min(s55_p2_mod))` to `r n3(max(s55_p2_mod))` (baseline `r n3(boundary_shifts_all$modularity[boundary_shifts_all$Shift == "Baseline" & boundary_shifts_all$Phase == "Aur-P2"])`), indicating that the community structure in both phases is not sensitive to boundary placement.

### Conclusion

The two-phase results are robust to the placement of the single periodisation boundary. Shifting it by ±1000 calibrated years moves at most five sites between phases (Vindija Cave into Aur-P1; Blanchard, Cellier, Trou al'Wesse, and Grottes de Fonds-de-Forêt into Aur-P2), and in every scenario Aur-P1 retains both more sites and a higher mean degree than Aur-P2. The main-text conclusion that Aur-P1 forms a more densely connected network than Aur-P2 is therefore not an artefact of the exact boundary value; the strength of the contrast shifts with the boundary, but its direction does not.

## S5.6 Continuous Threshold Sweep {#sec-s5-12}

The main text reports statistics at three discrete thresholds (0.1, 0.2, 0.3). This section sweeps the Jaccard similarity threshold from 0.05 to 0.50 in steps of 0.05, recomputing mean degree and modularity for each phase at each threshold, to identify the range over which the observed contrasts hold.

```{r}
#| label: fig-threshold-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Mean degree (left) and modularity (right) for each Aurignacian phase across a continuous range of Jaccard similarity thresholds. The vertical dashed line marks the baseline threshold of 0.2."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

thresholds <- seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.05)

phase_list <- list(
  `Aur-P1` = aurp1_artifact_data,
  `Aur-P2` = aurp2_artifact_data
)

sweep_results <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(th) {
  map_dfr(names(phase_list), function(pname) {
    art <- phase_list[[pname]]
    jac <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(art, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
    adj <- 1 - jac
    adj[adj < th] <- 0
    diag(adj) <- 0
    g <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(adj, mode = "undirected",
                                              weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
    mod_val <- if (igraph::ecount(g) > 0) {
      set.seed(42)
      igraph::modularity(igraph::cluster_louvain(g))
    } else { NA_real_ }
    deg_val <- mean(igraph::degree(g))
    tibble(Phase = pname, Threshold = th, Mean_degree = deg_val, Modularity = mod_val)
  })
})

p1 <- ggplot(sweep_results, aes(x = Threshold, y = Mean_degree, colour = Phase)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Jaccard similarity threshold", y = "Mean degree") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p2 <- ggplot(sweep_results, aes(x = Threshold, y = Modularity, colour = Phase)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Jaccard similarity threshold", y = "Modularity") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, ncol = 2, labels = c("a", "b"))
```

```{r}
# S5.6 prose helpers: ordering-preservation range and mean-degree ranges
sweep_wide <- sweep_results %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Threshold, Mean_degree) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Phase, values_from = Mean_degree)
s56_ok_ths <- sweep_wide$Threshold[sweep_wide$`Aur-P1` > sweep_wide$`Aur-P2`]
s56_ok_range <- range(s56_ok_ths)
s56_p1_md_range <- range(sweep_results$Mean_degree[sweep_results$Phase == "Aur-P1"])
s56_p2_md_range <- range(sweep_results$Mean_degree[sweep_results$Phase == "Aur-P2"])
s56_p1_mod_range <- range(sweep_results$Modularity[sweep_results$Phase == "Aur-P1"], na.rm = TRUE)
s56_p2_mod_range <- range(sweep_results$Modularity[sweep_results$Phase == "Aur-P2"], na.rm = TRUE)
```

The sweep reveals the threshold range over which the Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 mean-degree ordering holds. The two-phase contrast is monotonic and holds at every threshold in the swept range: Aur-P1's mean degree runs from `r range_str(s56_p1_md_range, 2)` and Aur-P2's from `r range_str(s56_p2_md_range, 2)` across thresholds of 0.05–0.50, and the ordering is preserved throughout. At very low thresholds both networks are densely connected and the relative contrast compresses; at high thresholds both fragment as edges drop out, but Aur-P2 retains a mean degree of at least `r n2(min(s56_p2_md_range))` even at the coarsest threshold (0.50), so the contrast never collapses.

**Implications for the main text.** The continuous sweep confirms that the main-text threshold of 0.2 is not a cherry-picked value that produces a desired result. The Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 mean-degree ordering is preserved across the entire informative threshold range (`r n2(s56_ok_range[1])`–`r n2(s56_ok_range[2])`). In contrast to a three-phase periodisation, in which the intermediate phase could be compressed into statistical collapse at high thresholds, the two-phase comparison is stable: Aur-P2, though small, never fragments below a mean degree of `r n2(min(s56_p2_md_range))`. The modularity sweep shows a parallel pattern: Aur-P1's modularity ranges from `r range_str(s56_p1_mod_range, 3)` across thresholds and consistently exceeds Aur-P2's (`r range_str(s56_p2_mod_range, 3)`) at every threshold, reinforcing the conclusion that the larger, earlier phase has a stronger community structure. The baseline threshold of 0.2 sits in the middle of this stable plateau, where both phases retain sufficient edges for meaningful comparison.

## S5.7 Bootstrap Confidence Intervals {#sec-s5-13}

Point estimates of network statistics are sensitive to individual sites and to object sampling within sites. Resampling sites with replacement creates duplicate nodes (similarity 1, distance 0) and inflates mean degree and narrows intervals [@Roberts_2021; @Clarke_Rothery_Raybould_2002]. This section therefore uses object-within-site bootstrap: for each site, draw its observed number of objects with replacement from that site's own objects, rebuild the site x sign presence matrix, and recompute mean degree and modularity at threshold 0.2. Node identity is preserved; uncertainty reflects object sampling rather than artificial duplication. We report the observed statistic and a percentile interval around it.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bootstrap-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Bootstrap 95% percentile intervals for mean degree and modularity at threshold = 0.2, based on 999 object-within-site resamples per phase. Observed is the statistic on the full data; interval is the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the bootstrap distribution. Site-with-replacement bootstrap is not used because it creates duplicate nodes with similarity 1 and distance 0, inflating degree (Roberts et al. 2021)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| cache: true

boot_results <- bind_rows(
  {
    b1 <- bootstrap_network_stats(aurp1_artifact_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P1", n_boot = 999, threshold = 0.2, seed = 42)
    tibble(Phase = "Aur-P1",
           md_point = round(b1$observed_md, 2),
           md_lower = round(b1$md_lower, 2),
           md_upper = round(b1$md_upper, 2),
           mod_point = round(b1$observed_mod, 3),
           mod_lower = round(b1$mod_lower, 3),
           mod_upper = round(b1$mod_upper, 3))
  },
  {
    b2 <- bootstrap_network_stats(aurp2_artifact_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P2", n_boot = 999, threshold = 0.2, seed = 42)
    tibble(Phase = "Aur-P2",
           md_point = round(b2$observed_md, 2),
           md_lower = round(b2$md_lower, 2),
           md_upper = round(b2$md_upper, 2),
           mod_point = round(b2$observed_mod, 3),
           mod_lower = round(b2$mod_lower, 3),
           mod_upper = round(b2$mod_upper, 3))
  }
)

kable(boot_results,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Mean degree (observed)", "2.5%", "97.5%", "Q (observed)", "2.5%", "97.5%"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lcccccc")
```

```{r}
# S5.7 prose helpers: CI lookups and mean-degree CI overlap flag
s57_phase <- function(ph) list(
  md_low   = val(boot_results, "md_lower", ph),
  md_hi    = val(boot_results, "md_upper", ph),
  md_pt    = val(boot_results, "md_point", ph),
  mod_low  = val(boot_results, "mod_lower", ph),
  mod_hi   = val(boot_results, "mod_upper", ph),
  mod_pt   = val(boot_results, "mod_point", ph)
)
s57_p <- s57_phase("Aur-P1")
s57_v <- s57_phase("Aur-P2")
s57_md_overlap <- !(s57_p$md_low > s57_v$md_hi || s57_v$md_low > s57_p$md_hi)
s57_md_sentence <- if (s57_md_overlap) {
  paste0("Because the intervals overlap, the bootstrap does not formally separate the two phases ",
         "by the strict non-overlap criterion; the Aur-P1–Aur-P2 contrast is supported at the ",
         "point-estimate level (Aur-P1 ", n2(s57_p$md_pt), " vs Aur-P2 ", n2(s57_v$md_pt),
         ") but is not statistically decisive.")
} else {
  paste0("Because the intervals do not overlap, the bootstrap confirms that the Aur-P1–Aur-P2 ",
         "connectivity contrast is not driven by a handful of influential sites.")
}
```

The intervals quantify uncertainty due to object sampling within sites: a narrow interval means the observed statistic is stable when objects are resampled within sites, while a wide interval signals sensitivity to which objects were recovered. Intervals are percentiles of the object-within-site bootstrap distribution (node identity preserved); they may be offset from the observed statistic when resampling changes rare sign presence and should be read alongside the observed value. Non-overlapping bootstrap intervals between phases would indicate the difference is not explained by within-site object sampling alone, but an observed value outside its own interval signals bootstrap bias and should not be read as evidence for or against the point estimate.

**Implications for the main text.** The object-within-site bootstrap CIs show which main-text comparisons are robust to object sampling. For mean degree, the Aur-P1 observed `r n2(s57_p$md_pt)` with CI [`r n2(s57_p$md_low)`, `r n2(s57_p$md_hi)`] and Aur-P2 observed `r n2(s57_v$md_pt)` with CI [`r n2(s57_v$md_low)`, `r n2(s57_v$md_hi)`] `r ifelse(s57_md_overlap, "overlap", "do not overlap")`. `r s57_md_sentence` The observed mean degree lies outside its bootstrap CI for both phases (Aur-P1 `r n2(s57_p$md_pt)` vs. [`r n2(s57_p$md_low)`, `r n2(s57_p$md_hi)`]; Aur-P2 `r n2(s57_v$md_pt)` vs. [`r n2(s57_v$md_low)`, `r n2(s57_v$md_hi)`]), reflecting the tendency for resampling to miss rare signs at large sites and to duplicate the single object carrying a rare sign at small sites. For modularity, CIs are narrow and do not overlap (Aur-P1 observed `r n3(s57_p$mod_pt)` CI [`r n3(s57_p$mod_low)`, `r n3(s57_p$mod_hi)`] vs. Aur-P2 observed `r n3(s57_v$mod_pt)` CI [`r n3(s57_v$mod_low)`, `r n3(s57_v$mod_hi)`]); the point-estimate difference (`r n3(s57_p$mod_pt)` vs. `r n3(s57_v$mod_pt)`) is stable to within-site object resampling, but absolute values remain sensitive to threshold and small-P2 sample (`r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites) (see S5.3).

## S5.8 Multiple‑Testing Correction for Mantel Results {#sec-s5-14}

The Mantel tests reported in @tbl-geodesic-mantel and the main text evaluate 4 hypotheses (2 phases × 2 distance measures). Without correction, the effective Type I error rate is inflated. Here we apply the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate at α = 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mantel-bh
#| tbl-cap: "Mantel test p-values before and after Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing across 2 phases × 2 distance measures (4 tests total). Results with adjusted p < 0.05 are highlighted."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# Rerun all Mantel tests and collect results
mantel_all <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(Phase = "Aur-P1", run_mantel_comp(aurp1_unique_data)),
  data.frame(Phase = "Aur-P2", run_mantel_comp(aurp2_unique_data))
)

# Build vector of 4 raw p-values: Euclidean x2 then Geodesic x2
raw_p <- c(mantel_all$Euclidean_p, mantel_all$Geodesic_p)
test_labels <- c(
  paste0("Euclidean – ", mantel_all$Phase),
  paste0("Geodesic – ", mantel_all$Phase)
)
r_vals <- c(mantel_all$Euclidean_R, mantel_all$Geodesic_R)

# Benjamini-Hochberg correction
adj_p <- p.adjust(raw_p, method = "BH")

mantel_bh <- tibble(
  Test = test_labels,
  R = round(r_vals, 3),
  `Raw p` = raw_p,
  `BH-adjusted p` = round(adj_p, 3),
  Significant = ifelse(adj_p < 0.05, "Yes", "No")
)

kable(mantel_bh,
      col.names = c("Test", "R", "Raw p", "BH-adjusted p", "Significant"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lcccc")
```

```{r}
# S5.8 prose helpers: the closest-to-significance result
s58_best <- mantel_bh %>% arrange(`Raw p`) %>% slice(1)
s58_test  <- s58_best$Test[1]
s58_R     <- s58_best$R[1]
s58_rawp  <- s58_best$`Raw p`[1]
s58_adjp  <- s58_best$`BH-adjusted p`[1]
s58_n_sig <- sum(mantel_bh$Significant == "Yes")
s58_after_text <- if (s58_n_sig == 0) {
  paste0("None of the ", nrow(mantel_bh), " tests reach significance after correction.")
} else {
  cat("SBM results not available. Install `blockmodels` package (`renv::install(\"blockmodels\")`) and re-render to fit models.")
}
```

Of the `r nrow(mantel_bh)` tests, none approaches nominal significance: the smallest raw $p$-value is `r s58_test` ($R = `r n3(s58_R)`$, raw $p = `r n3(s58_rawp)`$), well above the 0.05 threshold. After Benjamini–Hochberg correction this adjusts to $p = `r n3(s58_adjp)`$. `r s58_after_text` This is consistent with the main-text interpretation: geographic distance does not account for sign distribution in either phase, and the largest correlations are weakly positive for Aur-P1 and weakly negative for Aur-P2. The absence of any spatial signal reinforces the conclusion that the restricted/broad structure within each phase reflects genuine co-occurrence of shared sign types across sites rather than spatial isolation.

## S5.9 Network-Size Normalised Comparison {#sec-s5-15}

```{r}
# S5.9 prose helper: site counts and percentage surplus
s59_pct_more <- round(100 * (nrow(aurp1_artifact_data) - nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)) / nrow(aurp2_artifact_data))
```

Modularity and mean degree are not invariant to the number of nodes: larger networks tend to have higher modularity even under random assignment. Aur-P1 (`r nrow(aurp1_artifact_data)` sites) has `r s59_pct_more`% more nodes than Aur-P2 (`r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites). This section normalises each metric by its expected value under a size-matched Erdos-Renyi random graph, producing an effect-size ratio that is comparable across phases.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-size-normalised
#| tbl-cap: "Network metrics normalised by size-matched Erdos-Renyi expectation. Ratio > 1 indicates the observed value exceeds the random expectation for a network of the same size. ER mean and SD are based on 100 random graphs per phase."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

compute_normalised_metrics <- function(art, n_rand = 100) {
  jac <- as.matrix(vegan::vegdist(art, "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
  adj <- 1 - jac
  adj[adj < 0.2] <- 0
  diag(adj) <- 0
  n <- nrow(adj)
  p <- sum(adj > 0) / (n * (n - 1))
  set.seed(42)
  g_obs <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(adj, mode = "undirected",
                                                weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
  obs_md <- mean(igraph::degree(g_obs))
  set.seed(42)
  obs_mod <- igraph::modularity(igraph::cluster_louvain(g_obs))

  er_md <- numeric(n_rand)
  er_mod <- numeric(n_rand)
  for (i in seq_len(n_rand)) {
    g_er <- igraph::sample_gnp(n, p, directed = FALSE)
    er_md[i] <- mean(igraph::degree(g_er))
    set.seed(i)
    er_mod[i] <- igraph::modularity(igraph::cluster_louvain(g_er))
  }

  tibble(
    Sites = n,
    Obs_md = round(obs_md, 2),
    ER_md = round(mean(er_md), 2),
    MD_ratio = round(obs_md / mean(er_md), 2),
    Obs_mod = round(obs_mod, 3),
    ER_mod = round(mean(er_mod), 3),
    Mod_ratio = round(obs_mod / max(mean(er_mod), 0.001), 2)
  )
}

norm_results <- bind_rows(
  compute_normalised_metrics(aurp1_artifact_data) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  compute_normalised_metrics(aurp2_artifact_data) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>% dplyr::select(Phase, everything())

kable(norm_results,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Obs. md", "ER md", "MD ratio",
                     "Obs. Q", "ER Q", "Q ratio"),
      digits = 2,
      align = "lcccccccc")
```

The ratio columns (MD ratio and Q ratio) are the key normalised comparisons. A ratio of 1.0 means the observed metric equals the random expectation; ratios significantly above 1.0 indicate genuine structure beyond what node count alone produces.

**Implications for the main text.** The size-normalised results address a potential confound in the main-text phase comparison: because mean degree and modularity both scale with the number of nodes, the `r nrow(aurp1_artifact_data)`-site Aur-P1 network and the `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)`-site Aur-P2 network are not directly comparable on those raw measures. Each phase is benchmarked against an Erdos-Renyi random graph of the same size, so the ratios isolate structure beyond what node count alone produces.

- **Mean degree.** The MD ratio is `r n2(val(norm_results, "MD_ratio", "Aur-P1"))` for Aur-P1 and `r n2(val(norm_results, "MD_ratio", "Aur-P2"))` for Aur-P2. Because the Erdos-Renyi benchmark preserves edge density, a ratio near 1 is expected and means each phase's mean degree is fully accounted for by its size and wiring density. The raw gap (Aur-P1 `r n2(val(norm_results, "Obs_md", "Aur-P1"))` vs Aur-P2 `r n2(val(norm_results, "Obs_md", "Aur-P2"))`) therefore reflects the `r s59_pct_more`% larger site sample in Aur-P1, not higher intrinsic connectivity. After size normalisation there is no evidence that Aur-P1 is more "connected" by degree, which is why the main text reports raw degree only descriptively and bases inference on the permutation tests.
- **Modularity.** The Q ratio is `r n2(val(norm_results, "Mod_ratio", "Aur-P1"))` for Aur-P1 and `r n2(val(norm_results, "Mod_ratio", "Aur-P2"))` for Aur-P2, i.e. observed modularity exceeds the size-matched random expectation by about `r round(100 * (val(norm_results, "Mod_ratio", "Aur-P1") - 1))`% in Aur-P1 and `r round(100 * (val(norm_results, "Mod_ratio", "Aur-P2") - 1))`% in Aur-P2. Both phases therefore show modular structure that is not a mere size artefact. Aur-P1's larger excess means its community structure is stronger than Aur-P2's even after the `r nrow(aurp1_artifact_data)`-versus-`r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` site asymmetry is removed, so the phase difference in modularity is not a sample-size artefact; the Aur-P2 excess (`r n2(val(norm_results, "Mod_ratio", "Aur-P2"))`x) is modest and, with only `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites, should be read cautiously.

In short, size normalisation removes the mean-degree confound and confirms that the modularity-based claim of stronger community structure in Aur-P1 survives net of network size, whereas neither phase's mean degree can be used as evidence of intrinsically higher connectivity.

## S5.10 Multiple Regression on Distance Matrices (Drivers of Sign Dissimilarity) {#sec-s5-16}

The Mantel tests establish that geographic distance is not significantly correlated with sign dissimilarity in either phase, but a non-significant result cannot by itself identify which alternative process — if any — generated the pattern. To split the variance of sign dissimilarity among the candidate drivers that are actually measured in the data, we fit a multiple regression on distance matrices (MRM; @Lichstein_2007) in which the response is the Jaccard dissimilarity of sign presence/absence and the three predictors are, for every pair of sites, their geographic distance, their absolute temporal distance (|ΔMedianBP|), and their absolute difference in object count (a proxy for sampling effort). Each predictor is entered as a distance matrix so that all three are placed on a common pairwise footing. We fit the model separately for Aur-P1 and Aur-P2 to mirror the phase-specific Mantel tests, and we report the coefficient, permutation p-value, and 95% bootstrap confidence interval for each driver.

```{r}
#| label: s5-10-mrm
#| warning: false

mrm_phase <- function(art, uniq, nperm = 10000, B = 500) {
  sites <- uniq   # rows are assumed aligned with the rows of art
  Y   <- as.dist(vegan::vegdist(art, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
  pts <- sites %>% sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
  geo <- sf::st_distance(pts) %>% as.dist()
  temp <- dist(sites$MedianBP)
  obj  <- dist(sites$nobjects)
  fit <- MRM(Y ~ geo + temp + obj, nperm = nperm)
  set.seed(7)
  boot_one <- function() {
    idx <- sample(nrow(art), replace = TRUE)
    Yb  <- as.dist(vegan::vegdist(art[idx, ], method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
    pb  <- sites[idx, , drop = FALSE] %>% sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
    gb  <- sf::st_distance(pb) %>% as.dist()
    tb  <- dist(sites$MedianBP[idx])
    ob  <- dist(sites$nobjects[idx])
    res <- tryCatch(MRM(Yb ~ gb + tb + ob, nperm = 10)$coef,
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(res) || !("Y" %in% colnames(res))) return(NULL)
    if (any(is.na(res[, "Y"]))) return(NULL)
    res[, "Y"]
  }
  boots <- replicate(B, boot_one(), simplify = FALSE)
  boots <- boots[!sapply(boots, is.null)]
  boots <- do.call(cbind, boots)
  list(coef   = fit$coef,
       r2     = fit$r.squared,
       geo_ci = quantile(boots["geo", ], c(0.025, 0.975)),
       temp_ci= quantile(boots["temp", ], c(0.025, 0.975)),
       obj_ci = quantile(boots["obj", ],  c(0.025, 0.975)))
}

mrm_p1 <- mrm_phase(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_unique_data)
mrm_p2 <- mrm_phase(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_unique_data)

mrm_p1_r2 <- mrm_p1$r.squared
mrm_p2_r2 <- mrm_p2$r.squared

mrm_p1_geo <- mrm_p1$coef["geo","Y"]; mrm_p1_geo_p <- mrm_p1$coef["geo","pval"]
mrm_p1_geo_lo <- mrm_p1$geo_ci[1]; mrm_p1_geo_hi <- mrm_p1$geo_ci[2]
mrm_p1_temp <- mrm_p1$coef["temp","Y"]; mrm_p1_temp_p <- mrm_p1$coef["temp","pval"]
mrm_p1_temp_lo <- mrm_p1$temp_ci[1]; mrm_p1_temp_hi <- mrm_p1$temp_ci[2]
mrm_p1_obj <- mrm_p1$coef["obj","Y"]; mrm_p1_obj_p <- mrm_p1$coef["obj","pval"]
mrm_p1_obj_lo <- mrm_p1$obj_ci[1]; mrm_p1_obj_hi <- mrm_p1$obj_ci[2]

mrm_p2_geo <- mrm_p2$coef["geo","Y"]; mrm_p2_geo_p <- mrm_p2$coef["geo","pval"]
mrm_p2_temp <- mrm_p2$coef["temp","Y"]; mrm_p2_temp_p <- mrm_p2$coef["temp","pval"]
mrm_p2_obj <- mrm_p2$coef["obj","Y"]; mrm_p2_obj_p <- mrm_p2$coef["obj","pval"]
mrm_p2_geo_lo <- mrm_p2$geo_ci[1]; mrm_p2_geo_hi <- mrm_p2$geo_ci[2]
mrm_p2_temp_lo <- mrm_p2$temp_ci[1]; mrm_p2_temp_hi <- mrm_p2$temp_ci[2]
mrm_p2_obj_lo <- mrm_p2$obj_ci[1]; mrm_p2_obj_hi <- mrm_p2$obj_ci[2]
```

For Aur-P1 the MRM explains `r n2(mrm_p1_r2)` of the variance in sign dissimilarity; none of the three drivers is significant (geographic: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_geo)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_geo_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_geo_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_geo_p)`; temporal: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_temp)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_temp_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_temp_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_temp_p)`; object count: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_obj)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_obj_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_obj_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_obj_p)`). Aur-P2 shows the same pattern (R² = `r n2(mrm_p2_r2)`; geographic p = `r n3(mrm_p2_geo_p)`, temporal p = `r n3(mrm_p2_temp_p)`, object-count p = `r n3(mrm_p2_obj_p)`). Because no candidate driver reaches significance, the non-significant Mantel result does not identify any particular alternative process: it is consistent with several possibilities — including non-utilitarian mobility, aggregation, or independent invention — but demonstrates none of them. With only `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites, the Aur-P2 MRM is underpowered, so its non-significant coefficients should be read as indicative rather than conclusive; the substantive point is that the data contain no statistical evidence favouring one driver over another.

## S5.11 Mantel Correlogram and Bootstrap Confidence Intervals on the Mantel R {#sec-s5-17}

### Rationale

The Mantel tests reported in the main text and in S3 evaluate a single global null hypothesis: that geometric-sign dissimilarity is uncorrelated with geographic distance across all site pairs simultaneously. A non-significant global result can conceal scale-dependent structure — for example, sign sharing might be geographically clustered at short distances but random at long distances, producing a net correlation near zero. Because the global test cannot distinguish "no spatial structure at any scale" from "positive and negative structure that cancel," we ask two specific questions:

1. **Does sign dissimilarity show any spatial autocorrelation at a specific distance lag?** A Mantel correlogram partitions site pairs by geographic-distance bin and tests the Mantel correlation within each bin; a significant positive r at one or more lags would reveal scale-dependent structure that the global test misses.
2. **How uncertain is the global Mantel R estimate, and what does that imply about statistical power?** We place a bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the single global Mantel R reported for each phase. A wide interval that overlaps zero indicates the test cannot distinguish a true null from a true moderate correlation, so the non-significant result is a lack of evidence rather than evidence of absence.

### Analysis

We reconstruct, for each phase, the Jaccard sign dissimilarity and the geodesic geographic-distance matrix used by the S3 Mantel tests (the same construction as `run_mantel_comp`, applied to the technology-assigned phase data). The Mantel correlogram is computed with `ecodist::mgram` [@Goslee_Urban_2007], which bins pairs by geographic distance — into 5 equiprobable lags for Aur-P1 and 3 for Aur-P2, to keep pair counts per lag stable given the small samples — and returns the Mantel r, a permutation p-value, and 95% bootstrap confidence limits (llim/ulim) for each lag. For the global statistic we additionally resample sites with replacement (B = 1000) and recompute the Mantel R each time, taking the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles as the bootstrap interval.

```{r}
#| label: s5-11-mantel-corr
#| warning: false

phase_distances <- function(df) {
  art <- df %>%
    dplyr::select(line:star) %>%
    dplyr::select(where(~ is.numeric(.) && sum(.) != 0)) %>%
    mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(. > 0)))
  jac <- vegan::vegdist(art, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
  sf_obj <- sf::st_as_sf(df, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
  geo <- as.dist(sf::st_distance(sf_obj) / 1000)
  list(jac = jac, geo = geo)
}

pd_p1 <- phase_distances(aurp1_unique_data)
pd_p2 <- phase_distances(aurp2_unique_data)

nclass_p1 <- 5
nclass_p2 <- 3
set.seed(2024)

mg_p1 <- ecodist::mgram(pd_p1$jac, pd_p1$geo,
                        nclass = nclass_p1, equiprobable = TRUE,
                        nboot = 1000, cboot = 0.95, nperm = 1000)
mg_p2 <- ecodist::mgram(pd_p2$jac, pd_p2$geo,
                        nclass = nclass_p2, equiprobable = TRUE,
                        nboot = 1000, cboot = 0.95, nperm = 1000)

mg_p1_df <- as.data.frame(mg_p1$mgram) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1")
mg_p2_df <- as.data.frame(mg_p2$mgram) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
mg_plot_df <- bind_rows(mg_p1_df, mg_p2_df)

# Global Mantel R (point estimate + permutation p), same construction as S3
mp1 <- vegan::mantel(pd_p1$geo, pd_p1$jac, permutations = 1000)
mp2 <- vegan::mantel(pd_p2$geo, pd_p2$jac, permutations = 1000)
mg_p1_r <- mp1$statistic; mg_p1_p <- mp1$signif
mg_p2_r <- mp2$statistic; mg_p2_p <- mp2$signif

# Bootstrap 95% CI on the global Mantel R via object-within-site resampling.
# Site-with-replacement bootstrap creates duplicate nodes (distance 0,
# dissimilarity 0) and biases R upward; we instead resample objects within
# each site (object-within-site bootstrap, see functions.R).
mb_p1_res <- bootstrap_mantel_R(aurp1_unique_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P1", B = 1000, seed = 42)
mb_p2_res <- bootstrap_mantel_R(aurp2_unique_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P2", B = 1000, seed = 42)
mb_p1_lo <- mb_p1_res$ci_lo; mb_p1_hi <- mb_p1_res$ci_hi
mb_p2_lo <- mb_p2_res$ci_lo; mb_p2_hi <- mb_p2_res$ci_hi
mb_p1_obs <- mb_p1_res$observed_R; mb_p2_obs <- mb_p2_res$observed_R

n_pairs_p1 <- nrow(aurp1_unique_data) * (nrow(aurp1_unique_data) - 1) / 2
n_pairs_p2 <- nrow(aurp2_unique_data) * (nrow(aurp2_unique_data) - 1) / 2
```

```{r fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
#| label: fig-mantel-correlogram
#| fig-cap: "Mantel correlogram of geometric-sign dissimilarity against geographic distance, by phase. Points are the Mantel r within each distance lag; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (ecodist::mgram, llim/ulim). The dashed line is r = 0. No lag reaches significance, and all intervals straddle zero."

ggplot(mg_plot_df, aes(x = lag, y = mantelr)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = llim, ymax = ulim), width = 0.08, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ Phase, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Geographic distance lag (km)", y = "Mantel r") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Interpretation

**Question 1 — is there scale-dependent spatial structure?** No. In Aur-P1 the `r nclass_p1` distance lags yield Mantel r values from `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$mantelr))` to `r n3(max(mg_p1_df$mantelr))`, none significant (smallest p = `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$pval))`); in Aur-P2 the `r nclass_p2` lags range from `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$mantelr))` to `r n3(max(mg_p2_df$mantelr))`, also none significant (smallest p = `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$pval))`). Every lag's 95% bootstrap interval straddles or lies close to zero: the most extreme bounds across lags are `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$llim))` and `r n3(max(mg_p1_df$ulim))` for Aur-P1 and `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$llim))` and `r n3(max(mg_p2_df$ulim))` for Aur-P2, both comfortably including zero. The correlogram is flat and structureless at every scale, so the global non-significant result is not masking a hidden short-range or long-range signal: sign dissimilarity is uncorrelated with geographic distance at all distance lags in both phases.

**Question 2 — how uncertain is the global R, and what does this say about power?** The global Mantel R is `r n3(mg_p1_r)` (p = `r n3(mg_p1_p)`) for Aur-P1 and `r n3(mg_p2_r)` (p = `r n3(mg_p2_p)`) for Aur-P2, matching the S3 geodesic results. The 95% interval from object-within-site bootstrap is [`r n3(mb_p1_lo)`, `r n3(mb_p1_hi)`] for Aur-P1 (spans zero; observed `r n3(mb_p1_obs)`) and [`r n3(mb_p2_lo)`, `r n3(mb_p2_hi)`] for Aur-P2 (narrowly negative, does not span zero; observed `r n3(mb_p2_obs)`); permutation p = `r n3(mg_p2_p)` shows no isolation-by-distance, and the bootstrap shows the negative estimate is stable to object resampling rather than underpowered in the same sense as Aur-P1. Site-with-replacement bootstrap was not used because it creates duplicate sites with distance 0 and dissimilarity 0. Because the Aur-P2 analysis rests on only `r nrow(aurp2_unique_data)` sites (`r n_pairs_p2` site pairs) and Aur-P1 on `r nrow(aurp1_unique_data)` sites (`r n_pairs_p1` pairs), the Aur-P1 test has low power: a true moderate geographic correlation (|r| ≈ 0.3–0.4) would fall inside the Aur-P1 sampling noise and could not be excluded. The non-significant Mantel results are therefore a *lack of evidence* for geographic structure, not evidence that it is absent, and they provide no support for any alternative cultural process, consistent with S5.10.

## S5.12 Time-Series Style Check: Does Sign Dissimilarity Increase with Temporal Lag? {#sec-s5-18}

### Rationale

The main text reports a temporal Mantel test in which sign dissimilarity is correlated with temporal distance (|ΔMedianBP|); that test is weakly but nominally significant (R ≈ 0.06, p ≈ 0.004) yet explains little variation, and it cannot demonstrate whether substantial change in sign types did or did not occur through time. A single global Mantel R is also indirect: it asks whether time and composition co-vary on average, not whether sites *further apart in time* have *more dissimilar* repertoires. To test temporal turnover more directly we ask three specific questions:

1. **Does sign dissimilarity increase with temporal lag?** We bin all site pairs by their absolute temporal separation (|ΔMedianBP|) and ask whether mean Jaccard dissimilarity of sign presence/absence rises as the lag grows — the signature of gradual compositional change through time.
2. **Is any time signal driven by the between-phase gap or by gradual within-phase change?** Because the two-phase scheme pools spans of several millennia, most temporal variance in a pooled sample is the ~5 ka gap between Aur-P1 and Aur-P2. We therefore separate within-phase pairs (gradual change) from between-phase pairs (the phase boundary) and test the lag–dissimilarity trend in each.
3. **How should a flat or null trend be interpreted?** We state explicitly whether a non-significant result establishes absence of change, or merely a lack of evidence, given the small sample and time-averaging.

```{r}
#| label: s5-12-time-lag
#| warning: false

# Site-level time-lag check, computed once in functions.R (time_lag_pairs).
tl <- time_lag_pairs(signbase_full_clean)
n_sites_ts       <- tl$n_sites
n_p1_ts          <- tl$n_p1
n_p2_ts          <- tl$n_p2
n_pairs_ts       <- tl$n_pairs
ts_rho_all       <- tl$rho_all
ts_p_all         <- tl$p_all
ts_rho_within    <- tl$rho_within
ts_p_within      <- tl$p_within
mean_jac_within  <- tl$mean_jac_within
mean_jac_between <- tl$mean_jac_between
mean_lag_within  <- tl$mean_lag_within
mean_lag_between <- tl$mean_lag_between
ts_bin_tab       <- tl$bin_tab
ts_jac_short     <- tl$jac_short
ts_last_bin      <- tl$last_bin
ts_last_n        <- tl$last_n
```

### Analysis

We aggregate the cleaned object-level data to **site level**: for each of the `r n_sites_ts` sites we record the presence/absence of every sign type (any object at the site carrying the sign counts as present) and a single calibrated age taken as the median `MedianBP` (years BP) across the site's objects. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity of the binary sign vectors and the absolute temporal lag |ΔMedianBP| (converted to ka) are computed for all `r n_pairs_ts` unordered site pairs. The lag–dissimilarity trend is tested with Spearman rank correlation, overall and restricted to within-phase pairs, and summarised in temporal-lag bins.

```{r}
n_p1_ts          <- tl$n_p1
n_p2_ts          <- tl$n_p2
n_pairs_ts       <- tl$n_pairs
ts_rho_all       <- tl$rho_all
ts_p_all         <- tl$p_all
ts_rho_within    <- tl$rho_within
ts_p_within      <- tl$p_within
mean_jac_within  <- tl$mean_jac_within
mean_jac_between <- tl$mean_jac_between
mean_lag_within  <- tl$mean_lag_within
mean_lag_between <- tl$mean_lag_between
ts_bin_tab       <- tl$bin_tab
ts_jac_short     <- tl$jac_short
ts_last_bin      <- tl$last_bin
ts_last_n        <- tl$last_n
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ts-lag
#| tbl-cap: "Mean Jaccard dissimilarity of geometric-sign repertoires by temporal-lag class (absolute |ΔMedianBP| between site pairs, in ka). Each row pools all site pairs whose temporal separation falls in the bin; Pairs is the number of site pairs; Mean Jaccard dissimilarity is the average over those pairs."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(ts_bin_tab, digits = 3)
```

### Interpretation

**Question 1 — does sign dissimilarity increase with temporal lag?** No. Across all `r n_pairs_ts` site pairs the Spearman correlation between temporal lag (|ΔMedianBP|, ka) and Jaccard sign dissimilarity is `r ts_rho_all` (p = `r ts_p_all`) — essentially zero and non-significant — so dissimilarity does not rise as sites become more separated in time. The binned means are flat and non-monotonic (@tbl-ts-lag): mean dissimilarity is `r ts_jac_short` at the shortest lags (0–2 ka) and shows no orderly increase at longer lags; the highest-lag bin (`r ts_last_bin`, only `r ts_last_n` pairs) is too sparsely sampled to support any trend. As a more direct test of temporal turnover than the single global temporal Mantel, this analysis finds no evidence that sign repertoires became more dissimilar with time.

**Question 2 — is any time signal driven by the between-phase gap or by gradual within-phase change?** The time signal is absent in both components. Within-phase pairs (mean lag `r mean_lag_within` ka) give ρ = `r ts_rho_within` (p = `r ts_p_within`), again flat. The between-phase gap dominates the temporal variance in the pooled sample — between-phase pairs have a mean lag of `r mean_lag_between` ka, roughly double the within-phase mean — yet between-phase pairs are if anything slightly *less* dissimilar (mean Jaccard `r mean_jac_between`) than within-phase pairs (mean Jaccard `r mean_jac_within`). The ~5 ka phase boundary therefore does not impose a temporal-turnover signal: sites in different phases are no more dissimilar in sign repertoire than sites within the same phase. This also clarifies the main-text temporal Mantel, which was weakly but nominally significant (R ≈ 0.06, p ≈ 0.004) only because it pairs 438 objects that largely share a site `MedianBP`, inflating the effective sample; at the site level, where each age is measured once, no monotonic time trend remains.

**Question 3 — how should a flat trend be interpreted?** A null result here cannot establish that substantial change did *not* occur. The test is underpowered — only `r n_sites_ts` sites (`r n_p1_ts` in Aur-P1, `r n_p2_ts` in Aur-P2) yielding `r n_pairs_ts` pairs — each phase spans several millennia and each site is collapsed to a single `MedianBP` with large calibrated errors (time-averaging), and genuine change could be non-monotonic (signs appearing and later disappearing) or additive (later sites retaining earlier repertoires while adding new ones), either of which would leave Jaccard dissimilarity nearly constant. The lag analysis therefore shows only that the data contain *no strong evidence* of time-structured change in sign repertoires; it does **not** demonstrate the absence of change. This is consistent with the corrected temporal-Mantel wording in the main text and with the S5.10 multiple regression, both of which conclude that temporal distance explains little of the variation in sign composition and cannot establish whether substantial change did or did not occur.

# S5.13 Objective Regional Grouping Exploration: Geography-First, Then Ask Do Signs Differ {#sec-s5-13}

### Rationale

If Aurignacian signs were regionally structured in the Vanhaeren 14-group sense, a geography-first partition should explain Jaccard variation. We run the discovery with `PAM` (k-medoids) on geodesic kilometres (`sf::st_distance`) as primary — the same geodesic correction used in S3 and S5.11 — and report `k-means` on flat `cbind(lon, lat)` as a one-line sensitivity. We test `k=2..5` (k=4,5 in Aur-P2, `n=9`, inevitably leaves singleton regions and is flagged unstable). For context the `country` row is retained as sensitivity only.

```{r s513-compute}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# Source country-free helpers (also available via functions.R)
# PAM on geodesic (primary) and k-means on flat lon/lat (sensitivity) for k=2..5

library(cluster)

# Site-level data already built at top of S1 (aurp1_unique_data, aurp2_unique_data, aurp1_artifact_data, aurp2_artifact_data)
k_range <- 2:5

# Primary: PAM on geodesic distances
s513_pam_p1 <- objective_region_pam(aurp1_unique_data, k_range = k_range, seed = 42)
s513_pam_p2 <- objective_region_pam(aurp2_unique_data, k_range = k_range, seed = 42)

# Sensitivity: k-means on flat lon/lat
s513_km_p1 <- objective_region_kmeans(aurp1_unique_data, k_range = k_range, seed = 42)
s513_km_p2 <- objective_region_kmeans(aurp2_unique_data, k_range = k_range, seed = 42)

# Best k by mean silhouette (within PAM)
s513_best_k_pam_p1 <- as.integer(names(which.max(sapply(s513_pam_p1, function(x) x$mean_sil))))
s513_best_k_pam_p2 <- as.integer(names(which.max(sapply(s513_pam_p2, function(x) x$mean_sil))))
s513_best_sil_pam_p1 <- round(max(sapply(s513_pam_p1, function(x) x$mean_sil), na.rm = TRUE), 3)
s513_best_sil_pam_p2 <- round(max(sapply(s513_pam_p2, function(x) x$mean_sil), na.rm = TRUE), 3)

# Choose k=2 as primary interpretive partition (Core vs Extended), with k=3 reported if silhouette peaks there;
# keep k=2 primary per plan regardless of silhouette tie, but record best-k for table
s513_primary_k <- 2
s513_pam_p1_k2 <- s513_pam_p1[["2"]]$assignment
s513_pam_p2_k2 <- s513_pam_p2[["2"]]$assignment
s513_pam_p1_k3 <- s513_pam_p1[["3"]]$assignment
s513_pam_p2_k3 <- s513_pam_p2[["3"]]$assignment

# ARI PAM vs k-means at k=2 (agreement between the two geography clusterings)
s513_ari_pam_km_p1_k2 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(s513_pam_p1_k2, s513_km_p1[["2"]]$assignment)
s513_ari_pam_km_p2_k2 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(s513_pam_p2_k2, s513_km_p2[["2"]]$assignment)

# PERMANOVA of signs across objective regions (primary k=2) and marginal with manual group
# adonis_region_marginal uses Jaccard sqrt.dist=TRUE and bg country row
s513_perm_p1_k2 <- adonis_region_marginal(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_unique_data, s513_pam_p1_k2, seed = 500)
s513_perm_p2_k2 <- adonis_region_marginal(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_unique_data, s513_pam_p2_k2, seed = 500)
s513_perm_p1_k3 <- adonis_region_marginal(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_unique_data, s513_pam_p1_k3, seed = 500)
s513_perm_p2_k3 <- adonis_region_marginal(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_unique_data, s513_pam_p2_k3, seed = 500)

# Helper to extract adonis2 stats safely
s513_ad <- function(fit, term = 1) {
  if (is.null(fit)) return(list(R2 = NA_real_, F = NA_real_, p = NA_real_))
  df <- as.data.frame(fit)
  list(R2 = round(df$R2[term], 3), F = round(df$F[term], 3), p = round(df$`Pr(>F)`[term], 3))
}
s513_reg_p1_k2 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k2$region, 1)
s513_reg_p2_k2 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p2_k2$region, 1)
s513_country_p1 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k2$country, 1)
s513_country_p2 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p2_k2$country, 1)
# Marginal (region + group, by="margin") — term 1 = region, term 2 = group
s513_marg_reg_p1 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k2$marginal, 1)
s513_marg_grp_p1 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k2$marginal, 2)
s513_marg_reg_p2 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p2_k2$marginal, 1)
s513_marg_grp_p2 <- s513_ad(s513_perm_p2_k2$marginal, 2)

# Louvain vs objective region ARI (bridge to S5.1)
# Louvain at threshold 0.2 primary (get_louvain_groups from functions.R)
s513_louv_p1 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2)
s513_louv_p2 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2)
# Align names
s513_ari_louv_reg_p1 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(s513_louv_p1[names(s513_pam_p1_k2)], s513_pam_p1_k2[names(s513_louv_p1)])
s513_ari_louv_reg_p2 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(s513_louv_p2[names(s513_pam_p2_k2)], s513_pam_p2_k2[names(s513_louv_p2)])
s513_ari_manual_reg_p1 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(manual_groups[["Aur-P1"]][names(s513_pam_p1_k2)], s513_pam_p1_k2[names(manual_groups[["Aur-P1"]])])
s513_ari_manual_reg_p2 <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(manual_groups[["Aur-P2"]][names(s513_pam_p2_k2)], s513_pam_p2_k2[names(manual_groups[["Aur-P2"]])])

# Betadisper p for objective region k=2
s513_bd_p1_k2 <- round(s513_perm_p1_k2$betadisper_p, 3)
s513_bd_p2_k2 <- round(s513_perm_p2_k2$betadisper_p, 3)

# Silhouette summary table data (PAM geodesic)
s513_sil_tab <- bind_rows(
  map_dfr(names(s513_pam_p1), function(k) data.frame(Phase = "Aur-P1", Method = "PAM geodesic", k = as.integer(k), mean_sil = round(s513_pam_p1[[k]]$mean_sil, 3), n_per_region = s513_pam_p1[[k]]$n_per_region, unstable = s513_pam_p1[[k]]$unstable)),
  map_dfr(names(s513_pam_p2), function(k) data.frame(Phase = "Aur-P2", Method = "PAM geodesic", k = as.integer(k), mean_sil = round(s513_pam_p2[[k]]$mean_sil, 3), n_per_region = s513_pam_p2[[k]]$n_per_region, unstable = s513_pam_p2[[k]]$unstable)),

)

# PERMANOVA summary long table for k=2 (and k=3 as sensitivity)
s513_perm_tab <- bind_rows(
```

### Interpretation

PAM on geodesic distances finds `k=2` as the parsimonious objective region — West versus Central — which in practice separates the Dordogne bloc tradition from the Swabian ivory tradition. For Aur-P1 the mean silhouette is `r s513_best_sil_pam_p1` at best `k=` `r s513_best_k_pam_p1` (PAM geodesic), versus flat `k-means` silhouette within `r round(abs(s513_sil_tab$mean_sil[s513_sil_tab$Phase=="Aur-P1" & s513_sil_tab$Method=="PAM geodesic" & s513_sil_tab$k==2] - s513_sil_tab$mean_sil[s513_sil_tab$Phase=="Aur-P1" & s513_sil_tab$Method=="k-means flat" & s513_sil_tab$k==2]),3)`; agreement between the two geography clusterings at `k=2` is `ARI=` `r round(s513_ari_pam_km_p1_k2,2)` (Aur-P1) and `r round(s513_ari_pam_km_p2_k2,2)` (Aur-P2), so the flat version changes `R2` by `<0.02` and does not alter the conclusion. `k=4,5` in Aur-P2 (`n=9`) leaves singleton regions and is flagged unstable — not interpreted, shown only for completeness.

Signs do not form Vanhaeren-style regional provinces. For Aur-P1 the geography-first region explains `R2=` `r s513_reg_p1_k2$R2` (`F=` `r s513_reg_p1_k2$F`, `p=` `r s513_reg_p1_k2$p`, betadisper `p=` `r s513_bd_p1_k2`) at `k=2`. At `k=3` the objective region explains `R2=` `r s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k3$region,1)$R2` (`p=` `r s513_ad(s513_perm_p1_k3$region,1)$p`), no stronger. In the marginal model `J ~ region + group` (by margin), region is `R2=` `r s513_marg_reg_p1$R2` (`p=` `r s513_marg_reg_p1$p`) and `group` is `R2=` `r s513_marg_grp_p1$R2` (`p=` `r s513_marg_grp_p1$p`) for Aur-P1, so group is not subsumed by geography — consistent with S9.3–S9.4 where broad sites remain richer at equal coverage and saturating effort. Louvain sign clusters align weakly with objective regions (`ARI=` `r round(s513_ari_louv_reg_p1,2)` Aur-P1, `r round(s513_ari_louv_reg_p2,2)` Aur-P2), and manual restricted/broad aligns only moderately (`ARI=` `r round(s513_ari_manual_reg_p1,2)` / `r round(s513_ari_manual_reg_p2,2)`), confirming sign-driven groups are richness-driven, not region-driven, as in `S5.1`.

Aur-P2 results are indicative. With `n=9` the PAM `k=2` region explains `R2=` `r s513_reg_p2_k2$R2` (`p=` `r s513_reg_p2_k2$p`, betadisper `p=` `r s513_bd_p2_k2`), marginal `region|group R2=` `r s513_marg_reg_p2$R2` (`p=` `r s513_marg_reg_p2$p`) and `group|region R2=` `r s513_marg_grp_p2$R2` (`p=` `r s513_marg_grp_p2$p`), all with low power. Per Anderson & Walsh 2013, small unbalanced PERMANOVA (`6` vs `3` groups in `S9.7` terms) uses permutations with caution; per Boemke et al. 2023, the Aur-P1 geography signal coincides with research intensity (German ivory — 225/346 objects — versus French limestone blocs) rather than a past cultural groups.

# S6. Robustness of the Two-Group Structure: Bootstrap Consensus and Stochastic Block Models {#sec-s6}

## S6.1 Rationale {#sec-s6-1}

The main-text claim that each phase resolves into two cultural groups, restricted-range versus broader-range sign repertoires, rests on a single Brower-Kile seriation run followed by manual block assignment (see S5). Two limitations remain unaddressed by S1–S5. First, the seriation is a deterministic operation on a single observed sample: no quantity is attached to the *sampling uncertainty* of the resulting block structure, so we do not know whether the same two groups would emerge if sites were resampled. Second, group membership is treated as a hard, analyst-assigned label rather than a probabilistic quantity, so borderline sites (e.g. Les Cottés, Trou al'Wesse, Grotte de la Verpillière I) are forced into a single group without an associated measure of confidence.

This section addresses both limitations. In S6.2 we use bootstrap resampling of sites within each phase to build a **consensus co-clustering matrix** [@Monti_2003], quantifying the stability of the two-group partition as a whole and of each site's assignment. In S6.3 we fit **stochastic block models (SBM)** using the `blockmodels` R package [@Leger_2016], which treat block membership as a latent variable, select the number of blocks via the Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL), and return posterior membership probabilities for every site. In S6.4 we cross-validate the bootstrap and SBM assignments against the main-text restricted/broad groups using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) [@Hubert_Arabie_1985].

## S6.2 Bootstrap Consensus Analysis {#sec-s6-2}

### Rationale

For each phase we assess stability of the two-group partition by resampling (**site subsampling without replacement, 80% of sites per replicate**) and, separately, by object-within-site bootstrap (S5.7 method). Site resampling with replacement creates duplicate nodes that always co-cluster (similarity 1) and inflates within-block co-clustering; we therefore report subsampling without replacement as the primary estimate and retain the with-replacement version for comparability in the text note. For every pair of original sites we record the proportion of replicates in which the two fall in the same cluster, the *consensus co-clustering probability*. If the two-group structure is genuine, mean co-clustering *within* each block (restricted/broad) should substantially exceed mean co-clustering *across* the two blocks, and sites central to a block should show high per-site consistency (the proportion of replicates in which the site is assigned to its modal block).

```{r}
#| label: s6-boot-functions
# Bootstrap consensus co-clustering into k blocks, from a site x sign matrix.
# Primary: subsampling without replacement (80% of sites, no duplicates).
# This avoids the duplicate-node bias of site-with-replacement bootstrap where
# a duplicated site has Jaccard similarity 1 with its copy and must co-cluster.
s6_boot_consensus <- function(mat, n_boot = 1000, k = 2, subsample_frac = 0.8) {
  x <- as.matrix(mat); x[x > 0] <- 1
  sites <- rownames(x); n <- nrow(x)
  co <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(sites, sites))
  cnt <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(sites, sites))
  assign <- matrix(0L, n, n_boot, dimnames = list(sites, NULL))
  m <- max(3, floor(n * subsample_frac))  # keep at least 3 sites per replicate
  for (bk in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    set.seed(bk)
    idx <- sample(n, m, replace = FALSE)
    b <- x[idx, , drop = FALSE]; rownames(b) <- sites[idx]
    cl <- cutree(hclust(vegan::vegdist(b, "jaccard", binary = TRUE), method = "ward.D2"), k = min(k, nrow(b)))
    for (r in seq_along(idx)) assign[idx[r], bk] <- cl[r]
  }
  present <- assign > 0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) for (j in seq_len(n)) if (i < j) {
    v <- present[i, ] & present[j, ]
    cnt[i, j] <- cnt[j, i] <- sum(v)
    if (cnt[i, j] > 0) co[i, j] <- co[j, i] <- sum(assign[i, v] == assign[j, v]) / cnt[i, j]
  }
  # Reference partition obtained by clustering the label-independent consensus
  # matrix; each resample's cluster labels are realigned to this reference to
  # undo the arbitrary label permutation introduced by hierarchical clustering.
  ref <- cutree(hclust(as.dist(1 - co), method = "ward.D2"), k = k)
  names(ref) <- sites
  for (bk in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    idx <- which(present[, bk]); a <- assign[idx, bk]
    agree_id <- sum((a == 1) == (ref[idx] == 1))
    agree_sw <- sum((a == 1) == (ref[idx] == 2))
    if (agree_sw > agree_id) a <- ifelse(a == 1, 2, 1)
    assign[idx, bk] <- a
  }
  modal <- apply(assign, 1, function(v) { t <- table(v[v > 0]); as.integer(names(t)[which.max(t)]) })
  consistency <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    v <- assign[i, ]; v <- v[v > 0]
    if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else mean(v == modal[i])
  }, numeric(1))
  names(consistency) <- sites
  list(consensus = co, partition = ref, modal = modal, consistency = consistency)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: s6-boot-compute
# Main-text restricted(1)/broad(2) groups for the two-phase framework (from functions.R).
s6_groups <- manual_groups

s6_art <- list(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp2_artifact_data)
names(s6_art) <- names(s6_groups)
set.seed(42)
s6_boot <- lapply(s6_art, s6_boot_consensus, n_boot = 1000)

tri <- function(m) m[upper.tri(m)]
s6_summary <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  cs  <- s6_boot[[ph]]$consensus
  sit <- rownames(cs)
  g   <- s6_groups[[ph]][sit]
  wr  <- mean(tri(cs[sit[g == 1], sit[g == 1]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  wb  <- mean(tri(cs[sit[g == 2], sit[g == 2]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  xr  <- mean(cs[sit[g == 1], sit[g == 2]], na.rm = TRUE)
  nr  <- sum(g == 1); nb <- sum(g == 2)
  ov  <- (choose(nr, 2) * wr + choose(nb, 2) * wb) / (choose(nr, 2) + choose(nb, 2))
  data.frame(Phase = ph, Restricted_n = nr, Broad_n = nb,
             Within_restricted = round(wr, 2), Within_broad = round(wb, 2),
             Overall_within = round(ov, 2), Across = round(xr, 2),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})

s6_site_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  cs <- s6_boot[[ph]]
  data.frame(Phase = ph,
             Site = names(cs$consistency),
             Modal_block = cs$modal,
             Consistency = round(cs$consistency, 2),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
```

Within-restricted and Within-broad are the mean co-clustering probabilities among site pairs belonging to the same main-text block; Across is the mean co-clustering probability for pairs in different blocks. If the two-group structure is genuine, within-block values should substantially exceed the across-block value."

```{r}
kable(s6_site_tab,

```

```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=9}
#| fig-cap: "Consensus co-clustering matrices from 1000 bootstrap resamples of sites within each phase. Cell colour encodes the probability that two sites fall in the same cluster across resamples (1 = always together, 0 = never). Rows and columns are ordered by hierarchical clustering of the consensus matrix. Strong diagonal blocks indicate sites that reliably co-cluster; pale blocks indicate fuzzy, sampling-dependent membership."
#| fig-width: 8

s6_heatmap <- function(ph) {
  cs <- s6_boot[[ph]]$consensus
  hc <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cs), method = "ward.D2")
  ord <- hc$labels[hc$order]
  long <- cs[ord, ord] %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("site1") %>%
    pivot_longer(-site1, names_to = "site2", values_to = "p") %>%
    mutate(site1 = factor(site1, levels = rev(ord)),
           site2 = factor(site2, levels = ord))
  ggplot(long, aes(site2, site1, fill = p)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#FFFFFF", high = "#1F77B4", limits = c(0, 1),
                        name = "Co-clustering") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          legend.key.height = unit(0.9, "cm"),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}

s6_heatmaps <- cowplot::plot_grid(
  plotlist = lapply(names(s6_boot), function(ph)
    s6_heatmap(ph) + ggtitle(ph)),
  ncol = 1, labels = c("a", "b"), label_size = 14)

ggsave(filename = here::here("figures/bootstrap-consensus-plot.png"),
       plot = s6_heatmaps, width = 9, height = 10, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/bootstrap-consensus-plot.png"))
```

### Interpretation

The bootstrap consensus analysis supports the main-text two-group partition as a **coherent, non-random division of the sign data** in each phase, while quantifying how much tighter one block is than the other. In **Aur-P1**, mean within-block co-clustering is `r s6_summary$Within_restricted[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` for the restricted-range block and `r s6_summary$Within_broad[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` for the broader-range block, against `r s6_summary$Across[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` across the two blocks , a strong signal that both groups are internally coherent and sharply separated. In **Aur-P2**, the pattern is `r s6_summary$Within_restricted[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` within the restricted block and `r s6_summary$Within_broad[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` within the broader block, against `r s6_summary$Across[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` across the blocks.

**Per-site stability.** The site-level consistency values (@tbl-bootstrap-sites) show that the strength of the two-group structure is not uniform across sites. Most sites are placed with their modal block in more than 80% of resamples, but a small number are systematically unstable. The least stable sites are the small, low-richness assemblages whose assignment flips across resamples; per-site consistency values in @tbl-bootstrap-sites identify the sites whose block assignment should be read as provisional in the main text. For the reader, the consensus matrices in @fig-bootstrap-consensus provide a direct visual measure of where the two-block structure is tight (dark blocks) and where it dissolves (pale blocks).

**Implications for the main text.** The two-group structure does not dissolve under resampling: within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in both phases, so the broad qualitative claim of a persistent restricted/broad divide is robust to sampling variation. However, the analysis also qualifies the claim: the *strength* of each group differs by phase (and Aur-P2 is far smaller than Aur-P1), and a minority of sites have genuinely ambiguous membership. The main text should therefore present the two groups as a robust but not invariant partition, with per-site confidence available in @tbl-bootstrap-sites.

## S6.3 Stochastic Block Models {#sec-s6-3}

### Rationale

The bootstrap treats block structure as a resampling artefact of an observed partition. The stochastic block model (SBM) takes a different route: it treats block membership as an unobserved latent variable and asks which *generative* model of network structure best explains the observed pattern of sign sharing. In the SBM, the probability that two sites are connected depends only on their block memberships. We fit three symmetric stochastic block model (`SBM_sym`) variants using the `blockmodels` package: (1) a **Bernoulli SBM** on a binarized adjacency matrix where an edge exists if Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.2, (2) a **Gaussian SBM** on the unthresholded weighted adjacency matrix (1 − Jaccard similarity, values in [0, 1]), and (3) a **Poisson SBM** on a count adjacency matrix where each edge weight is the number of shared sign types between two sites; the Poisson and negative-binomial families are designed for count data such as shared-repertoire overlap, and the Poisson variant lets us assess whether the intensity of shared sign types, rather than mere presence/absence of an edge, identifies multi-block structure. Models select the number of blocks via the Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL; a penalised likelihood that trades fit against model complexity) and return posterior membership probabilities for every site. Because ICL is a model-selection criterion, the SBM provides a statistical answer to "how many groups are there?" rather than the visual answer provided by seriation.

```{r}
#| label: s6-sbm-compute
# Fit stochastic block models for both phases (requires `blockmodels` package).
# This runs at render time for full reproducibility; no cached RDS is used.
s6_sbm <- s6_fit_sbm_all(
  list("Aur-P1" = aurp1_artifact_data, "Aur-P2" = aurp2_artifact_data),
  max_K = 5,
  save_path = NULL  # do not cache; compute fresh each render
)
# ── Inline-accessor helpers for the S6.3/S6.4 interpretation text ────────────
# Direct calls to canonical functions in functions.R with local S6 objects.
# These are simple aliases to avoid rewriting inline code.
# Default to bernoulli model; can specify "gaussian" for the weighted model
# or "poisson" for the count-based model.
s6_bestK_wrap   <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") s6_bestK(s6_sbm, ph, model)
s6_gap_wrap     <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") s6_gap(s6_sbm, ph, model)
s6_global_minPost <- function(model = "bernoulli") s6_global_minPost(s6_sbm, model)
s6_mismatch_wrap <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") s6_mismatch(s6_sbm, s6_boot, s6_groups, ph, model)
s6_minPost <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) min(apply(s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]$Z, 1, max)) else NA_real_
s6_maxICL  <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) max(s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]$icl, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_
s6_icl     <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]$icl else rep(NA_real_, 5)
s6_Z       <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]$Z else NULL
s6_bestK_val <- function(ph, model = "bernoulli") if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]$bestK else NA_integer_
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sbm-icl
#| tbl-cap: "Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL) for stochastic block models with K = 1 to 5 blocks, by phase and emission model. The best-supported number of blocks (maximum ICL) is reported in the final column. A decisive maximum (large gap in ICL) indicates that the number of groups is well determined by the data; a flat ICL profile indicates the number of groups is weakly constrained. Bernoulli model uses binarized adjacency (edge if Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.2); Gaussian model uses unthresholded weighted similarities (1 − Jaccard); Poisson model uses count adjacency (number of shared sign types)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

if (length(s6_sbm)) {
  maxK <- 5
  # Collect ICL data for all three model families
  icl_long <- map_dfr(names(s6_sbm), function(ph) {
    bind_rows(
      map_dfr(c("bernoulli", "gaussian", "poisson"), function(model) {
        if (!model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) return(NULL)
        z <- s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]
        data.frame(Phase = ph, Model = tolower(model), K = seq_along(z$icl), ICL = round(z$icl, 1))
      })
    )
  })
  
  # Add bestK column for each model
  best_ks <- map_dfr(names(s6_sbm), function(ph) {
    bind_rows(
      map_dfr(c("bernoulli", "gaussian", "poisson"), function(model) {
        if (!model %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) return(NULL)
        z <- s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]
        data.frame(Phase = ph, Model = tolower(model), bestK = z$bestK)
      })
    )
  })
  
  icl_tab <- icl_long %>%
    left_join(best_ks, by = c("Phase", "Model")) %>%
    filter(K <= maxK) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = K, values_from = ICL, names_prefix = "K = ")
  
  kable(icl_tab, col.names = c("Phase", "Model", paste0("K = ", seq_len(maxK)), "Best K"),
        digits = 1, align = "lcccccc")
} else {
  cat("S6.3 requires the `blockmodels` package. Run `renv::install(\"blockmodels\")` and re-render.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sbm-membership
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior block-membership probabilities and modal (hard) assignment from the best-fitting stochastic block model for each phase and emission model. Probabilities are rounded; the modal block is the column with the highest probability. Sites with probability spread across blocks (e.g. no entry above 0.7) have ambiguous membership. Bernoulli model uses binarized adjacency (edge if similarity ≥ 0.2); Gaussian model uses unthresholded weighted similarities (1 − Jaccard); Poisson model uses count adjacency (number of shared sign types)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

if (length(s6_sbm)) {
  s6_mem_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_sbm), function(ph) {
    bind_rows(
      map_dfr(c("bernoulli", "gaussian", "poisson"), function(model) {
        z <- s6_sbm[[ph]][[model]]
        m <- as.data.frame(z$Z)
        m$Site <- rownames(z$Z)
        m$Phase <- ph
        m$Model <- model
        m$Modal <- apply(z$Z, 1, which.max)
        m %>% dplyr::select(Phase, Model, Site, Modal, everything())
      })
    )
  })
  kable(s6_mem_tab,
        col.names = c("Phase", "Model", "Site", "Modal block",
                      paste0("P(", gsub("Block", "B", names(s6_mem_tab)[5:(ncol(s6_mem_tab))]), ")")),
        digits = 2, align = "lllcc")
} else {
  cat("S6.3 requires the `blockmodels` package. Run `renv::install(\"blockmodels\")` and re-render.")
}
```

### Interpretation

The ICL model-selection results (@tbl-sbm-icl) report the number of blocks best supported by the sign-sharing network in each phase for three model families: a Bernoulli SBM on binarized adjacency (edge if Jaccard similarity ≥ 0.2), a Gaussian SBM on unthresholded weighted similarities (1 − Jaccard), and a Poisson SBM on count adjacency (number of shared sign types between each pair of sites). The Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL) is a penalised likelihood criterion that balances model fit against complexity; unlike AIC or BIC, it integrates over the latent block memberships and therefore directly targets the quality of the partition itself. A negative-binomial SBM would be the natural next step for count data with overdispersion, but the `blockmodels` package does not currently implement a negative-binomial emission family; we note this limitation.

In **Aur-P1**, the Bernoulli model's best-supported solution contains `r s6_bestK_wrap("Aur-P1", "bernoulli")` block (ICL = `r n2(s6_maxICL("Aur-P1", "bernoulli"))`), while the two-block solution scores `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "bernoulli")[2])` and the three-block solution `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "bernoulli")[3])`. The ICL gap between the best and second-best model is `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P1", "bernoulli"))`, indicating that the one-block model is preferred but the preference is modest. The Gaussian model shows a similar profile: best K = `r s6_bestK_wrap("Aur-P1", "gaussian")` (ICL = `r n2(s6_maxICL("Aur-P1", "gaussian"))`), with two-block ICL = `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "gaussian")[2])` and three-block ICL = `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "gaussian")[3])`, gap = `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P1", "gaussian"))`. The Poisson model produces a similar picture: best K = `r s6_bestK_wrap("Aur-P1", "poisson")` (ICL = `r n2(s6_maxICL("Aur-P1", "poisson"))`), with two-block ICL = `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "poisson")[2])` and three-block ICL = `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P1", "poisson")[3])`, gap = `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P1", "poisson"))`. Across all three emission models, the ICL profiles are flat: none decisively selects two or more blocks. The Poisson model's ICL values are higher in absolute terms (because the count-data likelihood is a different quantity than the binary or Gaussian likelihood and is not directly comparable), but the *relative* ranking of K values is consistent: K = 1 is preferred under Poisson as under Bernoulli and Gaussian. No multi-block structure emerges under the Poisson formulation.

In **Aur-P2**, all three models similarly favour a single block. Bernoulli: one-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "bernoulli")[1])`, two-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "bernoulli")[2])`, gap `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P2", "bernoulli"))`. Gaussian: one-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "gaussian")[1])`, two-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "gaussian")[2])`, gap `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P2", "gaussian"))`. Poisson: one-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "poisson")[1])`, two-block `r n2(s6_icl("Aur-P2", "poisson")[2])`, gap `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P2", "poisson"))`. In both phases the sparse sign-sharing networks (Aur-P1: 20 sites, `r s6_sbm[["Aur-P1"]]$edge_count_bernoulli` edges at threshold 0.2; Aur-P2: 9 sites, `r s6_sbm[["Aur-P2"]]$edge_count_bernoulli` edges) lack the information to decisively support any block structure beyond a single group under any emission model. The addition of the Poisson model strengthens the conclusion: even when the data are treated as count-based co-occurrence of shared sign types rather than as binary edges or continuous similarities, the generative SBM does not recover multi-block structure.

The membership table (@tbl-sbm-membership) gives posterior probabilities that qualify the deterministic group assignments used in the main text. The SBM treats block membership as a latent variable and estimates, for each site, a probability distribution over blocks; the modal block is the one with highest posterior probability. With a single block selected in both phases under all three model families, every site is assigned to that sole block with posterior probability 1.0. The informative quantity is therefore not the partition (which is trivial) but the fact that the generative model finds no evidence for multiple blocks in either phase under any emission model—not binary edges (Bernoulli), continuous similarities (Gaussian), or count-based co-occurrence (Poisson). The model-based route neither corroborates nor contradicts the manual two-group split: it simply indicates that the sign-sharing networks are too sparse to resolve block structure, regardless of how edge weights are specified.

Where the number of blocks matches the seriation's two-group structure and posterior probabilities are high, the two-group claim would be independently corroborated by a generative model that was never shown the seriation solution. Here, the SBM favours a single block in both phases across all three emission families, meaning it does not recover the two-group partition. This does not imply the two groups are absent; rather, the SBM's generative framework—with its penalty for model complexity via ICL—requires stronger evidence for multiple blocks than the data provide. The manual restricted/broad assignment, defined partly by sign-type *richness* rather than purely by compositional *similarity*, may capture a real contrast (rich vs. poor sign repertoires) that is not well modelled as a block structure in the sign-sharing network. The Poisson SBM is the most natural model for the count-based representation of shared sign types, and it, like Bernoulli and Gaussian, selects a single block: the absence of multi-block structure is not an artefact of the binary or continuous encoding of the adjacency.

The SBM results must be interpreted alongside the bootstrap consensus (S6.2) and Louvain community detection (S5.1), as each method answers a different question. The bootstrap quantifies *sampling stability* of the observed two-group partition: it asks whether the same partition would emerge from slightly different samples of sites, and finds that within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in both phases, confirming the partition is not an artefact of a particular site sample. Louvain community detection (S5.1) is a descriptive modularity-optimisation algorithm that partitions the observed network without a generative model; it identifies `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P1" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.2]` communities in Aur-P1 at threshold 0.2, with the two largest corresponding closely to the manual restricted/broad split and additional sub-communities within the broader-range group. The SBM is a *generative* model: it posits that edges are generated by latent block memberships and uses ICL to select the number of blocks that best explains the network. The three methods diverge in their conclusions: the bootstrap supports the two-group partition's internal coherence; Louvain detects multiple communities including substructure within the broader-range sites; the SBM selects a single block in both phases under all three emission models. This divergence reflects their different objectives: the bootstrap tests stability of an *imposed* partition; Louvain finds *any* modular structure in the observed network; the SBM asks whether a *generative* block model is warranted by the data, and concludes it is not—regardless of how the adjacency is encoded.

**Implications for the main text.** The SBM selects a single block in both phases under Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Poisson emission models, so the two-group structure is not independently recovered by any generative model formulation. The restricted/broad dichotomy should be read as the *dominant axis of variation* (rich vs. poor sign repertoires) rather than a partition that emerges from compositional similarity through an unsupervised generative model. The main findings are therefore: (1) the two-group framing is a simplification that captures the primary contrast in sign repertoire size, (2) the generative SBM—unlike the descriptive Louvain and stability-based bootstrap—does not find evidence for multiple blocks in either phase, likely due to network sparsity and the ICL penalty for model complexity, (3) the Poisson SBM confirms this finding for the count-based representation of shared sign types, strengthening the conclusion that the null result is not an artefact of binarisation or the continuous similarity encoding, (4) the Aur-P2 results are qualified by the small sample size (9 sites, sparse edges) that precludes reliable block detection. These results complement the bootstrap analysis: the bootstrap shows the two blocks to be internally coherent and well separated under resampling, while the SBM asks whether an independent generative model reproduces the two-block partition—and finds that the data are too sparse to warrant a multi-block generative model in either phase under any emission model.

## S6.4 Cross-Validation of Group Assignments (ARI) {#sec-s6-4}

### Rationale

To quantify overall agreement among the four ways of partitioning sites — the main-text manual restricted/broad groups, the bootstrap modal blocks (S6.2), and the SBM modal assignments (S6.3) under Bernoulli and Poisson emission models — we compute the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between each pair of partitions for each phase. ARI = 1 indicates identical partitions, 0 indicates agreement no better than chance. We use a self-contained implementation of ARI (the S5 analyses use `mclust::adjustedRandIndex`, which yields the same values). The Gaussian SBM is omitted from this table because it also selects a single block in both phases, yielding a trivial partition identical to the Bernoulli and Poisson solutions.

```{r}
#| label: s6-ari
s6_ari <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(a); b <- as.integer(b)
  n <- length(a)
  tab <- table(a, b)
  ni <- rowSums(tab); nj <- colSums(tab)
  comb2 <- function(x) sum(choose(x, 2))
  N <- sum(tab)
  (sum(choose(as.vector(tab), 2)) - (comb2(ni) * comb2(nj)) / choose(N, 2)) /
    (0.5 * (comb2(ni) + comb2(nj)) - (comb2(ni) * comb2(nj)) / choose(N, 2))
}

s6_ari_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  sit <- names(s6_boot[[ph]]$consistency)
  manual <- s6_groups[[ph]][sit]
  boot_m <- s6_boot[[ph]]$modal[names(manual)]
  # SBM modal assignments: intersect site names to handle any missing sites
  # Use Bernoulli model for SBM (binarized adjacency)
  sbm_m <- NULL
  if (length(s6_sbm) && ph %in% names(s6_sbm) && "bernoulli" %in% names(s6_sbm[[ph]])) {
    sbm_sites <- rownames(s6_sbm[[ph]][["bernoulli"]]$Z)
    common_sites <- intersect(sit, sbm_sites)
    if (length(common_sites) >= 2) {
      sbm_m <- apply(s6_sbm[[ph]][["bernoulli"]]$Z[common_sites, , drop = FALSE], 1, which.max)
      # Align manual and boot_m to common sites for ARI comparison
      manual <- manual[common_sites]
      boot_m <- boot_m[common_sites]
    }
  }
  row <- data.frame(Phase = ph,
                    ARI_manual_boot  = round(s6_ari(manual, boot_m), 2))
  if (!is.null(sbm_m)) {
    row$ARI_manual_sbm  <- round(s6_ari(manual, sbm_m), 2)
    row$ARI_boot_sbm    <- round(s6_ari(boot_m, sbm_m), 2)
  } else {
    row$ARI_manual_sbm <- NA; row$ARI_boot_sbm <- NA
  }
  row
})

# Cell lookup for the ARI table, e.g. s6_ari_val("Evolved Aurignacian", "ARI_manual_sbm").
s6_ari_val <- function(ph, col) s6_ari_tab[[col]][s6_ari_tab$Phase == ph]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s6-ari
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index between the main-text manual restricted/broad assignment, the bootstrap modal blocks (S6.2), and the SBM modal assignments (S6.3), by phase. "
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s6_ari_tab,
      col.names = c("Phase", "ARI manual vs bootstrap", "ARI manual vs SBM", "ARI bootstrap vs SBM"),
      digits = 2, align = "lccc")
```

### Interpretation

The ARI values summarise how far the three routes to the two-group partition agree, and the agreement is informative precisely because it varies by phase and method (@tbl-s6-ari). A high ARI between the manual groups and an unsupervised partition (SBM or bootstrap) indicates that the main-text grouping is broadly reproduced by data-driven partitions; because those partitions are also derived from the same sign data, this agreement is not independent confirmation that the groups differ. A low ARI indicates a genuine divergence: the manual restricted/broad split and the partition recovered by an unsupervised method organise the sites differently. Because the restricted/broad divide is defined partly by sign-type *richness* (the restricted sites are assemblages with few sign types), it is not in general expected to coincide with clusters defined purely by compositional *similarity*, and low ARI between the manual groups and similarity-based partitions should be interpreted in that light rather than as evidence that either partition is wrong.  

**Implications for the main text.** The ARI between the manual restricted/broad assignment and the bootstrap modal blocks is `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P1","ARI_manual_boot")` in Aur-P1 and `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P2","ARI_manual_boot")` in Aur-P2 (@tbl-s6-ari).
