In Aur-P1 this means the bootstrap recovers the manual two-group partition exactly: the main-text claim that Aur-P1 resolves into restricted-range and broader-range sign-repertoire groups is robustly supported and is not an artefact of the particular site sample. In Aur-P2 the value of `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P2","ARI_manual_boot")` means the bootstrap recovers the manual partition only weakly, so the main-text Aur-P2 two-group claim rests on a markedly weaker evidence base than the Aur-P1 claim and is best treated as a provisional pattern. The SBM columns are undefined for the Bernoulli model (and Gaussian model) because both select a single block in both phases (S6.3), yielding a trivial partition where all sites share the same block assignment; consequently no meaningful two-group ARI can be computed. The SBM's result that the sign-sharing networks are too sparse to support more than one block is consistent with the bootstrap finding that the Aur-P2 partition is the less robust of the two. These agreements are among partitions derived from the same sign data, so they establish the *recovery and stability* of the two-group structure rather than independent confirmation that the groups differ — that question is addressed in @sec-s6-6.

## S6.5 Summary of Implications {#sec-s6-5}

Taken together, S6 provides three converging but graded lines of evidence for the main-text two-group claim. (1) **Resampling stability**: within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in every phase (@fig-bootstrap-consensus, @tbl-bootstrap-summary), so the partition does not arise from a particular sample of sites. (2) **Model selection**: the SBM attaches posterior probabilities to each site's membership (@tbl-sbm-membership) and reports the number of blocks best supported by the sign-sharing network in each phase for two emission models—Bernoulli (binarized adjacency) and Gaussian (unthresholded similarities) (@tbl-sbm-icl). Both model families select a single block in both Aur-P1 and Aur-P2, indicating that the sparse sign-sharing networks do not provide sufficient evidence for a multi-block generative model—this is a null result for block structure, not a contradiction of the two-group contrast. (3) **Cross-validation**: ARI between the manual, bootstrap, and SBM partitions quantifies their agreement (@tbl-s6-ari). The three routes are mutually informative but not redundant: the bootstrap shows the two blocks to be internally coherent and well separated under resampling; the SBM finds the data too sparse to warrant a multi-block generative model under either emission model; and the manual assignment captures the dominant axis of variation in sign repertoire size. The circularity of the main-text PerMANOVA itself is addressed separately in @sec-s6-6, which validates the grouping on withheld data rather than on the data used to define it.

# S6.6 Circularity-Breaking Validation of the Restricted/Broad Group Difference {#sec-s6-6}

## Rationale

The restricted/broad groups were defined from the same sign-composition data that the main-text PerMANOVA later tests, so its p-values cannot be read as *independent* confirmation that the groups differ. Louvain, bootstrap and stochastic block model analyses (S5, S6) also operate on that same underlying dataset, so they do not remove the circularity either. To address this directly we implement three complementary methods that break the circularity, each following a distinct validation strategy:

- **(A) Maximally-selected achieved-significance test:** the optimal two-group split is re-derived from *randomised* data in every permutation, and the observed optimal split is compared against that null. This controls for the fact that the grouping was itself optimised to maximise separation.
- **(B) Cross-validation on withheld data:** the grouping is validated on data that did not contribute to its definition. We do this at two levels — (i) site level: leave-one-site-out k-nearest-neighbour classification, where each held-out site is predicted from the other sites only; and (ii) object level: the two-group rule is learned from one random half of each site's objects and tested, by PerMANOVA, on the *other* half.
- **(C) Group-free gradient PerMANOVA:** instead of asserting discrete groups, sign composition is regressed on continuous predictors that are independent of the distance matrix (log object count and site richness). Regressing the Jaccard dissimilarity on its own first PCoA axis is tautological and not used here; a valid gradient test must use a predictor not derived from the same matrix.

All three are exploratory companions to, not replacements for, the main-text PerMANOVA, which we present as descriptive rather than confirmatory, framed as selective inference on data-adaptive groups [@Gao_Bien_Witten_2022; @Neufeld_2024]. P-values from 100 dependent splits are reported as median p, proportion significant, and Brown's method for dependent p-values [@Brown_1975; @Poole_2016], not Fisher's method which assumes independence. Jaccard results are shown alongside Simpson turnover (which removes the richness-nestedness component) because the richness median split is tautological under Jaccard.

```{r}
# ── S6.6 computation: circularity-breaking validation ────────────────────────
# Align manual group labels to the site x sign artifact matrices (rownames = sites).
aurp1_grp <- aurp1_unique_data$group[match(rownames(aurp1_artifact_data),
                                           aurp1_unique_data$site_name)]
aurp2_grp <- aurp2_unique_data$group[match(rownames(aurp2_artifact_data),
                                           aurp2_unique_data$site_name)]

sign_cols_all <- intersect(colnames(aurp1_artifact_data), colnames(aurp2_artifact_data))

# (A) Maximally-selected achieved-significance test
s6_6_bestP1 <- best_split_permtest(aurp1_artifact_data, group = aurp1_grp, B = 999, seed = 1,
                                   null_type = "curveball")
s6_6_bestP2 <- best_split_permtest(aurp2_artifact_data, group = aurp2_grp, B = 999, seed = 1,
                                   null_type = "curveball")

# (B-i) Site-level leave-one-out cross-validated group recovery
s6_6_cvP1 <- cv_group_accuracy(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_grp, k = 1, B = 999, seed = 1)
s6_6_cvP2 <- cv_group_accuracy(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_grp, k = 1, B = 999, seed = 1)

# (B-ii) Object-level holdout: groups from one half of objects, test on the other
s6_6_objP1 <- cv_permanova_objectsplit(
  signbase_full_clean %>% filter(phase2 == "Aur-P1") %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, all_of(sign_cols_all)),
  sign_cols_all, B_rep = 100, B_perm = 499, seed = 1)
s6_6_objP2 <- cv_permanova_objectsplit(
  signbase_full_clean %>% filter(phase2 == "Aur-P2") %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, all_of(sign_cols_all)),
  sign_cols_all, B_rep = 100, B_perm = 499, seed = 1)

# (C) Group-free gradient PerMANOVA on predictors independent of D
# Use log object count and richness, not the PCoA axis of the same D
s6_6_D1 <- vegdist(aurp1_artifact_data, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
s6_6_D2 <- vegdist(aurp2_artifact_data, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
gradP1_pred <- gradient_predictors(aurp1_unique_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P1")
gradP2_pred <- gradient_predictors(aurp2_unique_data, signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P2")
s6_6_gradP1_log <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D1, gradP1_pred$log_nobjects)
s6_6_gradP2_log <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D2, gradP2_pred$log_nobjects)
s6_6_gradP1_rich <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D1, gradP1_pred$richness)
s6_6_gradP2_rich <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D2, gradP2_pred$richness)
# Keep PCoA-axis result only to show tautology, not as validation
s6_6_gradP1_pcoa <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D1, cmdscale(s6_6_D1, k = 1)[, 1])
s6_6_gradP2_pcoa <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D2, cmdscale(s6_6_D2, k = 1)[, 1])

# Summary table
s6_6_tab <- data.frame(
  Method = c("A: Maximally-selected split (P1)", "A: Maximally-selected split (P2)",
             "B-i: LOOCV site classification (P1)", "B-i: LOOCV site classification (P2)",
             "B-ii: Object-half holdout Jaccard (P1)", "B-ii: Object-half holdout Jaccard (P2)",
             "B-ii: Object-half holdout Simpson (P1)", "B-ii: Object-half holdout Simpson (P2)",
             "C: Gradient log(nobjects) (P1)", "C: Gradient log(nobjects) (P2)",
             "C: Gradient richness (P1)", "C: Gradient richness (P2)"),
  Statistic = c(round(s6_6_bestP1$observed_best_F, 2), round(s6_6_bestP2$observed_best_F, 2),
                 paste0(round(s6_6_cvP1$accuracy, 2), " acc"), paste0(round(s6_6_cvP2$accuracy, 2), " acc"),
                 paste0(round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant * 100), "% sig, med p=", round(s6_6_objP1$median_p, 3)),
                 paste0(round(s6_6_objP2$prop_significant * 100), "% sig, med p=", round(s6_6_objP2$median_p, 3)),
                 paste0(round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant_sim * 100), "% sig, med p=", round(s6_6_objP1$median_p_sim, 3)),
                 paste0(round(s6_6_objP2$prop_significant_sim * 100), "% sig, med p=", round(s6_6_objP2$median_p_sim, 3)),
                 paste0("R2=", s6_6_gradP1_log$R2), paste0("R2=", s6_6_gradP2_log$R2),
                 paste0("R2=", s6_6_gradP1_rich$R2), paste0("R2=", s6_6_gradP2_rich$R2)),
  `p-value` = c(round(s6_6_bestP1$p_value, 3), round(s6_6_bestP2$p_value, 3),
                 round(s6_6_cvP1$p_value, 3), round(s6_6_cvP2$p_value, 3),
                 paste0("Brown ", format.pval(s6_6_objP1$browns_p, digits=3), " (Fisher ", format.pval(s6_6_objP1$combined_p, digits=3), ")"),
                 paste0("Brown ", format.pval(s6_6_objP2$browns_p, digits=3), " (Fisher ", format.pval(s6_6_objP2$combined_p, digits=3), ")"),
                 paste0("Brown ", format.pval(s6_6_objP1$browns_p_sim, digits=3)),
                 paste0("Brown ", format.pval(s6_6_objP2$browns_p_sim, digits=3)),
                 s6_6_gradP1_log$p, s6_6_gradP2_log$p,
                 s6_6_gradP1_rich$p, s6_6_gradP2_rich$p))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s6-6-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Circularity-breaking validation of the restricted/broad group difference. Method A re-derives the optimal two-group split from randomised data (Curveball null). Method B validates on withheld data: (B-i) site-level leave-one-out k-NN classification (label smoothness check, not independent validation; permutation p) and (B-ii) object-level holdout where groups are defined from one random half of each site's objects and tested on the other half. B-ii reports median p, proportion significant, and Brown's method for dependent p-values with Fisher p for reference; Jaccard and Simpson turnover versions are shown because the richness median split is tautological under Jaccard. Method C is group-free gradient PerMANOVA on predictors independent of the distance matrix (log object count, richness); PCoA-axis result is not used as validation. A significant B-ii Brown p indicates recoverability from independent objects."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
kable(s6_6_tab, digits = 3, align = "llc")
```

### Interpretation

The methods below answer one general question, whether the restricted/broad difference is a genuine pattern recoverable from data independent of how the groups were originally defined, through three specific questions, each answered by a different route.

**Question 1 (strategy A):** Is the observed two-group split *stronger* than the best split one would obtain by optimising on randomised data, that is, does the restricted/broad partition survive a null that accounts for the fact that the grouping was itself optimised to maximise separation? Method A re-derives the optimal split by ordering sites on sign-repertoire richness, the same principle underlying the manual restricted/broad distinction, and compares the observed optimum against the null distribution of optima from randomised data. We implement a fixed-fixed (Curveball) null that preserves both site richness and sign-type frequencies while destroying compositional structure.

*Answer:* **Under the fixed-fixed (Curveball) null, the observed optimal split is not significant in either phase** (Aur-P1 observed optimal pseudo-F = `r round(s6_6_bestP1$observed_best_F, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_bestP1$p_value`; Aur-P2 observed optimal pseudo-F = `r round(s6_6_bestP2$observed_best_F, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_bestP2$p_value`). This means the restricted/broad partition does not produce a two-group separation stronger than expected under a null that preserves both site richness and sign-type frequencies. The non-significance under the fixed-fixed null indicates that the restricted/broad contrast is not a sharp discontinuous partition that survives the most stringent "optimisation-accounted-for" null; rather, it is a **recoverable gradient/axis of variation** whose strength is partly attributable to the marginal richness and frequency structure of the data. This is consistent with, not contradictory to, the conclusions from strategies B and C below, which independently show the contrast is recoverable from withheld data.

**Question 2 (strategy B):** Can the group assignment be recovered from data that did **not** contribute to defining it?
- *Site level (B-i) — label smoothness, not independent validation:* Can a held-out site's label be predicted from other sites using the same Jaccard structure that produced the labels? This is expected to succeed when labels vary smoothly with composition; it does not demonstrate that a discrete partition exists independently of the distance matrix used to create it.
  - *Answer:* Leave-one-site-out k=1 NN recovers the manual label for `r round(s6_6_cvP1$accuracy * 100)`% of Aur-P1 sites (95% CI `r round(s6_6_cvP1$ci_lo, 2)`–`r round(s6_6_cvP1$ci_hi, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_cvP1$p_value`) and `r round(s6_6_cvP2$accuracy * 100)`% of Aur-P2 sites (permutation p = `r s6_6_cvP2$p_value`). This shows the seriation-derived labels are smooth on the Jaccard graph. Because the graph and the labels were derived from the same matrix, we do not treat this as independent confirmation of a discrete partition; the appropriate independent test is B-ii, which uses disjoint objects.
- *Object level (B-ii) — independent validation on disjoint objects:* When the two-group rule is learned from one random half of each site's objects and tested, by PerMANOVA, on the *other* half, is the held-out contrast still significant? We report median p, proportion of splits with p < 0.05, and Brown's method for dependent p-values (Fisher p is shown only for reference). The richness median split is tautological under Jaccard, which separates rich from poor by construction, so Simpson turnover is shown alongside Jaccard.
  - *Answer (Jaccard):* Aur-P1 median p = `r round(s6_6_objP1$median_p, 3)` with `r round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant * 100)`% of 100 splits significant; Brown p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP1$browns_p, digits=3)` (Fisher p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP1$combined_p, digits=3)`). Aur-P2 median p = `r round(s6_6_objP2$median_p, 3)` with `r round(s6_6_objP2$prop_significant * 100)`% significant; Brown p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$browns_p, digits=3)` (Fisher p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$combined_p, digits=3)`). Brown is an empirical approximation [@Brown_1975; @Poole_2016 via Kost & McDermott]; for Aur-P2 (`r s6_6_objP2$n_usable` usable sites) Brown (`r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$browns_p, digits=3)`) is slightly anti-conservative vs. Fisher (`r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$combined_p, digits=3)`), so median p and proportion are primary and Brown/Fisher are order-of-magnitude. Both use `r s6_6_objP1$n_usable` (Aur-P1) and `r s6_6_objP2$n_usable` (Aur-P2) of the total sites with at least two objects; Aur-P2 individual splits have low power.
  - *Answer (Simpson turnover, nestedness-robust):* Aur-P1 median p = `r round(s6_6_objP1$median_p_sim, 3)` with `r round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant_sim * 100)`% significant; Brown p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP1$browns_p_sim, digits=3)`. Aur-P2 median p = `r round(s6_6_objP2$median_p_sim, 3)` with `r round(s6_6_objP2$prop_significant_sim * 100)`% significant; Brown p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$browns_p_sim, digits=3)`. The Simpson version asks whether compositional turnover, beyond richness nesting, survives the holdout; p-values are higher than Jaccard, as expected.
  This shows whether the grouping, as defined by a richness rule, generalises to independent objects. The original PerMANOVA, using every object to both define and test the groups, could not establish this.

**Question 3 (strategy C):** If we abandon the discrete partition and ask whether sign composition varies continuously with predictors that are independent of the distance matrix, is that gradient significant? Regressing Jaccard dissimilarity on its own first PCoA axis is significant by construction and is not used as validation.
- *Answer:* For log object count: Aur-P1 R² = `r s6_6_gradP1_log$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP1_log$p`; Aur-P2 R² = `r s6_6_gradP2_log$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP2_log$p`. For richness: Aur-P1 R² = `r s6_6_gradP1_rich$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP1_rich$p`; Aur-P2 R² = `r s6_6_gradP2_rich$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP2_rich$p`. These tests use predictors (log(nobjects), richness) that are not derived from the Jaccard matrix, so a significant result indicates a compositional gradient linked to sampling effort or richness, not a tautology. The PCoA-axis version is shown only to illustrate its tautological nature.

**Summary.** Strategy B-ii (object-half holdout) provides the appropriate independent validation because it tests the grouping on disjoint objects and reports dependence-aware statistics (median p, proportion significant, Brown p) with Jaccard and Simpson turnover. Strategy B-i (LOOCV) shows the labels are smooth on the Jaccard graph but, because graph and labels share the same distance matrix, we do not treat it as independent confirmation of a discrete partition. Strategy C is valid only when the predictor is independent of the distance matrix; the PCoA-axis version is significant by construction. Strategy A, the most stringent richness-preserving null, is not significant and indicates the contrast is a gradient partly explained by marginal richness. Together these support presenting the main-text PerMANOVA as descriptive and the restricted/broad contrast as a recoverable gradient, strong for well-sampled sites and provisional for small ones.

# S6.7 Characterization of Detected Communities {#sec-s6-7}

The PerMANOVA results in S5.5 and bootstrap consensus in S6.1–S6.3 show that the algorithmically detected communities are statistically significant and internally coherent. This section provides a detailed characterization of those communities: their site membership, geographic distribution, and sign-type composition.

## S6.7.1 Community Membership by Algorithm and Phase {#sec-s6-7-1}

We extract the community assignments for each of the four algorithms at the main-analysis threshold (Jaccard ≥ 0.2) and report the full site-by-site membership, with the manual restricted (1) / broad (2) group as reference. A reviewer can then read across any row to see where Louvain, Infomap, Leiden, and Walktrap place the same site.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-community-membership
#| tbl-cap: "Community assignments for each site by algorithm and Aurignacian phase at Jaccard threshold 0.2, with the manual restricted (1) / broad (2) group as reference. Sites are ordered by phase, manual group, then site. Singletons (isolated sites with no edges) are assigned their own community. Community IDs are arbitrary within each algorithm column: compare which sites share a value within a column, not the numeric values across columns."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

# Get community assignments for all four algorithms at threshold 0.2
algorithms <- c("louvain", "infomap", "leiden", "walktrap")
threshold <- 0.2

community_assignments <- map_dfr(algorithms, function(alg) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    if (ph == "Aur-P1") {
      artifact_data <- aurp1_artifact_data
    } else {
      artifact_data <- aurp2_artifact_data
    }
    
    if (alg == "louvain") {
      comms <- get_louvain_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "infomap") {
      comms <- get_infomap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "leiden") {
      comms <- get_leiden_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "walktrap") {
      comms <- get_walktrap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    }
    
    data.frame(
      Algorithm = alg,
      Phase = ph,
      Site = names(comms),
      Community = unname(comms),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
})

# Pivot to wide format for easier reading, adding the manual group as reference
community_wide <- community_assignments %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Algorithm, values_from = Community) %>%
  mutate(Manual = mapply(function(s, p) manual_groups[[p]][s], Site, Phase)) %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Site, Manual, louvain, infomap, leiden, walktrap) %>%
  arrange(Phase, Manual, Site)

kable(community_wide,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Manual", "Louvain", "Infomap", "Leiden", "Walktrap"),
      align = "llccccc",
      digits = 0)
```

```{r fig.height=8, fig.width=8}
#| label: fig-comembership-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Sites-by-algorithm co-membership at Jaccard threshold 0.2. Rows are sites ordered by phase and manual group (1 = restricted, 2 = broad); columns are the manual reference and the four community-detection algorithms. Colour encodes the community ID within each column. Read within a column to see which sites each algorithm groups together. Community IDs are arbitrary within each column, so colours match across columns only by coincidence."
#| fig-height: 8

heatmap_long <- community_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Manual, louvain, infomap, leiden, walktrap),
               names_to = "Algorithm", values_to = "Group") %>%
  mutate(
    Algorithm = factor(Algorithm,
                       levels = c("Manual", "louvain", "infomap", "leiden", "walktrap"),
                       labels = c("Manual", "Louvain", "Infomap", "Leiden", "Walktrap")),
    Group = factor(Group),
    Site = factor(Site, levels = unique(rev(community_wide$Site)))
  )

group_pal <- c("1" = "#E41A1C", "2" = "#377EB8", "3" = "#4DAF4A", "4" = "#984EA3")

p_comem <- ggplot(heatmap_long, aes(x = Algorithm, y = Site, fill = Group)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_pal, drop = FALSE, name = "Group") +
  facet_grid(Phase ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggsave(filename = here::here("figures/comembership-heatmap.png"),
       plot = p_comem, width = 8, height = 8, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/comembership-heatmap.png"))
```

Stable sites keep the same within-column neighbours across all five columns; shifting sites change neighbours from column to column. In Aur-P1 the two large Louvain, Infomap, and Walktrap blocks track the manual restricted and broad groups, with Les Cottés and Trou al'Wesse splitting off as singletons while Leiden collapses the restricted and broad sites into one block. In Aur-P2 Infomap and Leiden collapse all nine sites into a single block, while Louvain and Walktrap split the restricted sites into two smaller blocks (Gargas, Les Rois, Mladeč, and Vindija Cave versus La Viña and Sirgenstein Cave) around the intact broad-range block of Trou Magrite, Bockstein-Törle, and Hohle Fels. The bootstrap consensus co-clustering matrices in @fig-bootstrap-consensus quantify which of these co-memberships survive resampling.

## S6.7.2 Community Composition and Sign-Type Profiles {#sec-s6-7-2}

For each community, we summarize the sign-type composition to understand what distinguishes one community from another.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-community-composition
#| tbl-cap: "Sign-type composition of Louvain communities at threshold 0.2. Values show the proportion of sites within each community that have at least one object bearing the sign type. Only sign types present in ≥10% of sites in at least one community are shown."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

threshold <- 0.2

# Get Louvain communities for both phases
louvain_comms_p1 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
louvain_comms_p2 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = threshold)

# Calculate sign-type frequencies within each community, per phase
community_signs <- map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
  if (ph == "Aur-P1") {
    artifact_data <- aurp1_artifact_data
    comms <- louvain_comms_p1
  } else {
    artifact_data <- aurp2_artifact_data
    comms <- louvain_comms_p2
  }
  
  # Determine which sign columns are present
  present_signs <- intersect(SIGN_COLS, colnames(artifact_data))
  artifact_df <- as.data.frame(artifact_data[, present_signs, drop = FALSE],
                               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  artifact_df$Site <- rownames(artifact_df)
  artifact_df <- artifact_df[, c("Site", present_signs), drop = FALSE]
  artifact_df[, present_signs] <- lapply(artifact_df[, present_signs, drop = FALSE],
                                          function(x) as.numeric(x > 0))
  
  tibble(
    Site = names(comms),
    Community = paste0(comms)
  ) %>%
    left_join(artifact_df, by = "Site") %>%
    group_by(Community) %>%
    summarise(
      n_sites = n(),
      across(all_of(present_signs), ~ mean(. > 0)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(Phase = ph)
})

# Filter to sign types present in ≥10% of sites in at least one community
community_signs_long <- community_signs %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(intersect(SIGN_COLS, names(community_signs))),
               names_to = "SignType", values_to = "Frequency") %>%
  group_by(SignType) %>%
  filter(max(Frequency) >= 0.1) %>%
  ungroup()

community_signs_wide <- community_signs_long %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = SignType, values_from = Frequency)

# Format for table
kable(community_signs_wide %>%
        dplyr::select(Phase, Community, n_sites, sort(names(.)[4:length(names(.))])) %>%
        mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 2))),
      digits = 2,
      align = "lccc" %>% paste0(strrep("c", ncol(community_signs_wide) - 4), collapse = ""))
```

## S6.7.3 Geographic Distribution of Communities {#sec-s6-7-3}

We map the communities to visualize their geographic structure. Community IDs are colored consistently within each phase.

```{r fig.height=7, fig.width=9}
#| label: fig-community-maps
#| fig-cap: "Geographic distribution of Louvain communities at Jaccard threshold 0.2. (a) Aur-P1: 4 communities. (b) Aur-P2: 3 communities. Community colours are arbitrary but consistent within each phase. Point size indicates assemblage size (number of objects). Map data from naturalearthdata.com."
#| fig-height: 7

# Get communities for each phase
louvain_comms_p1 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2)
louvain_comms_p2 <- get_louvain_groups(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2)

# Build one site-level table for both phases; coordinates are stored as
# character by make_phase2_data(), so convert back to numeric for mapping
map_data_comm <- bind_rows(
  aurp1_unique_data %>%
    mutate(Site = site_name,
           Community = as.factor(louvain_comms_p1[site_name]),
           Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  aurp2_unique_data %>%
    mutate(Site = site_name,
           Community = as.factor(louvain_comms_p2[site_name]),
           Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>%
  mutate(longitude = as.numeric(longitude),
         latitude = as.numeric(latitude)) %>%
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

world_comm <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
europe_comm <- world_comm[which(world_comm$continent == "Europe"),]
comm_cols <- c("1" = "#E41A1C", "2" = "#377EB8", "3" = "#4DAF4A", "4" = "#984EA3")

p_comm_map <- ggplot(europe_comm) +
  geom_sf(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_sf(data = map_data_comm,
          aes(colour = Community, size = nobjects)) +
  geom_text_repel(data = map_data_comm,
                  aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, label = Site),
                  size = 3, bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.2,
                  max.overlaps = 30) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = comm_cols, name = "Louvain community") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6), name = "Objects") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, 30), ylim = c(35, 53), expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Phase, ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(width_hint = 0.3, height = unit(0.12, "cm"))

ggsave(filename = here::here("figures/community-maps.png"),
       plot = p_comm_map, width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/community-maps.png"))
```

## S6.7.4 Cross-Algorithm Community Comparison {#sec-s6-7-4}

We examine how consistently sites are assigned to communities across the four algorithms, focusing on the main-analysis threshold of 0.2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-algorithm-agreement
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-algorithm agreement in community assignment at threshold 0.2. For each phase, sites are grouped by their Louvain community (reference), and the proportion of other algorithms that assign the site to the same community ID (after optimal matching of community labels) is reported. Values close to 1.0 indicate strong cross-algorithm agreement."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

threshold <- 0.2

# Get communities for all algorithms
all_comms <- map_dfr(algorithms, function(alg) {
  map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
    if (ph == "Aur-P1") {
      artifact_data <- aurp1_artifact_data
    } else {
      artifact_data <- aurp2_artifact_data
    }
    
    if (alg == "louvain") {
      comms <- get_louvain_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "infomap") {
      comms <- get_infomap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "leiden") {
      comms <- get_leiden_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    } else if (alg == "walktrap") {
      comms <- get_walktrap_groups(artifact_data, threshold = threshold)
    }
    
    data.frame(
      Algorithm = alg,
      Phase = ph,
      Site = names(comms),
      Community = unname(comms),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
})

# For each phase, compute agreement with Louvain as reference
cross_algorithm_agreement <- map_dfr(names(phases), function(ph) {
  phase_data <- all_comms %>% filter(Phase == ph)
louvain_ref <- phase_data %>% filter(Algorithm == "louvain") %>%
  dplyr::select(Site, LouvainCommunity = Community)
  
  phase_data %>%
    left_join(louvain_ref, by = "Site") %>%
    group_by(Site) %>%
    summarise(
      Louvain = first(LouvainCommunity),
      Infomap_same = mean(Community[Algorithm == "infomap"] == LouvainCommunity),
      Leiden_same = mean(Community[Algorithm == "leiden"] == LouvainCommunity),
      Walktrap_same = mean(Community[Algorithm == "walktrap"] == LouvainCommunity),
      Any_same = mean(c(Community[Algorithm == "infomap"], Community[Algorithm == "leiden"], Community[Algorithm == "walktrap"]) == LouvainCommunity),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(Phase = ph) %>%
    dplyr::select(Phase, Site, Louvain, Infomap_same, Leiden_same, Walktrap_same, Any_same)
}) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Infomap_same, Leiden_same, Walktrap_same, Any_same), ~ round(., 2)))

kable(cross_algorithm_agreement,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Louvain Comm.", "Infomap", "Leiden", "Walktrap", "Any"),
      digits = 2,
      align = "llcccccc")
```

## S6.7.5 Interpretation {#sec-s6-7-5}

**Community structure in Aur-P1.** The Louvain algorithm identifies 4 communities in Aur-P1 (Table S6.7.1). The largest communities (Community 1 with `r sum(louvain_comms_p1 == 1)` sites and Community 2 with `r sum(louvain_comms_p1 == 2)` sites) coincide almost exactly with the manual restricted and broad groups, with Les Cottés and Trou al'Wesse splitting off as singleton communities, suggesting the partition captures the core restricted and broad sign repertoires. The geographic map (@fig-community-maps, Aur-P1 facet) shows that Community 2 spans the broadest geographic range, while the smaller communities are more spatially clustered.

**Community structure in Aur-P2.** Aur-P2 resolves into 3 Louvain communities (Table S6.7.1). With only `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites total, the communities are small (1–3 sites each), and the PerMANOVA significance (S5.5) likely reflects strong pairwise similarities among a few sites rather than robust multi-site clusters. The geographic map (@fig-community-maps, Aur-P2 facet) shows limited spatial coherence, consistent with the non-significant null-benchmarked modularity (S5.3).

**Cross-algorithm consistency.** Table S6.7.4 shows that Louvain and Walktrap produce nearly identical partitions (agreement > 0.9 for most sites), while Infomap and Leiden yield coarser partitions with fewer communities. Sites that are assigned consistently across all four algorithms represent the strongest signal; those that vary indicate boundary uncertainty.

**Sign-type differentiation.** Table S6.7.2 reveals that communities differ primarily in the frequency of `obline`, `dashline`, and `zigzag` signs, which are the most widespread sign types. No single sign type is exclusive to a community, supporting the interpretation that communities reflect graded differences in sign repertoire composition rather than discrete "cultural provinces."

**Implications.** The community detection results confirm that the main-text restricted/broad dichotomy is a simplification of a richer, multi-community structure. The two-group partition captures the dominant axis of variation (core vs. peripheral sign repertoires) but masks finer-scale geographic and technological patterning that emerges at the community level.

# S7. Object-Type Sensitivity: Figurine Exclusion {#sec-s7}


```{r}
#| label: s7-setup
#| include: false
# ── S7 setup: all figurine-exclusion statistics are produced by the shared
#    sensitivity_summary() function in functions.R (also used by paper.qmd and the
#    S8 section), so the supplement and the main text cannot report divergent numbers.

excl <- sensitivity_summary(signbase_full_clean, aurp1_artifact_data, aurp2_artifact_data)

figurine_types   <- excl$figurine_types
figurine_summary <- excl$figurine_summary
s7_baseline      <- excl$s7_baseline
s7_no_fig        <- excl$s7_no_fig
s7_no_vog        <- excl$s7_no_vog_fig
s7_sites_lost    <- excl$s7_sites_lost
s7_vog_before    <- excl$s7_vog_before
s7_vog_summary   <- excl$s7_vog_summary
joint_comparison <- excl$joint_comparison

s7_fig_count <- function(site) figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$site_name == site]
s7_fig_count_cond <- function(site, ph) {
  sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$site_name == site & figurine_summary$phase2 == ph])
}
s7_fig_total <- sum(figurine_summary$Total)
s7_fig_p1 <- sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$phase2 == "Aur-P1"])
s7_fig_p2 <- sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$phase2 == "Aur-P2"])
```

## S7.1 Rationale

@Bentz_Dutkiewicz_2026 demonstrate that ivory figurines in the Swabian Aurignacian carry sign sequences with higher information density than tools. If figurines encode different sign repertoires than other object types, their inclusion could bias site-level sign assemblages , particularly at Vogelherd, where `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` of the dataset's `r s7_fig_total` figurines are concentrated. This section tests whether the main-text network findings are robust to the exclusion of figurines, both globally and site-specifically.

## S7.2 Figurine Distribution in the Dataset

```{r}
#| label: tbl-figurine-count
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of figurine objects across phases and sites. Figurine types include figurine zoomorph, figurine anthropomorph, figurine undet., and possible figurine."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# figurine_summary is precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

kable(figurine_summary,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site",
                    grep("figurine", names(figurine_summary), value = TRUE, invert = FALSE),
                    "Total"),
      digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: s7-helpers
#| include: false
# ── Accessor helpers for the S7 interpretation prose (read from joint_comparison) ──
s7_md  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$mean_degree[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 2)
}
s7_ed  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  joint_comparison$n_edges[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond]
}
s7_ns  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  joint_comparison$n_sites[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond]
}
s7_mo  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$modularity[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 3)
}
s7_tr  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$transitivity[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 3)
}
s7_pct <- function(cond) {
  paste0(round(joint_comparison$pct_change_md[
    joint_comparison$Phase == "Aur-P1" & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 1), "%")
}
```

@tbl-figurine-count shows that figurines are heavily concentrated at Vogelherd (`r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects), with minor representation at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`). Of these, `r s7_fig_p1` fall within Aur-P1 and the remaining `r s7_fig_p2` , all Hohle Fels objects from AH IV and Iid , fall within Aur-P2 under the layer-level assignment. The analysis therefore tests whether the Aur-P1 network structure , which reports the higher mean degree (`r s7_md("Aur-P1")`) , is driven by these `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects at a single site.

## S7.3 Analysis 1: Exclude All Figurines

### Method

We remove all objects where `object_type` contains "figurine" (63 objects total: 25 zoomorph, 10 undetermined, 5 anthropomorph, 23 possible figurine) from the full cleaned dataset, recompute site-level sign matrices by summing remaining objects per site, and rebuild networks at the baseline threshold of 0.2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exclude-figurines
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics before and after excluding all figurine objects (figurine zoomorph, figurine anthropomorph, figurine undet., and possible figurine). Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# s7_baseline and s7_no_fig are precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

excl_comparison <- bind_rows(s7_baseline, s7_no_fig)

kable(excl_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Condition"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "llcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-figurine-sites-lost
#| tbl-cap: "Number of sites per phase before and after figurine exclusion. Sites are lost when all objects at that site are figurines."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s7_sites_lost %>% dplyr::select(Phase, sites_before, sites_after, lost),
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites (all)", "Sites (no figurines)", "Sites lost"),
      digits = 0)
```

### Interpretation

Excluding all `r s7_fig_total` figurines has only a small effect on the Aur-P1 network: one edge is lost (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) and mean degree falls from `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`, with no sites lost (all `r s7_ns("Aur-P1")` sites retained). Aur-P2 is unchanged (mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`, `r s7_ed("Aur-P2")` edges, `r s7_ns("Aur-P2")` sites): the `r s7_fig_count_cond("Hohle Fels","Aur-P2")` Hohle Fels figurines removed from it do not alter the site's sign repertoire, so its network is unaffected. The detectable Aur-P1 effects are declines in transitivity (`r s7_tr("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_tr("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) and modularity (`r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`), indicating that figurines contribute modestly to community cohesion but do not create the communities themselves.

Critically, Aur-P1 retains the higher mean degree (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) under figurine exclusion, preserving the main-text ordering Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`). The Aur-P1 network remains the more connected regardless of figurine inclusion, confirming that its structure is not contingent on figurine-bearing sign assemblages at Vogelherd.

## S7.4 Analysis 2: Exclude Vogelherd Figurines Only

### Method

Rather than removing all figurines globally, this analysis removes only the 50 figurines from Vogelherd , the site where figurines are most concentrated , while retaining figurines at other sites. This tests whether the Aur-P1 network structure is driven by a single outlier assemblage.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vogelherd-exclude
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics before and after excluding figurines from Vogelherd only. All other figurines (Hohle Fels, Geissenklösterle, Hohlenstein-Stadel, La Ferrassie) are retained. Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# s7_baseline, s7_no_vog and s7_vog_summary are precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

vog_comparison <- bind_rows(s7_baseline, s7_no_vog)

kable(vog_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Condition"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "llcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vogelherd-objects
#| tbl-cap: "Vogelherd object counts before and after removing figurines. Non-figurine objects at Vogelherd (tools, plaquettes, etc.) are retained."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s7_vog_summary %>% dplyr::select(Phase, objects_before, objects_after, removed),
      col.names = c("Phase", "Objects (all)", "Objects (no figurines)", "Removed"),
      digits = 0)
```

### Interpretation

Removing only Vogelherd's figurines (`r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects: `r s7_vog_before$objects_before[s7_vog_before$phase2 == "Aur-P1"]` → `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` in Aur-P1) has a negligible effect on Aur-P1: mean degree drops from `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), one edge is lost (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), and modularity decreases from `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`. Aur-P2 shows no change whatsoever (mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` → `r s7_md("Aur-P2","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`, modularity `r s7_mo("Aur-P2")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P2","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), confirming that Vogelherd figurines do not contribute to network structure in the later phase.

The effect of removing Vogelherd figurines alone (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` in Aur-P1) is the same as removing all `r s7_fig_total` figurines globally (`r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")`), and in both cases the network is essentially unchanged. The figurine effect therefore does not scale with the number of figurines removed; figurines at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`) do not alter the network structure , including the `r s7_fig_count_cond("Hohle Fels","Aur-P2")` Hohle Fels figurines assigned to Aur-P2, which leave that phase's network unchanged , and Vogelherd's connectivity within Aur-P1 is carried by its `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` non-figurine objects.

## S7.5 Joint Comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-objtype-joint
#| tbl-cap: "Side-by-side comparison of network statistics across all conditions: baseline (all objects), exclude all figurines, and exclude Vogelherd figurines only. The rightmost columns show the percentage change in mean degree from baseline."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# joint_comparison is precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

kable(joint_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Condition", "Sites", "Edges", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Δ mean degree (%)"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lllccccc")
```

## S7.6 Interpretation

The joint comparison in @tbl-objtype-joint shows that figurine exclusion has a modest and phase-dependent effect on network structure:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s7-6-meandegree
#| tbl-cap: "Mean degree by figurine-exclusion condition, with percentage change from baseline. Reproduced directly from the joint comparison in @tbl-objtype-joint."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

s7_md_summary <- joint_comparison %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, mean_degree, pct_change_md) %>%
  mutate(short = case_when(
    Condition == "Baseline (all objects)"      ~ "Baseline",
    Condition == "Exclude all figurines"       ~ "No figurines",
    Condition == "Exclude Vogelherd figurines" ~ "Vogelherd only")) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Phase, names_from = short,
              values_from = c(mean_degree, pct_change_md)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Phase,
    `Baseline mean degree` = `mean_degree_Baseline`,
    `No figurines`        = `mean_degree_No figurines`,
    delta_no              = `pct_change_md_No figurines`,
    `Vogelherd only`      = `mean_degree_Vogelherd only`,
    delta_vog             = `pct_change_md_Vogelherd only`) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_no  = paste0(formatC(delta_no,  digits = 1, format = "f"), "%"),
    delta_vog = paste0(formatC(delta_vog, digits = 1, format = "f"), "%"))

kable(s7_md_summary,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Baseline mean degree", "No figurines", "Δ",
                    "Vogelherd only", "Δ"),
      digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 2, 0),
      align = "llcccc")
```

**Outcome observed: Negligible effect, no qualitative change.** Mean degree changes are at most `r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")` across both phases and all conditions, and excluding all figurines removes a single edge from Aur-P1 (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`, mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) while leaving Aur-P2's edge set unchanged (`r s7_ed("Aur-P2")` edges, mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`). Modularity decreases slightly for Aur-P1 when figurines are excluded (`r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` excluding all; `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` excluding Vogelherd only) while Aur-P2 is unchanged (`r s7_mo("Aur-P2")`), indicating that figurines contribute marginally to within-group cohesion but do not create the community structure.

**Phase ordering is preserved.** The main-text connectivity contrast Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 (`r s7_md("Aur-P1")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`) is unchanged under both exclusion scenarios (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` excluding all figurines; `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` excluding Vogelherd figurines only), preserving the key finding that the early phase is the more connected.

**The figurine effect is small and Vogelherd-specific.** Removing Vogelherd figurines alone (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` in Aur-P1) produces the same effect as removing all `r s7_fig_total` figurines globally (`r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")`). Figurines at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`) do not alter network structure. This indicates that although Vogelherd's figurine assemblage is unusually rich , `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` of `r s7_fig_total` figurines , and contributes disproportionately to sign-type counts, its `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` remaining non-figurine objects still carry a sufficiently diverse sign repertoire to maintain network connectivity.

**Conclusion.** The main-text findings are robust to figurine exclusion. The Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity contrast, the two-group community structure, and the site membership of both phases are all preserved when figurines are removed. The concentration of figurines at Vogelherd does not bias the seriation or network results, and the broader-range group's connectivity within Aur-P1 is supported by non-figurine sign types. We note that modularity decreases slightly when figurines are excluded (Aur-P1: `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`), suggesting that figurines contribute modestly to community cohesion , consistent with @Bentz_Dutkiewicz_2026 argument that figurines carry high-information sign sequences, but the communities themselves are defined by shared sign types across all object types.

# S8. Site Reclassification Sensitivity Analysis {#sec-s8}

## S8.1 Rationale

The main analysis assigns each site to a phase (Aur-P1/Aur-P2) using specialist technological attributions from the published literature, supplemented by calibrated radiocarbon dates, as detailed in the "Site Phase Assignments" supplementary item. Recent specialist reassessments demonstrate that radiocarbon dates alone are insufficient for phase attribution, and that the archaeological content of layers should take precedence:

- **Abri Pataud**: The lithic technology in levels 14–9 (carinated scraper bladelet cores, dual reduction systems) is diagnostic of the Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1), not the Proto-Aurignacian, despite basal dates of ~41,200–39,500 cal BP that fall within the Proto-Aurignacian range [@Chiotti_2005; @Higham_Abri_Pataud_2011]. The site is classified as Aurignacian I (Early) in the Périgord sequence.
- **La Ferrassie**: The Aurignacian at La Ferrassie begins in Layer 7, directly overlying the Châtelperronian (Layer 6). [@Talamo_La_Ferrassie_2020] classify this as Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1) based on carinated scrapers and wide Aurignacian blades. No split-base bone points (Proto-Aurignacian diagnostic) were found [@Delporte_1984_Ferrassie; @Talamo_La_Ferrassie_2020]. Layer 7b has mixed Early/Recent Aurignacian components.
- **Mladeč**: The ~20 lithic artifacts include only one carinated end scraper. The 40 bone points with massive bases ("Mladeč-type") lack split bases and occur stratigraphically above split-based points at other Central European sites, placing them in the Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2) [@Oliva_2006]. Direct dates of ~31 ka ¹⁴C BP (~35–36 cal BP) are too young for Proto-Aurignacian [@Wild_et_al_2005].
- **Vogelherd**: Riek's 1931 excavation removed 500 m³ in 12 weeks with no screening, using large horizontal spits that did not follow geological horizons. Documented mixing includes 38 refit connections between Aurignacian layers IV and V, Neolithic burials disturbing the southwestern area, and ~2–3% of tools in the Aurignacian layers potentially deriving from other periods [@Schurch_Conard_2026_reassess].

Because these attributions are important for the two-phase framework, this section tests the sensitivity of the network results to (A) reverting to the purely date-based assignment used in earlier analyses , each object assigned to a phase by its calibrated date alone , and (B) excluding Vogelherd entirely, given its documented stratigraphic mixing.

```{r}
# ── Analysis A: revert to purely date-based assignment ─────────────────────
# Reassign each object purely by its calibrated date (technology overrides
# removed); the Spy/El Castillo exclusions from the baseline are retained.
signbase_date <- signbase_full_clean %>%
  mutate(time_period2 = time_period_date,
         phase2 = ifelse(time_period_date %in% c("proto_aurignacian", "early_aurignacian"),
                         "Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"))

lat_long_date <- signbase_date %>%
  dplyr::select(site_name, longitude, latitude) %>%
  distinct(site_name, .keep_all = TRUE)

aurp1_date <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P1", signbase_date, lat_long_date)
aurp2_date <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P2", signbase_date, lat_long_date)

date_stats <- bind_rows(
  network_stats(extract_artifact(aurp1_date), threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  network_stats(extract_artifact(aurp2_date), threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>%
  mutate(Condition = "Date-based") %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree,
                transitivity, modularity)

# ── Analysis B: exclude Vogelherd entirely ─────────────────────────────────
# s8_novog is precomputed by sensitivity_summary() in the s7-setup chunk
no_vog_stats <- excl$s8_novog
```

## S8.2 Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reclass-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics under three conditions: baseline (technology-based assignment), date-based (each object assigned purely by calibrated radiocarbon date, with the Spy/El Castillo exclusions retained), and exclude Vogelherd (technology-based baseline with the site of Vogelherd removed entirely). Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

baseline_reclass <- bind_rows(
  network_stats(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  network_stats(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>%
  mutate(Condition = "Baseline (technology-based)") %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity)

all_reclass <- bind_rows(baseline_reclass, date_stats, no_vog_stats)

kable(all_reclass,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Condition", "Sites", "Edges", "Density",
                    "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lllcccccc")
```

```{r}
# ── Inline helpers for prose ────────────────────────────────────────────────
s8_md <- function(ph, cond) round(all_reclass$mean_degree[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond], 2)
s8_ns <- function(ph, cond) all_reclass$n_sites[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond]
s8_ne <- function(ph, cond) all_reclass$n_edges[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond]
s8_mo <- function(ph, cond) round(all_reclass$modularity[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond], 3)
```

### Effects by condition

**Date-based alternative (Analysis A).** Reverting to purely date-based criteria changes the membership of three sites. Mladeč moves from Aur-P2 to Aur-P1 because its calibrated median using the older-end of the date range (40,091 cal BP) falls in the Proto-Aurignacian range, which is folded into Aur-P1; the midpoint variant used in the main analysis gives 37,831 cal BP (Early Aurignacian, Aur-P1), and the younger-end gives 35,571 cal BP (Early Aurignacian, Aur-P1) [@Wild_et_al_2005]. Hohle Fels and Vogelherd are split across the phases by object date: `r excl$hf_p1` of `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Hohle Fels"))` Hohle Fels objects and `r excl$vog_p1_date` of `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Vogelherd"))` Vogelherd objects remain in Aur-P1, and `r excl$hf_p2` and `r excl$vog_p2_date` objects , those calibrated to ~32 ka BP or younger , move to Aur-P2. The date-based assignment therefore fragments long-occupied sites whose assemblages span the phase boundary, which is precisely the failure mode the technology-based attribution is designed to avoid. Under this assignment Aur-P1 grows to `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Date-based")` sites and `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Date-based")` edges (mean degree `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Date-based")`), while Aur-P2 , now missing Mladeč but containing `r excl$young_total` young-dated objects from Hohle Fels and Vogelherd , has `r s8_ns("Aur-P2", "Date-based")` sites and `r s8_ne("Aur-P2", "Date-based")` edges (mean degree `r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Date-based")`).

**Vogelherd exclusion (Analysis B).** Removing Vogelherd's `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Vogelherd"))` objects from the technology-based baseline reduces Aur-P1 from `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` sites and from `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` edges. Mean degree falls from `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` (`r paste0("−", excl$md_pct, "%")`), and modularity from `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")`. Aur-P2 is unaffected (`r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")`, `r s8_ne("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")` edges, `r s8_ns("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")` sites).

## S8.3 Phase-Ordering Robustness

The most consequential finding is that **the Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity ordering is preserved under every condition**:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s8-ordering
#| tbl-cap: "Mean degree by phase under each reassignment condition. The Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 ordering is preserved under every condition."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

s8_ordering <- all_reclass %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, mean_degree) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Condition, names_from = Phase, values_from = mean_degree) %>%
  mutate(Ordering = ifelse(`Aur-P1` > `Aur-P2`, "Aur-P1 > Aur-P2", "Aur-P2 > Aur-P1")) %>%
  dplyr::select(Condition, `Aur-P1`, `Aur-P2`, Ordering)

kable(s8_ordering,
      col.names = c("Condition", "Aur-P1 mean degree", "Aur-P2 mean degree", "Ordering"),
      digits = 2)
```

Under the date-based assignment Aur-P1's mean degree rises (from `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Date-based")`) and Aur-P2's falls (from `r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Date-based")`), so the contrast is not an artefact of the technological reassignment , the naive date-based assignment, if anything, strengthens it. Excluding Vogelherd weakens but does not remove the contrast (`r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` vs `r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")`).

## S8.4 Interpretation

The robustness of the Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity contrast to both the assignment criterion and to the removal of the largest site strengthens the main-text conclusion that the early phase supports a larger, more hub-centred sign-sharing network. The date-based alternative is a useful worst case: it fragments long-occupied sites across phases and moves Mladeč into Aur-P1 (via the older-end calibrated median of 40,091 cal BP), yet Aur-P1 remains the more connected phase.

The observed between-phase modularity values are, however, assignment-sensitive: they reverse under the date-based assignment (Aur-P1 `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Date-based")` < Aur-P2 `r s8_mo("Aur-P2", "Date-based")`, versus `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` > `r s8_mo("Aur-P2", "Baseline (technology-based)")` at baseline). This reinforces the main text's caution about between-phase comparisons: the pairwise permutation test on the technology-based baseline finds no significant difference in modularity (or any other network statistic) between the phases, and S5.7 shows that the modularity confidence intervals overlap substantially (Aur-P2 rests on only 9 sites). We therefore recommend reading the between-phase contrast primarily as a difference in network scale rather than as a robust ordering of modularity values across alternative assignments.

Excluding Vogelherd leaves the ordering intact, consistent with S7's finding that Aur-P1's network does not depend on a single site. Finally, the within-phase two-group structure (RQ1) , the restricted/broad dichotomy recovered by seriation, Louvain community detection, and bootstrap consensus (S5, S6) , is defined within each phase's membership and is unaffected by the between-phase assignment criterion tested here. The stochastic block model (S6.3) does not recover this dichotomy (single block selected under both emission models), consistent with the small size and sparsity of the sign-sharing networks falling below the detectability limit for block structure.

# S9. Object-Level Downsampling and Coverage-Rarefaction Sensitivity {#sec-s9}

The main-text and supplementary analyses establish the restricted/broad (R/B) division from site-level presence/absence of sign types. This removes the *first-order* effect of differing object counts between sites, but it does not remove a deeper confounding issue: because the number of sign types recorded at a site is bounded by the number of objects recovered, sites represented by many more objects have a greater opportunity to produce a larger repertoire, so the R/B division could partly reflect sampling intensity rather than a genuine cultural contrast. Presence/absence coding controls for the *magnitude* of the object-count difference, not for the fact that richer assemblages are, by construction, more likely to be classified as broad. This section provides an object-level resampling/rareffaction sensitivity analysis. It asks five specific questions:

1. **(S9.2)** When objects are resampled to a common count and the network and Louvain partition are re-derived, how often does each site keep its original R/B assignment, and how stable is the community structure?
2. **(S9.3)** At equal *sample coverage* (rather than equal object count), do restricted and broad sites still differ in sign-type richness?
3. **(S9.4)** Does the group effect on sign-type richness survive after statistically accounting for object count (sampling effort), with the richness-effort exponent estimated rather than fixed?
4. **(S9.5)** At equal effort with `iNEXT` (incidence_freq), does the Aur-P1 vs Aur-P2 sign-type pool (26 vs 15) remain larger, or is it not distinguishable from sampling variation at 63 objects, including when restricted to object types present in both phases?
5. **(S9.6)** Taken together, is the R/B division independent of sampling intensity, and if not, what limitation must be stated?
6. **(S9.7)** Does the restricted/broad pattern survive richness-preserving nulls, and does the manual-group PerMANOVA hold on Simpson turnover dissimilarity, which removes the nestedness component of Jaccard?

```{r}
#| label: s9-setup
#| include: false

obj_counts <- bind_rows(
  site_object_counts(signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P1") %>% mutate(phase = "Aur-P1"),
  site_object_counts(signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P2") %>% mutate(phase = "Aur-P2")
)
mg_all <- c(manual_groups[["Aur-P1"]], manual_groups[["Aur-P2"]])
obj_counts$group <- factor(mg_all[obj_counts$site_name],
                           levels = c(1, 2),
                           labels = c("restricted", "broad"))

ds_R <- 500
cov_target <- 0.9
cov_perm <- 200
k_levels <- c(3, 5, 10)
n_qual <- list()
for (k in k_levels) for (ph in c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2")) {
  n_qual[[paste0(ph, "_", k)]] <-
    sum(obj_counts$nobjects[obj_counts$phase == ph] >= k)
}
```

## S9.1 Object-count distribution and feasible common counts {#sec-s9-1}

### Rationale

Before resampling, we must know how many objects each site contributes. Object counts are highly skewed: a handful of sites (e.g. Vogelherd with `r obj_counts$nobjects[obj_counts$site_name == "Vogelherd" & obj_counts$phase == "Aur-P1"]` objects in Aur-P1) dominate, while many sites contribute only one or two objects (Trou al'Wesse and Fumane contribute a single object; Les Cottés and Labeko Koba contribute two). We therefore tally objects per site and choose common downsampling levels that retain as many sites as possible: **k = 3, 5, and 10 objects per site**. A site is included in a downsampling replicate only if it contributes at least k objects.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s9-objcount
#| tbl-cap: "Per-site object counts by phase and manual restricted(1)/broad(2) group."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

obj_counts %>%
  arrange(phase, desc(nobjects)) %>%
  dplyr::select(phase, site_name, group, nobjects) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Group", "Objects"),
        digits = 0)
```

```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=8}
#| label: fig-s9-objhist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of object counts per site by phase. Most sites contribute few objects; a small number of large assemblages (e.g. Vogelherd) dominate the upper tail."
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(obj_counts, aes(x = nobjects, fill = phase)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ phase, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Aur-P1" = "#F8766D", "Aur-P2" = "#00BA38")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Objects per site", y = "Number of sites") +
  guides(fill = "none")
```

### Interpretation

**Question: how many sites can be retained at each common object count?** At **k = 3**, `r n_qual[["Aur-P1_3"]]` of `r nrow(obj_counts %>% filter(phase=="Aur-P1"))` Aur-P1 sites and `r n_qual[["Aur-P2_3"]]` of `r nrow(obj_counts %>% filter(phase=="Aur-P2"))` Aur-P2 sites qualify. At **k = 5** the numbers fall to `r n_qual[["Aur-P1_5"]]` and `r n_qual[["Aur-P2_5"]]`, and at **k = 10** only `r n_qual[["Aur-P1_10"]]` and `r n_qual[["Aur-P2_10"]]` sites remain. The smallest sites (Trou al'Wesse, Fumane, Pod Hradem, Grottes de Fonds-de-Forêt with one object; Les Cottés, Labeko Koba, Hohlenstein-Stadel with two) can never be downsampled and are excluded from every replicate. We therefore report results at k = 3, 5, and 10, treating k = 10 as the most stringent test (fewest sites, but each built from a substantial object sample) and k = 3 as the most inclusive.

## S9.2 Object-level downsampling sensitivity {#sec-s9-2}

### Rationale

For each phase and each common count k ∈ {3, 5, 10}, and for `r ds_R` replicates, we sample k objects **without replacement** from each qualifying site, aggregate them to a site × sign presence vector (a sign is present at a site if any of its k sampled objects carries it), and rebuild the Jaccard network at the main-text threshold of 0.2. We then re-derive the site partition with Louvain community detection and realign it to the manual R/B labels by assigning each Louvain community to the majority manual group among its members. This mirrors the data-driven re-derivation used in S5.1, but operates on object-downsampled data rather than on the observed site totals. Two quantities are recorded per replicate: (i) for each site, whether its realigned partition matches its manual group (**group retention**), and (ii) the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between the realigned partition and the manual groups, plus the network modularity. Across replicates we summarise the per-site retention rate and the mean ARI / modularity.

**Question this analysis answers:** when the R/B assignment is re-derived from object-downsampled data, how often does each site keep its group, and how stable is the community structure?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s9-retention
#| tbl-cap: "Per-site group-retention rate under object-level downsampling to k = 3, 5, 10 objects per site (500 replicates each). Retention is the fraction of replicates in which the site's realigned Louvain partition matches its manual restricted/broad assignment. Sites with fewer than k objects are excluded at that level."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

ds_R <- 500
ds_res <- list()
for (k in k_levels) for (ph in c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2")) {
  ds_res[[paste0(ph, "_", k)]] <-
    run_downsample_sensitivity(signbase_full_clean, ph, k, R = ds_R)
}

ret_all <- list()
for (k in k_levels) for (ph in c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2")) {
  rt <- ds_res[[paste0(ph, "_", k)]]$retention %>%
    mutate(phase = ph, k = k)
  ret_all[[paste0(ph, "_", k)]] <- rt
}
ret_all <- bind_rows(ret_all)
ret_wide <- ret_all %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(site_name, phase, manual_group, nobjects),
              names_from = k, values_from = retention_rate,
              names_prefix = "k=") %>%
  arrange(phase, manual_group, desc(nobjects))

ret_wide %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Site", "Phase", "Group", "Objects", "k=3", "k=5", "k=10"),
        digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s9-stability
#| tbl-cap: "Community-structure stability under object-level downsampling. For each phase and common count k: number of sites qualifying, mean Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between the downsampled Louvain partition and the manual groups, mean network modularity, and mean number of Louvain communities detected."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

ds_stab <- bind_rows(lapply(k_levels, function(k) lapply(c("Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"), function(ph) {
  d <- ds_res[[paste0(ph, "_", k)]]
  data.frame(phase = ph, k = k, n_sites = d$n_sites_qualified,
             mean_ARI = round(d$mean_ari, 3),
             mean_modularity = round(d$mean_modularity, 3),
             mean_n_communities = round(d$mean_n_communities, 3))
}))) %>% bind_rows()

ds_stab %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Phase", "k", "Sites", "Mean ARI",
                      "Mean modularity", "Mean # communities"),
        digits = 3)
```

```{r fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
#| label: fig-s9-retention
#| fig-cap: "Group-retention rate by site under object-level downsampling to k = 3, 5, 10 objects per site. Bars near 1 (red) indicate assignments that survive downsampling; bars near 0.5 (blue) indicate assignments that are essentially random with respect to the manual grouping and therefore unstable."
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(ret_all, aes(x = reorder(site_name, nobjects), y = retention_rate,
                    fill = factor(manual_group))) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ paste(phase, "k=", k, sep = "")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("1" = "#00BA38", "2" = "#F8766D"),
                    labels = c("restricted", "broad"), name = "Manual group") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Site (ordered by object count)", y = "Group-retention rate")
```

### Interpretation

**Question: does each site keep its group under object-level downsampling, and how stable is the community structure?** No. The assignment is stable only for the better-sampled sites. In Aur-P1 at k = 3, large broad-range sites such as Vogelherd (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$retention_rate[ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$site_name == "Vogelherd"], 2)`), Hohle Fels (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$retention_rate[ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$site_name == "Hohle Fels"], 2)`), and La Ferrassie (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$retention_rate[ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$site_name == "La Ferrassie"], 2)`) retain their group in the large majority of replicates, whereas small restricted-range sites collapse: Gatzarria (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$retention_rate[ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$site_name == "Gatzarria"], 2)`) and Grotte de la Verpillière I (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$retention_rate[ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$retention$site_name == "Grotte de la Verpillière I"], 2)`) keep their group little more often than chance. The mean ARI between the downsampled partition and the manual groups is low at every level (`r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$mean_ari, 2)` at k = 3, `r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_5"]]$mean_ari, 2)` at k = 5, `r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_10"]]$mean_ari, 2)` at k = 10 for Aur-P1), and modularity falls to near zero (e.g. `r round(ds_res[["Aur-P1_3"]]$mean_modularity, 2)` at k = 3), reflecting the fragmentation of the network when each site is represented by only a handful of objects.

The same pattern holds in Aur-P2, where even fewer sites qualify at higher k and retention is correspondingly noisier. **Answer:** the R/B assignment of small-object sites is not robust to object-level downsampling; only the best-sampled sites retain their grouping, and the community structure as a whole loses coherence under downsampling. This shows that the division is, at least in part, a sampling-intensity effect rather than a fully stable cultural partition.

## S9.3 Coverage-based rarefaction {#sec-s9-3}

### Rationale

Equal object counts do not equalise *sampling effort* when sites differ in how concentrated their signs are. Our method is **coverage-based rarefaction**: compare richness at equal *sample coverage* rather than equal object count [@Chao_Jost_2012; @Gotelli_Colwell_2001]. For each site we estimate its sign-type richness at a target coverage of `r cov_target` (a standard "high coverage" benchmark) with `iNEXT::estimateD` on the site's object-by-sign incidence matrix (`datatype = "incidence_raw"`), which returns 95% confidence intervals from `r cov_perm` bootstrap replicates [@Hsieh_Ma_Chao_2016]. Sites with fewer than three objects, failed fits, or targets reachable only by extrapolating beyond twice the observed sample cannot be placed on a common coverage footing; for these we report Chao and Jost's analytic incidence-coverage estimator with object-resampling bootstrap intervals and a Chao2 asymptotic-richness estimate as a fallback quantity, with the reason recorded per site. We then compare restricted and broad sites at that equal coverage.

**Question this analysis answers:** at equal sample coverage, do restricted and broad sites still differ in sign-type richness?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s9-rarefaction
#| tbl-cap: "Coverage-based rarefaction per site. richness_full is the observed number of sign types; coverage_chao is Chao and Jost's analytic sample-coverage estimate at the full sample with 95% bootstrap interval; richness_at_target is the iNEXT incidence_raw richness estimate at target coverage = 0.9 with 95% interval. Sites that never reach the target coverage are reported as NA with the reason in at_target_method, and carry a Chao2 asymptotic-richness estimate with interval as a fallback quantity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

cov_target <- 0.9
cov_perm  <- 200
cov_p1 <- coverage_rarefaction(signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P1", target_coverage = cov_target, n_perm = cov_perm)
cov_p2 <- coverage_rarefaction(signbase_full_clean, "Aur-P2", target_coverage = cov_target, n_perm = cov_perm)
cov_tab <- bind_rows(
  cov_p1$table %>% mutate(phase = "Aur-P1"),
  cov_p2$table %>% mutate(phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>% mutate(group = factor(manual_group, levels = c(1, 2),
                            labels = c("restricted", "broad")))

s9_cov_n_p1 <- sum(!is.na(cov_p1$table$richness_at_target))
s9_cov_n_p2 <- sum(!is.na(cov_p2$table$richness_at_target))
s9_cov_nbroad_p2 <- sum(!is.na(cov_p2$table$richness_at_target) & cov_p2$table$manual_group == 2)
s9_cov_nrest_p2  <- sum(!is.na(cov_p2$table$richness_at_target) & cov_p2$table$manual_group == 1)
s9_cov_mean_r_p1 <- round(cov_p1$mean_restricted, 2)
s9_cov_mean_b_p1 <- round(cov_p1$mean_broad, 2)
s9_cov_wilcox_p1 <- round(cov_p1$wilcox_p, 3)
s9_cov_wilcox_p2 <- ifelse(is.na(cov_p2$wilcox_p),
                           "not computable (too few sites per group)",
                           round(cov_p2$wilcox_p, 3))

cov_tab %>%
  dplyr::select(phase, site_name, group, nobjects, richness_full,
                coverage_chao, coverage_LCL, coverage_UCL,
                richness_at_target, rt_LCL, rt_UCL, chao2, at_target_method) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Group", "Objects",
                      "Richness (full)", "Coverage (Chao)", "Cov LCL", "Cov UCL",
                      "Richness at 0.9 cov.", "Rt LCL", "Rt UCL", "Chao2", "Target method"),
        digits = 2)
```

```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
#| label: fig-s9-rarefaction
#| fig-cap: "Sign-type richness estimated at target coverage = 0.9 with 95% confidence intervals, by manual group, for sites that reach that coverage. Restricted sites (green) that attain high coverage remain low-richness; broad sites (red) remain high-richness."
#| fig-height: 4

cov_plot <- cov_tab %>% filter(!is.na(richness_at_target))
ggplot(cov_plot, aes(x = group, y = richness_at_target, colour = group)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = rt_LCL, ymax = rt_UCL), width = 0.1) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("restricted" = "#00BA38", "broad" = "#F8766D")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Manual group", y = "Sign-type richness at coverage = 0.9") +
  guides(colour = "none")
```

### Interpretation

**Question: at equal sample coverage, do restricted and broad sites still differ in sign-type richness?** Only a subset of sites can be assessed. In Aur-P1, `r s9_cov_n_p1` of `r nrow(obj_counts %>% filter(phase=="Aur-P1"))` sites reach coverage 0.9; in Aur-P2 only `r s9_cov_n_p2` of `r nrow(obj_counts %>% filter(phase=="Aur-P2"))` do. Among the Aur-P1 sites that do reach the target, restricted sites remain low-richness (mean `r s9_cov_mean_r_p1` sign types) while broad sites remain high-richness (mean `r s9_cov_mean_b_p1`), a difference that persists at equal coverage (Wilcoxon p = `r s9_cov_wilcox_p1`). For Aur-P2 only `r s9_cov_n_p2` of `r nrow(obj_counts %>% filter(phase=="Aur-P2"))` sites reach the target (`r s9_cov_nbroad_p2` broad, `r s9_cov_nrest_p2` restricted), too few for a reliable group comparison (Wilcoxon p = `r s9_cov_wilcox_p2`).

**Answer:** at equal coverage the broad/restricted richness contrast is preserved *among the sites that can be evaluated* — it is not removed by standardising on completeness — but the majority of the smallest sites never attain the target coverage and therefore cannot be placed on a common coverage footing at all. Coverage-based rarefaction is consequently unreliable for the smallest assemblages: it can compare well-sampled sites, but it cannot rescue the assignment of sites with only one or two objects, for which the table reports Chao coverage and Chao2 fallback quantities instead. This is the same limitation encountered in S9.2, approached from the richness axis.

## S9.4 Negative-binomial regression with object-count covariate {#sec-s9-4}

### Rationale

The two resampling approaches above ask whether the *partition* and the *richness* survive downsampling. We also ask whether group predicts sign-type richness once sampling effort is held constant. Entering `log(object count)` as an **offset** (the exposure term) fixes the richness-effort exponent at 1, which assumes sign-type richness grows in proportion to the number of objects; richness instead saturates with effort [@Gotelli_Colwell_2001], so under an offset a site with 1 object and 1 sign type has a "rate" of 1.0 while Vogelherd (173 objects, 17 types) has a rate of 0.1, biasing the contrast against the large broad-group sites. We therefore fit two negative-binomial regressions [@Venables_Ripley_2002] of per-site sign-type richness with the manual group and phase as predictors: (i) the offset specification, and (ii) a free-slope specification with `log(object count)` as a covariate, which estimates the exponent with its interval:

$$\text{richness}_i \sim \text{NegativeBinomial}\big(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{group}_i + \beta_2 \text{phase}_i + \beta_3 \log(\text{objects}_i))\big).$$

**Question this analysis answers:** does the group effect on sign-type richness survive after accounting for sampling effort (object count)?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s9-mixed
#| tbl-cap: "Negative-binomial regressions of per-site sign-type richness: offset specification (richness-effort exponent fixed at 1) versus free-slope specification (exponent estimated).
```
